# DataFusion Advanced — 12) Object stores and remote data access

This section follows the dense, agent-facing technical-reference style of the Cyclopts source material. 

## 12.0 Version anchor

Current package anchor: **`datafusion==54.0.0`**, released **June 29, 2026**, requiring **Python >=3.10**. DataFusion Python is a Rust-backed Python binding over Apache Arrow DataFusion with SQL/DataFrame execution, optimized plans, PyArrow/Pandas-compatible exchange, and file/data-source support. ([PyPI][1])

```bash id="qclncj"
python -m pip install "datafusion==54.0.0"
```

```python id="zww7sx"
import datafusion
assert datafusion.__version__ == "54.0.0"
```

---

## 12.1 Object-store invariant

DataFusion remote IO is built around explicit `ObjectStore` registration inside a `SessionContext`.

```text id="ue6l43"
remote URI
  -> URI scheme / host
  -> registered ObjectStore
  -> file scan / listing table / Parquet reader
  -> DataFrame logical plan
  -> ExecutionPlan
  -> RecordBatch stream
```

The public Python docs list supported object stores as **AmazonS3**, **GoogleCloud**, **Http**, **LocalFileSystem**, and **MicrosoftAzure**. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

```python id="8qjk6a"
from datafusion import SessionContext
from datafusion.object_store import AmazonS3

ctx = SessionContext()

s3 = AmazonS3(
    bucket_name="my-bucket",
    region="us-east-1",
)

ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3, None)
ctx.register_parquet("events", "s3://my-bucket/events/")
```

---

## 12.2 Object-store module capability map

```python id="vi1ymw"
from datafusion.object_store import (
    AmazonS3,
    GoogleCloud,
    Http,
    LocalFileSystem,
    MicrosoftAzure,
)
```

| Store class       | URI family                                          | Typical target                       | Main use                            |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| `AmazonS3`        | `s3://bucket/path`                                  | AWS S3 / S3-compatible object stores | cloud Parquet/CSV/JSON scans        |
| `GoogleCloud`     | `gs://bucket/path`                                  | Google Cloud Storage                 | GCS data lakes                      |
| `MicrosoftAzure`  | `az://`, `abfs://`, deployment-specific Azure paths | Azure Blob / ADLS-style storage      | Azure data lakes                    |
| `Http`            | `http://...`, `https://...`                         | HTTP-accessible objects              | public/static remote files          |
| `LocalFileSystem` | `file://...` or local path integration              | local disks / mounted volumes        | explicit local object-store mapping |

The rendered `datafusion.object_store` API page exposes these store classes as module contents, while the data-source guide gives a concrete S3 registration example using `AmazonS3`, `ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3, None)`, and `ctx.register_parquet(...)`. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 12.3 Core registration API: `ctx.register_object_store(...)`

### Signature

```python id="uf30sa"
ctx.register_object_store(
    schema: str,
    store: Any,
    host: str | None = None,
) -> None
```

`register_object_store(schema, store, host=None)` adds a new object store into the session; `schema` is the data-source schema, `store` is the object store object, and `host` is the URL host. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

```python id="t9q7a7"
ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3_store, None)
ctx.register_object_store("gs://", gcs_store, None)
ctx.register_object_store("https://", http_store, "example.com")
```

### Deregistration

```python id="1h6tcy"
ctx.deregister_object_store(
    schema: str,
    host: str | None = None,
) -> None
```

`deregister_object_store(schema, host=None)` removes an object store from the session; the docs describe `schema` with examples such as `"s3://"` and `host` with examples such as a bucket name. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

```python id="osencq"
ctx.deregister_object_store("s3://", None)
ctx.deregister_object_store("s3://", "my-bucket")
```

---

## 12.4 Registration key model: `schema` + optional `host`

```text id="2drdzu"
registration lookup key:
  schema: URI scheme prefix, e.g. "s3://", "gs://", "https://"
  host: optional URI host, e.g. bucket name, account host, domain name

URI:
  s3://my-bucket/path/file.parquet
  ├─ schema = "s3://"
  ├─ host   = "my-bucket"
  └─ path   = "/path/file.parquet"
```

The official S3 example registers with `schema="s3://"` and `host=None`, then reads a path of the form `s3://{bucket_name}/...`. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

```python id="e0t0da"
path = "s3://yellow-trips/"
ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3, None)
ctx.register_parquet("trips", path)
```

**Agent rule:** use `schema` for protocol routing; use `host` only when deliberately scoping an object-store registration to one URI host/bucket/domain. If a store object is already bucket/container-specific, keep `path` and constructor bucket/container aligned.

---

## 12.5 Amazon S3

## 12.5.1 Basic S3 registration

```python id="u3v82c"
import os

from datafusion import SessionContext
from datafusion.object_store import AmazonS3

ctx = SessionContext()

bucket_name = "yellow-trips"
region = "us-east-1"

s3 = AmazonS3(
    bucket_name=bucket_name,
    region=region,
    access_key_id=os.getenv("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"),
    secret_access_key=os.getenv("AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"),
)

ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3, None)

ctx.register_parquet("trips", f"s3://{bucket_name}/")
df = ctx.table("trips")
```

This pattern is the official DataFusion Python object-store example: construct `AmazonS3` with `bucket_name`, `region`, `access_key_id`, and `secret_access_key`; register it under `"s3://"`; then register a Parquet path using `s3://{bucket_name}/`. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

---

## 12.5.2 Practical constructor surface

The rendered AutoAPI page lists `AmazonS3` but does not expand its constructor. The current public source exposes an `AmazonS3` constructor shape equivalent to:

```python id="rmp598"
AmazonS3(
    bucket_name: str,
    region: str | None = None,
    access_key_id: str | None = None,
    secret_access_key: str | None = None,
    session_token: str | None = None,
    endpoint: str | None = None,
    allow_http: bool = False,
    imdsv1_fallback: bool = False,
)
```

The current source uses `AmazonS3Builder::from_env()`, then applies explicit region, access key, secret key, session token, endpoint, IMDSv1 fallback, bucket name, and HTTP allowance when provided. Verify the constructor with `help(AmazonS3)` in the pinned wheel before locking production code. ([GitHub][7])

```python id="6kb9cx"
s3 = AmazonS3(
    bucket_name="my-bucket",
    region=os.environ["AWS_REGION"],
    access_key_id=os.environ.get("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"),
    secret_access_key=os.environ.get("AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"),
    session_token=os.environ.get("AWS_SESSION_TOKEN"),
)
```

S3-compatible endpoint / MinIO-style pattern:

```python id="6g3vwi"
s3 = AmazonS3(
    bucket_name="my-bucket",
    region="us-east-1",
    endpoint="http://localhost:9000",
    access_key_id=os.environ["MINIO_ACCESS_KEY"],
    secret_access_key=os.environ["MINIO_SECRET_KEY"],
    allow_http=True,
)

ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3, None)
ctx.register_parquet("events", "s3://my-bucket/events/")
```

---

## 12.5.3 S3 credential policy

```text id="s0fk95"
Preferred:
  IAM role / workload identity / environment-backed provider chain
  short-lived credentials
  session token for assumed roles
  deployment secret manager -> environment/runtime injection
  no source-code secrets
  no notebooks with raw keys
  no committed .env files

Acceptable in local dev:
  environment variables
  local credential profile if supported by runtime provider
  ephemeral test credentials
  MinIO test keys in local-only compose files

Avoid:
  hardcoded access_key_id / secret_access_key
  long-lived shared IAM user credentials
  logging constructor kwargs
  registering global context with tenant-specific credentials
```

DataFusion’s S3 example demonstrates loading AWS access key and secret key from environment variables rather than hardcoding literals. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

---

## 12.6 Google Cloud Storage

## 12.6.1 Practical constructor surface

The object-store module exposes `GoogleCloud`; current source shows a constructor shape equivalent to:

```python id="p5iu00"
GoogleCloud(
    bucket_name: str,
    service_account_path: str | None = None,
)
```

The current source builds a `GoogleCloudStorageBuilder` with a bucket name and optionally a service-account path. Verify the constructor in the installed wheel when version-pinning. ([GitHub][7])

```python id="tvpaka"
from datafusion.object_store import GoogleCloud

gcs = GoogleCloud(
    bucket_name="my-gcs-bucket",
    service_account_path=os.environ.get("GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS"),
)

ctx.register_object_store("gs://", gcs, None)
ctx.register_parquet("events", "gs://my-gcs-bucket/events/")
```

## 12.6.2 GCS credential policy

```text id="1dq0lp"
Preferred:
  GCP workload identity / service account binding
  service-account path injected through environment/config
  secret-manager controlled credential files
  no credential JSON committed to repo

Local dev:
  GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS path
  short-lived test service account

Avoid:
  embedding service-account JSON in code
  storing service-account file path in query builders
  sharing one global context across tenants/projects
```

## 12.7 Microsoft Azure

## 12.7.1 Practical constructor surface

The object-store module exposes `MicrosoftAzure`; current source shows a constructor shape equivalent to:

```python id="znd2j7"
MicrosoftAzure(
    container_name: str,
    account: str | None = None,
    access_key: str | None = None,
    bearer_token: str | None = None,
    client_id: str | None = None,
    client_secret: str | None = None,
    tenant_id: str | None = None,
    sas_query_pairs: list[tuple[str, str]] | None = None,
    use_emulator: bool | None = None,
    allow_http: bool | None = None,
    use_fabric_endpoint: bool | None = None,
)
```

The current source starts from environment-backed Azure builder state, then applies container name, account/access key, bearer token, client-secret triplet, SAS authorization pairs, emulator mode, HTTP allowance, and Fabric endpoint flag. The source enforces that `client_id`, `client_secret`, and `tenant_id` are either all set or all absent. Verify against the pinned installed wheel. ([GitHub][7])

```python id="d34xli"
from datafusion.object_store import MicrosoftAzure

az = MicrosoftAzure(
    container_name=os.environ["AZURE_STORAGE_CONTAINER"],
    account=os.environ.get("AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT"),
    access_key=os.environ.get("AZURE_STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY"),
)

ctx.register_object_store("az://", az, None)
ctx.register_parquet("events", "az://my-container/events/")
```

Service principal pattern:

```python id="1o1kgy"
az = MicrosoftAzure(
    container_name=os.environ["AZURE_STORAGE_CONTAINER"],
    account=os.environ["AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT"],
    client_id=os.environ["AZURE_CLIENT_ID"],
    client_secret=os.environ["AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET"],
    tenant_id=os.environ["AZURE_TENANT_ID"],
)
```

SAS pattern:

```python id="w69e8j"
az = MicrosoftAzure(
    container_name=os.environ["AZURE_STORAGE_CONTAINER"],
    account=os.environ["AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT"],
    sas_query_pairs=[
        ("sv", os.environ["AZURE_SAS_SV"]),
        ("sig", os.environ["AZURE_SAS_SIG"]),
        # plus remaining SAS pairs, preferably loaded from secret manager
    ],
)
```

## 12.7.2 Azure credential policy

```text id="2y1e66"
Preferred:
  managed identity / workload identity where available
  short-lived SAS for scoped read paths
  service principal credentials from secret manager
  no SAS token in source code
  no account key in source code

Local dev:
  emulator with allow_http/use_emulator only in dev
  explicit env-based account/container config

Avoid:
  mixing credential modes in one constructor
  logging SAS pairs
  checking SAS query strings into tests
  reusing one context across containers with different auth scopes
```

---

## 12.8 HTTP object store

## 12.8.1 Practical constructor surface

The object-store module exposes `Http`; current source shows:

```python id="t9bpdf"
Http(url: str)
```

The source parses the URL and configures an `HttpStore` from the URL origin when parsing succeeds. ([GitHub][7])

```python id="qt1jke"
from datafusion.object_store import Http

http = Http("https://example.com/data/")

ctx.register_object_store("https://", http, "example.com")
ctx.register_parquet("remote_events", "https://example.com/data/events.parquet")
```

## 12.8.2 HTTP deployment policy

```text id="jxqjm8"
Use HTTP store for:
  public static files
  signed URLs
  internal artifact server
  reproducible public datasets

Avoid HTTP store for:
  high-churn authenticated APIs
  endpoints requiring complex request signing per object
  row-level APIs
  paginated REST sources
  mutable HTTP resources without caching/versioning
```

**Agent rule:** treat HTTP as file/object retrieval, not a general REST connector.

---

## 12.9 Local filesystem object store

## 12.9.1 Practical constructor surface

The object-store module exposes `LocalFileSystem`; current source shows:

```python id="53hn9z"
LocalFileSystem(
    prefix: str | None = None,
)
```

If a prefix is supplied, the local filesystem store is created with that prefix; otherwise it uses the default local filesystem store. ([GitHub][7])

```python id="1pfisf"
from datafusion.object_store import LocalFileSystem

local = LocalFileSystem(prefix="/data/lake")

ctx.register_object_store("file://", local, None)
ctx.register_parquet("events", "file:///data/lake/events/")
```

## 12.9.2 Local-vs-cloud path policy

```text id="rtadh3"
Local:
  POSIX/Windows path semantics
  process filesystem permissions
  container mount visibility
  local disk failure/ephemerality
  fast metadata but non-portable paths

Cloud:
  URI semantics
  bucket/container/account scopes
  object-store consistency/latency/cost
  credential provider chain
  network errors/retries
  path prefixes are object keys, not directories
```

**Agent rule:** do not assume local path behavior applies to cloud object stores. Directory listing, rename, overwrite, latency, consistency, and permissions differ.

---

# 12.10 URI schemas and path resolution

## 12.10.1 URI decomposition

```text id="rqtiyc"
s3://my-bucket/events/part-0.parquet
├─ scheme/schema: s3://
├─ host:          my-bucket
└─ object path:   events/part-0.parquet

gs://my-bucket/events/part-0.parquet
├─ scheme/schema: gs://
├─ host:          my-bucket
└─ object path:   events/part-0.parquet

https://example.com/data/events.parquet
├─ scheme/schema: https://
├─ host:          example.com
└─ path:          /data/events.parquet

file:///data/events/part-0.parquet
├─ scheme/schema: file://
├─ host:          usually empty/localhost
└─ path:          /data/events/part-0.parquet
```

`register_object_store` takes the URI schema and optional host as lookup keys; `register_listing_table` can assemble multiple files from locations in an `ObjectStore` instance, making object-store registration relevant for remote multi-file tables. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

---

## 12.10.2 Object-store-backed file registration

```python id="m2bwej"
ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3, None)

ctx.register_parquet(
    name="events",
    path="s3://my-bucket/events/",
    table_partition_cols=[("dt", "utf8")],
    parquet_pruning=True,
)
```

```python id="1rtagd"
ctx.register_listing_table(
    name="events_listing",
    path="s3://my-bucket/events/",
    table_partition_cols=[("dt", "utf8")],
    file_extension=".parquet",
    schema=events_schema,
)
```

`register_listing_table(...)` registers multiple files as a single table and creates a table that can assemble files from locations in an `ObjectStore` instance. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

---

## 12.10.3 Path alignment rules

```text id="g7tpae"
S3:
  AmazonS3(bucket_name="b")
  path should normally begin s3://b/...

GCS:
  GoogleCloud(bucket_name="b")
  path should normally begin gs://b/...

Azure:
  MicrosoftAzure(container_name="c", account="a")
  path must match the URI scheme/account/container convention expected by registered store

HTTP:
  Http("https://example.com/base/")
  register host example.com when scoping
  path should use same origin

Local:
  LocalFileSystem(prefix="/data")
  file:// URI and prefix must point to visible mounted path
```

**Agent rule:** constructor bucket/container/account and URI host/path must agree. Mismatched bucket/container names produce “no suitable object store” or object-not-found style failures.

---

# 12.11 Credential management patterns

## 12.11.1 Secure context factory

```python id="6k0avi"
from __future__ import annotations

import os
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

from datafusion import SessionContext
from datafusion.object_store import AmazonS3, GoogleCloud, MicrosoftAzure


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class S3StoreConfig:
    bucket: str
    region: str
    endpoint: str | None = None
    allow_http: bool = False


def register_s3(ctx: SessionContext, cfg: S3StoreConfig) -> None:
    s3 = AmazonS3(
        bucket_name=cfg.bucket,
        region=cfg.region,
        access_key_id=os.environ.get("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"),
        secret_access_key=os.environ.get("AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"),
        session_token=os.environ.get("AWS_SESSION_TOKEN"),
        endpoint=cfg.endpoint,
        allow_http=cfg.allow_http,
    )

    ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3, None)
```

**Credential boundary:** the query builder never sees credentials.

```python id="qgvsxi"
def register_sources(ctx: SessionContext, bucket: str) -> None:
    ctx.register_parquet("events", f"s3://{bucket}/events/")
```

---

## 12.11.2 Bootstrap-vs-query separation

```python id="61indq"
def bootstrap_remote_context() -> SessionContext:
    ctx = SessionContext()
    register_s3(ctx, S3StoreConfig(bucket="prod-events", region="us-east-1"))
    ctx.register_parquet("events", "s3://prod-events/events/")
    return ctx


def build_report(ctx: SessionContext):
    return ctx.sql("""
        SELECT country, count(*) AS n
        FROM events
        GROUP BY country
    """)
```

**Agent rule:** object-store registration belongs to deployment/bootstrap; SQL/DataFrame builders should only reference logical table names.

---

## 12.11.3 Secrets policy matrix

| Secret type         | Recommended source                               | Avoid                                |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| AWS access key      | IAM role / secret manager / env injection        | hardcoded string                     |
| AWS session token   | STS/assume-role env injection                    | persisted local file in repo         |
| GCP service account | workload identity / secret-mounted file          | JSON literal in code                 |
| Azure SAS           | secret manager / short-lived runtime injection   | logged query string                  |
| Azure account key   | secret manager / managed identity where possible | notebook cell literal                |
| MinIO dev creds     | local `.env` excluded from VCS                   | production reuse                     |
| HTTP signed URL     | short-lived config injected at runtime           | source-controlled URL with signature |

---

# 12.12 Local vs cloud operational differences

```text id="rj9d9y"
Local filesystem:
  low latency
  POSIX-ish semantics
  mount visibility matters
  single-machine scope
  path permissions from OS/container
  renames often cheap/atomic

Cloud object stores:
  higher latency
  object key namespace, not true directories
  list operations may be expensive
  credentials required
  network and throttling errors possible
  rename often copy+delete semantics
  request/egress cost matters
  read-after-write/consistency behavior provider-specific
```

**Agent advisory:**

```text id="k7fa84"
Do not test only with local files and assume cloud behavior.
Add remote integration tests for:
  path prefix
  credentials
  listing
  partition discovery
  compressed files
  Parquet pruning
  large object reads
```

---

# 12.13 Object-store-backed Parquet pattern

```python id="73bp53"
from __future__ import annotations

import os
import pyarrow as pa

from datafusion import SessionContext
from datafusion.object_store import AmazonS3


EVENTS_SCHEMA = pa.schema([
    ("event_id", pa.string()),
    ("user_id", pa.int64()),
    ("country", pa.string()),
    ("amount", pa.float64()),
    ("event_ts", pa.timestamp("us")),
])


def make_s3_context(bucket: str, region: str) -> SessionContext:
    ctx = SessionContext()

    s3 = AmazonS3(
        bucket_name=bucket,
        region=region,
        access_key_id=os.environ.get("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"),
        secret_access_key=os.environ.get("AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"),
        session_token=os.environ.get("AWS_SESSION_TOKEN"),
    )

    ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3, None)

    ctx.register_parquet(
        name="events",
        path=f"s3://{bucket}/events/",
        table_partition_cols=[("dt", pa.string())],
        parquet_pruning=True,
        file_extension=".parquet",
        schema=EVENTS_SCHEMA,
    )

    return ctx
```

Value case:

```text id="k3qmpp"
remote Parquet scan
predicate row-group pruning
partition column filtering
SQL-visible logical table
credentials isolated in bootstrap
query code independent of storage backend
```

---

# 12.14 Multi-store / multi-environment configuration

```python id="eq6909"
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StorageSpec:
    kind: Literal["local", "s3", "gcs", "azure", "http"]
    table: str
    uri: str
    bucket_or_container: str | None = None
    region: str | None = None
    schema: str | None = None


def register_remote_table(ctx: SessionContext, spec: StorageSpec) -> None:
    # Object-store registration should happen in a separate bootstrap layer.
    ctx.register_parquet(
        name=spec.table,
        path=spec.uri,
        schema=spec.schema,
        parquet_pruning=True,
        file_extension=".parquet",
    )
```

Recommended split:

```text id="i0w3tj"
Storage bootstrap:
  credentials
  object-store constructor
  ctx.register_object_store(...)

Table bootstrap:
  logical table names
  remote URIs
  schema/partition/file extension
  ctx.register_parquet / register_listing_table

Query layer:
  ctx.table("events")
  ctx.sql("SELECT ... FROM events")
```

---

# 12.15 Host-scoped registration pattern

```python id="yuggfl"
# Generic scheme-level store.
ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3_for_bucket_a, None)

# Host-scoped store.
ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3_for_bucket_a, "bucket-a")
```

Use host-scoped registration when:

```text id="yyjwmc"
one context has multiple stores under same scheme
bucket/container/account-level credentials differ
same URI scheme maps to multiple trust zones
tenant-specific buckets are isolated inside one context
```

Prefer context-per-tenant when:

```text id="o3wvs4"
credentials must not coexist
temporary views are tenant-specific
query text is untrusted
schema/table namespace leakage must be impossible
```

`deregister_object_store(schema, host)` mirrors the same schema/host key shape and can remove a store by scheme and host. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

---

# 12.16 HTTP and signed URL pattern

```python id="y9509h"
from datafusion.object_store import Http

ctx = SessionContext()

http = Http("https://datasets.example.com/")
ctx.register_object_store("https://", http, "datasets.example.com")

ctx.register_parquet(
    "public_events",
    "https://datasets.example.com/events/part-0.parquet",
)
```

Signed URL caveats:

```text id="jgihe8"
Signed URLs:
  include credentials in URL query string
  can leak through logs/plans/errors
  expire while query is running
  are poor fit for multi-file listing unless every object path is signed/accessible
```

**Agent rule:** prefer authenticated object-store constructor credentials over signed URLs for multi-file datasets; use signed URLs for bounded, single-object reads only.

---

# 12.17 Object-store-backed listing table pattern

```python id="7dq9je"
ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3, None)

ctx.register_listing_table(
    name="events",
    path="s3://my-bucket/events/",
    table_partition_cols=[
        ("dt", "utf8"),
        ("region", "utf8"),
    ],
    file_extension=".parquet",
    schema=events_schema,
)
```

`register_listing_table(...)` registers multiple files as a single table and uses an object store to assemble files from locations; it accepts table partition columns, file extension, schema, and file sort order. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

Use when:

```text id="pfbdij"
remote prefix contains many files
file extension filtering matters
partition columns are directory-derived
object store listing is required
single logical table should span many objects
```

---

# 12.18 Security posture for LLM-generated systems

```text id="tqtzzo"
Hard rules:
  - no credentials in prompt-visible generated SQL
  - no credentials in DataFrame query builders
  - no credentials in code snippets committed to repo
  - no signed URLs in logs
  - no global SessionContext with user-specific object stores
  - no user-controlled object-store URI without allowlist

Safe boundaries:
  - bootstrap reads secrets from env/secret manager
  - register object stores once per context
  - register logical tables by controlled URI prefixes
  - query builders operate over table names only
  - untrusted SQL runs read-only and table-allowlisted
```

---

# 12.19 URI allowlist policy

```python id="z87l0y"
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AllowedPrefix:
    table: str
    uri_prefix: str


_ALLOWED_PREFIXES = {
    "events": AllowedPrefix("events", "s3://prod-events/events/"),
    "users": AllowedPrefix("users", "s3://prod-users/users/"),
}


def register_allowed_parquet(ctx: SessionContext, table: str, suffix: str = "") -> None:
    if table not in _ALLOWED_PREFIXES:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown table: {table}")

    prefix = _ALLOWED_PREFIXES[table].uri_prefix
    if ".." in suffix or suffix.startswith("/"):
        raise ValueError("Unsafe suffix")

    ctx.register_parquet(
        table,
        prefix + suffix,
        parquet_pruning=True,
        file_extension=".parquet",
    )
```

**Agent rule:** dynamic remote paths must be constrained by prefix allowlists. Never let an LLM or user provide an arbitrary cloud URI directly to `register_parquet`, `register_listing_table`, or `read_*`.

# 12.20 Testing patterns

## 12.20.1 Local object-store smoke test

```python id="17e97g"
from datafusion.object_store import LocalFileSystem

def test_local_object_store(tmp_path):
    ctx = SessionContext()
    local = LocalFileSystem(prefix=str(tmp_path))

    ctx.register_object_store("file://", local, None)

    path = tmp_path / "events.parquet"
    write_test_parquet(path)

    ctx.register_parquet("events", f"file://{path}")
    assert ctx.sql("SELECT count(*) AS n FROM events").to_pydict()["n"][0] > 0
```

## 12.20.2 S3 config unit test without exposing secrets

```python id="g7lqiz"
def test_s3_config_reads_env(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID", "test-key")
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY", "test-secret")
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_SESSION_TOKEN", "test-token")

    ctx = SessionContext()
    register_s3(ctx, S3StoreConfig(bucket="test-bucket", region="us-east-1"))

    # Validate registration path only; real S3 read belongs in integration tests.
```

## 12.20.3 Remote integration test marker

```python id="g6av0k"
import os
import pytest

@pytest.mark.integration
@pytest.mark.skipif(
    not os.environ.get("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"),
    reason="S3 credentials not configured",
)
def test_s3_parquet_read():
    ctx = make_s3_context(
        bucket=os.environ["TEST_S3_BUCKET"],
        region=os.environ["AWS_REGION"],
    )

    out = ctx.sql("SELECT count(*) AS n FROM events").to_pydict()
    assert out["n"][0] >= 0
```

# 12.21 Anti-pattern catalog

## Anti-pattern: credentials in query builders

```python id="c76v85"
def build_report():
    s3 = AmazonS3(
        bucket_name="prod",
        access_key_id="AKIA...",
        secret_access_key="secret",
    )
```

Correct:

```python id="ni1vq2"
def bootstrap_context():
    ctx = SessionContext()
    register_s3(ctx, S3StoreConfig(bucket="prod", region="us-east-1"))
    return ctx


def build_report(ctx):
    return ctx.sql("SELECT * FROM events")
```

---

## Anti-pattern: arbitrary user-controlled URI

```python id="9ak3fv"
ctx.register_parquet("user_table", user_supplied_uri)
```

Correct:

```python id="iqvhhr"
register_allowed_parquet(ctx, table="events", suffix=safe_suffix)
```

---

## Anti-pattern: global context with cloud credentials

```python id="xp4syf"
ctx = SessionContext.global_ctx()
ctx.register_object_store("s3://", tenant_store, None)
```

Correct:

```python id="20hwk8"
ctx = SessionContext()
ctx.register_object_store("s3://", tenant_store, None)
```

---

## Anti-pattern: local-only tests for cloud path logic

```text id="uhy7zw"
Problem:
  local path semantics do not validate object-store listing, credentials, host mapping, network errors, or URI scheme routing.
```

Correct:

```text id="zghl6t"
Use:
  unit tests for config construction
  local tests for schema/query logic
  integration tests for actual cloud URI + object-store registration
```

---

## Anti-pattern: signed URLs in logs

```python id="hpr4lc"
logger.info("reading %s", signed_url)
```

Correct:

```python id="l2beg2"
logger.info("reading remote object", extra={"scheme": "https", "host": "datasets.example.com"})
```

# 12.22 Deployment checklist

```text id="iysswl"
Object-store support:
  [ ] Import from datafusion.object_store.
  [ ] Register object store with ctx.register_object_store(schema, store, host=None).
  [ ] Register remote files/tables after object-store registration.
  [ ] Use register_listing_table for multi-file object-store tables.

Credentials:
  [ ] Load from environment / identity provider / secret manager.
  [ ] Keep secrets out of query builders.
  [ ] Keep secrets out of SQL strings.
  [ ] Keep secrets out of logs and plan snapshots.
  [ ] Use short-lived credentials where possible.
  [ ] Use context-per-tenant when credentials differ.

URI policy:
  [ ] Document supported URI schemes.
  [ ] Use prefix allowlists for dynamic paths.
  [ ] Align constructor bucket/container with URI host.
  [ ] Document local-vs-cloud behavior differences.
  [ ] Test path resolution in target deployment.

S3:
  [ ] bucket_name matches s3://bucket path.
  [ ] region configured.
  [ ] endpoint/allow_http only for S3-compatible/local dev.
  [ ] session_token supported for temporary credentials.

GCS:
  [ ] bucket_name matches gs://bucket path.
  [ ] service_account_path / workload identity handled outside query code.

Azure:
  [ ] container/account path convention documented.
  [ ] one credential mode selected.
  [ ] SAS/account keys never logged.

HTTP:
  [ ] host-scoped registration.
  [ ] avoid long-lived signed URLs in code/logs.
  [ ] use for file/object reads, not REST APIs.

Local:
  [ ] prefix maps to mounted path.
  [ ] container path visibility tested.
```

## 12.23 Section compression for LLM agents

```text id="knj557"
Object-store module:
  from datafusion.object_store import AmazonS3, GoogleCloud, Http, LocalFileSystem, MicrosoftAzure

Registration:
  ctx.register_object_store(schema: str, store: Any, host: str | None = None) -> None
  ctx.deregister_object_store(schema: str, host: str | None = None) -> None

Supported stores:
  AmazonS3
  GoogleCloud
  Http
  LocalFileSystem
  MicrosoftAzure

S3 pattern:
  s3 = AmazonS3(bucket_name=bucket, region=region,
                access_key_id=os.getenv("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"),
                secret_access_key=os.getenv("AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"),
                session_token=os.getenv("AWS_SESSION_TOKEN"),
                endpoint=None,
                allow_http=False)
  ctx.register_object_store("s3://", s3, None)
  ctx.register_parquet("events", f"s3://{bucket}/events/")

GCS pattern:
  gcs = GoogleCloud(bucket_name=bucket, service_account_path=os.getenv("GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS"))
  ctx.register_object_store("gs://", gcs, None)
  ctx.register_parquet("events", f"gs://{bucket}/events/")

Azure pattern:
  az = MicrosoftAzure(container_name=container, account=account, access_key=os.getenv("AZURE_STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY"))
  ctx.register_object_store("az://", az, None)

HTTP pattern:
  http = Http("https://example.com/base/")
  ctx.register_object_store("https://", http, "example.com")

Local pattern:
  local = LocalFileSystem(prefix="/data/lake")
  ctx.register_object_store("file://", local, None)

URI rule:
  URI scheme maps to schema.
  URI host maps to host/bucket/domain.
  URI path maps to object key/path.

Best practices:
  credentials outside code
  object-store registration in bootstrap
  query builders use registered table names
  dynamic URIs require allowlists
  context per tenant when credentials differ
  document local vs cloud path behavior
  use register_listing_table for multi-file remote prefixes
  test actual cloud object-store registration in integration tests
```

# DataFusion Advanced — 13) Joins and relational composition

This section follows the dense, agent-facing technical-reference style of the Cyclopts source material. 

## 13.0 Core join model

```text id="p6ys96"
DataFrame join API:
  df.join(...)
    column-name equi-join API

  df.join_on(...)
    expression-predicate join API
    supports equality and inequality predicates
    equality predicates are optimized

SQL join API:
  ctx.sql("SELECT ... FROM a JOIN b ON ...")
```

`DataFrame.join(...)` supports `inner`, `left`, `right`, `full`, `semi`, and `anti` joins; it requires either `on` or both `left_on` and `right_on`, and it exposes `coalesce_duplicate_keys=True` by default. `DataFrame.join_on(...)` accepts one or more `Expr` predicates, supports inequality predicates, and the docs state equality predicates are correctly optimized. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 13.1 API surface map

| API                                                  | Join condition form            |                      Best for | Supports inequality? | Duplicate key handling                            |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ----------------------------: | -------------------: | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `df.join(right, on="id")`                            | same column name(s)            |            ordinary equi-join |                   no | `coalesce_duplicate_keys`                         |
| `df.join(right, left_on="a", right_on="b")`          | different left/right key names |            ordinary equi-join |                   no | key columns remain distinct unless same-name `on` |
| `df.join_on(right, left.col("a") == right.col("b"))` | expression predicates          |           equi/non-equi joins |                  yes | manual projection/aliasing                        |
| SQL `JOIN ... ON ...`                                | SQL expression                 | analyst SQL / query migration |                  yes | SQL projection controls output                    |

---

# 13.2 `df.join(...)`: equi-join API

## 13.2.1 Signatures

```python id="ycjuji"
df.join(
    right: DataFrame,
    on: str | Sequence[str],
    how: Literal["inner", "left", "right", "full", "semi", "anti"] = "inner",
    *,
    left_on: None = None,
    right_on: None = None,
    join_keys: None = None,
    coalesce_duplicate_keys: bool = True,
) -> DataFrame
```

```python id="odmtf5"
df.join(
    right: DataFrame,
    on: None = None,
    how: Literal["inner", "left", "right", "full", "semi", "anti"] = "inner",
    *,
    left_on: str | Sequence[str],
    right_on: str | Sequence[str],
    join_keys: tuple[list[str], list[str]] | None = None,
    coalesce_duplicate_keys: bool = True,
) -> DataFrame
```

```python id="afpjs7"
df.join(
    right: DataFrame,
    on: None = None,
    how: Literal["inner", "left", "right", "full", "semi", "anti"] = "inner",
    *,
    join_keys: tuple[list[str], list[str]],
    left_on: None = None,
    right_on: None = None,
    coalesce_duplicate_keys: bool = True,
) -> DataFrame
```

The `join_keys` tuple form is documented as deprecated; generated code should prefer `on=...` or `left_on=...` / `right_on=...`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 13.2.2 Same-name key join: `on=...`

```python id="ch4471"
joined = left.join(
    right,
    on="id",
    how="inner",
)
```

Multi-column same-name key join:

```python id="zrvx13"
joined = left.join(
    right,
    on=["tenant_id", "user_id"],
    how="left",
)
```

SQL equivalent:

```sql id="0onerg"
SELECT *
FROM left_table l
JOIN right_table r
  ON l.id = r.id;
```

Agent rules:

```text id="zjnbjw"
Use on=... only when key names are identical on both sides.
Use list[str] for composite keys.
Document output schema when coalesce_duplicate_keys is True.
Set coalesce_duplicate_keys=False only when both key columns are required downstream.
```

---

## 13.2.3 Different-name key join: `left_on` / `right_on`

```python id="30l7yd"
joined = left.join(
    right,
    left_on="customer_id",
    right_on="id",
    how="inner",
)
```

Composite different-name key join:

```python id="tp6y1d"
joined = left.join(
    right,
    left_on=["tenant_id", "customer_id"],
    right_on=["tenant", "id"],
    how="left",
)
```

The join guide demonstrates `left.join(right, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", how="inner")`, and describes `left`, `full`, `semi`, and `anti` behavior with the same `left_on` / `right_on` form. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

Agent rules:

```text id="uwtojd"
Use left_on/right_on when key names differ.
Left and right key lists must be same length and semantically aligned by position.
Prefer explicit projection after join to avoid accidental duplicate columns.
```

---

# 13.3 Join type semantics

## 13.3.1 `inner`

```python id="bxxdzd"
left.join(right, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", how="inner")
```

```text id="1w3bv1"
inner:
  keep only rows with matching keys on both sides
  output includes joined columns from both inputs
  unmatched left rows dropped
  unmatched right rows dropped
```

The join guide states that inner join includes only rows containing common values between the join columns in both DataFrames. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 13.3.2 `left`

```python id="2z24sb"
left.join(right, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", how="left")
```

```text id="szfhzu"
left:
  preserve all left rows
  attach matching right rows
  unmatched right-side fields become NULL
```

The join guide describes left join as returning all rows from the left DataFrame and matching rows from the right; missing right matches become nulls. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 13.3.3 `right`

```python id="fwbgm7"
left.join(right, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", how="right")
```

```text id="od9ow2"
right:
  preserve all right rows
  attach matching left rows
  unmatched left-side fields become NULL
```

The SQL reference describes right outer join as including all right-side rows and producing null values for the left side when no match exists. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 13.3.4 `full`

```python id="lpn6j5"
left.join(right, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", how="full")
```

```text id="6qarsc"
full:
  preserve all rows from both sides
  matched rows combine
  unmatched left rows have NULL right fields
  unmatched right rows have NULL left fields
```

The Python join guide describes full join as returning all rows from both tables, with nulls for unmatched fields. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 13.3.5 `semi`

```python id="evklwx"
left.join(right, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", how="semi")
```

```text id="o6xlwq"
semi:
  keep left rows that have at least one match in right
  output only left columns
  does not project right columns
  useful for existence filtering
```

The Python guide states that left semi join retrieves matching rows from the left table while omitting duplicates with multiple matches in the right table; the SQL reference says left semi join returns rows from the left that have at least one right match and projects only left columns. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 13.3.6 `anti`

```python id="01psn0"
left.join(right, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", how="anti")
```

```text id="wdo1j7"
anti:
  keep left rows that have no match in right
  output only left columns
  useful for exclusion / orphan detection / incremental load gaps
```

The Python guide describes left anti join as showing all rows from the left table without any matching row in the right table, excluding left rows with at least one right match. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 13.3.7 Join type decision table

| Need                                                 | Use     |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| enrich matching rows only                            | `inner` |
| preserve fact table rows while adding dimension data | `left`  |
| preserve dimension/reference rows and attach facts   | `right` |
| reconcile both sides, show unmatched from both       | `full`  |
| filter left rows to those with a match               | `semi`  |
| filter left rows to those without a match            | `anti`  |

---

# 13.4 Duplicate key handling: `coalesce_duplicate_keys`

## 13.4.1 Default behavior

```python id="kqg7xc"
joined = left.join(right, on="id", how="inner")
```

Starting in DataFusion-Python 51.0.0, joins coalesce columns with identical names in the `on` fields by default; this reduces ambiguous column-selection problems after joins. The behavior can be disabled with `coalesce_duplicate_keys=False`. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

```text id="7el9tl"
left columns:   id, customer
right columns:  id, name

left.join(right, "id")
output:
  id, customer, name
```

---

## 13.4.2 Disable key coalescing

```python id="vdvp31"
joined = left.join(
    right,
    on="id",
    how="inner",
    coalesce_duplicate_keys=False,
)
```

```text id="c02qge"
left columns:   id, customer
right columns:  id, name

left.join(right, "id", coalesce_duplicate_keys=False)
output:
  id, customer, id, name
```

The join guide shows the default coalesced output containing one `id` column, and the disabled form containing both left and right `id` columns. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 13.4.3 Coalescing policy

```text id="h87s0b"
Use coalesce_duplicate_keys=True when:
  same-name keys are semantically identical
  one output key column is desired
  downstream code expects unambiguous key names

Use coalesce_duplicate_keys=False when:
  left/right key values must be audited independently
  full/right joins require provenance inspection
  data-quality checks compare key normalization behavior
  output schema must expose both physical key columns
```

Agent rule:

```text id="tnjhnr"
Always document join-key naming behavior.
For public output schemas, explicitly select/alias output columns after joins.
Do not rely on implicit duplicate-column names for stable APIs.
```

---

# 13.5 Expression joins: `join_on(...)`

## 13.5.1 Signature

```python id="t6waax"
df.join_on(
    right: DataFrame,
    *on_exprs: Expr,
    how: Literal["inner", "left", "right", "full", "semi", "anti"] = "inner",
) -> DataFrame
```

`join_on(...)` joins two DataFrames using one or more expression predicates. The docs state join predicates must be `Expr` objects, typically built with `datafusion.col()`, and that expression predicates support inequality predicates; equality predicates are correctly optimized. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 13.5.2 Simple expression equi-join

```python id="4z2ga0"
from datafusion import col

joined = left.join_on(
    right,
    col("a") == col("b"),
    how="inner",
)
```

The API docs show a unique-column example using `left.join_on(right, col("a") == col("b")).sort(col("x")).to_pydict()`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 13.5.3 Qualified expression equi-join

```python id="z4h13u"
joined = left.join_on(
    right,
    left.col("id") == right.col("id"),
    how="inner",
)
```

`DataFrame.col()` should be used on each DataFrame before joins to obtain fully qualified column references; these references can be used in the join predicate and later to disambiguate columns with the same names. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Projection after ambiguous join:

```python id="j4bmul"
out = joined.select(
    left.col("id"),
    left.col("val").alias("left_val"),
    right.col("val").alias("right_val"),
)
```

The API docs demonstrate this exact pattern: join on `left.col("id") == right.col("id")`, then select `left.col("id")`, `left.col("val")`, and `right.col("val").alias("rval")`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 13.5.4 Multi-predicate expression join

```python id="f4dd2c"
joined = left.join_on(
    right,
    left.col("tenant_id") == right.col("tenant_id"),
    left.col("user_id") == right.col("id"),
    how="inner",
)
```

Equivalent explicit conjunction:

```python id="zc7odb"
joined = left.join_on(
    right,
    (left.col("tenant_id") == right.col("tenant_id"))
    & (left.col("user_id") == right.col("id")),
    how="inner",
)
```

Agent rule:

```text id="gm4vso"
Prefer multiple join_on predicates for multiple simple equality conditions.
Use explicit & when the predicate shape mixes equality and inequality.
Always parenthesize boolean comparisons when using & or |.
```

---

## 13.5.5 Inequality join

```python id="q6k13e"
joined = intervals.join_on(
    events,
    events.col("event_ts") >= intervals.col("start_ts"),
    events.col("event_ts") < intervals.col("end_ts"),
    how="inner",
)
```

SQL equivalent:

```sql id="b25w5j"
SELECT *
FROM intervals i
JOIN events e
  ON e.event_ts >= i.start_ts
 AND e.event_ts <  i.end_ts;
```

`join_on(...)` is the API for expression predicates, including inequality predicates. Equality predicates are optimized, while general inequality predicates express non-equi join logic that may have different execution costs depending on optimizer/runtime support and data sizes. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text id="vif1d7"
Use join_on for:
  interval joins
  range joins
  non-equal time validity joins
  composite predicates
  qualified-column disambiguation

For performance:
  keep equality predicates explicit when present
  isolate range predicates from equality predicates when possible
  inspect optimized_logical_plan() and execution_plan()
```

---

# 13.6 `df.col(...)` and ambiguous schemas

## 13.6.1 Problem

```text id="swf4fr"
left schema:
  id, val

right schema:
  id, val

after join:
  id, val, id, val   or coalesced key + duplicate non-key val
```

Unqualified `col("val")` can become ambiguous after joins.

## 13.6.2 Correct pattern

```python id="eiuzzm"
joined = left.join_on(
    right,
    left.col("id") == right.col("id"),
    how="inner",
)

out = joined.select(
    left.col("id").alias("id"),
    left.col("val").alias("left_val"),
    right.col("val").alias("right_val"),
)
```

The docs explicitly recommend `DataFrame.col()` before the join to get fully qualified references for join predicates and disambiguating result columns. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 13.6.3 Strict projection helper

```python id="oysjh3"
def select_join_output(joined, left, right):
    return joined.select(
        left.col("id").alias("id"),
        left.col("val").alias("left_val"),
        right.col("val").alias("right_val"),
    )
```

Agent rule:

```text id="dlsvme"
For generated join code:
  never project duplicate-name columns unqualified
  always alias duplicate non-key columns
  prefer explicit output projection immediately after join
```

---

# 13.7 Join-key naming behavior

## 13.7.1 Same key name

```python id="u25sid"
joined = left.join(right, on="id", how="inner")
```

Default output:

```text id="3x3t99"
id, left_non_key..., right_non_key...
```

Because `coalesce_duplicate_keys=True` by default for identical names in `on` fields. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

## 13.7.2 Different key names

```python id="5h7h7r"
joined = left.join(
    right,
    left_on="customer_id",
    right_on="id",
    how="inner",
)
```

Expected schema policy:

```text id="pdakjv"
left key:  customer_id
right key: id
both key columns are semantically distinct names
explicit projection recommended
```

Example:

```python id="elsg70"
out = joined.select(
    left.col("customer_id").alias("customer_id"),
    right.col("id").alias("provider_id"),
    left.col("customer"),
    right.col("name").alias("provider_name"),
)
```

## 13.7.3 Documentation rule

```text id="iqgz07"
Every generated join specification should declare:
  left relation
  right relation
  join type
  left key expression(s)
  right key expression(s)
  duplicate-key coalescing policy
  output projection and aliases
```

---

# 13.8 Join optimizer considerations

## 13.8.1 Equality predicates

DataFusion’s Python API docs explicitly state that equality predicates in `join_on(...)` are correctly optimized. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Recommended shape:

```python id="acvbde"
joined = left.join_on(
    right,
    left.col("tenant_id") == right.col("tenant_id"),
    left.col("user_id") == right.col("user_id"),
    how="inner",
)
```

Avoid hiding equality inside opaque or unnecessary computed expressions:

```python id="0qoh34"
# Less optimizer-friendly shape.
joined = left.join_on(
    right,
    (left.col("user_id") + 0) == right.col("user_id"),
)
```

## 13.8.2 Equality + range predicates

```python id="4ob9tu"
joined = facts.join_on(
    dimension,
    facts.col("entity_id") == dimension.col("entity_id"),
    facts.col("ts") >= dimension.col("valid_from"),
    facts.col("ts") < dimension.col("valid_to"),
    how="inner",
)
```

Agent guidance:

```text id="qd0872"
Keep the equality predicate explicit.
Add range predicates separately.
Inspect optimized_logical_plan() for join/filter placement.
Benchmark range joins with production-scale cardinalities.
```

## 13.8.3 Plan inspection

```python id="i9lo8c"
print(joined.optimized_logical_plan().display())
print(joined.execution_plan().display_indent())
```

Use plan inspection to verify join type, filter placement, projection pruning, and physical execution shape before tuning.

---

# 13.9 Relational composition patterns

## 13.9.1 Dimension enrichment

```python id="7gz8ia"
enriched = facts.join(
    dim_users,
    left_on="user_id",
    right_on="id",
    how="left",
)

out = enriched.select(
    facts.col("event_id"),
    facts.col("user_id"),
    dim_users.col("country").alias("user_country"),
    facts.col("amount"),
)
```

Value case:

```text id="1j45g4"
preserve all facts
attach nullable dimension attributes
left join is standard dimension enrichment
```

---

## 13.9.2 Existence filter

```python id="uf1uzy"
active_user_events = events.join(
    active_users,
    left_on="user_id",
    right_on="id",
    how="semi",
)
```

Value case:

```text id="x6d0xe"
keep events whose user exists in active_users
avoid projecting right columns
avoid duplicate multiplication from multiple right matches
```

Semi join returns only matching rows from the left side and projects only left columns. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 13.9.3 Anti-join orphan detection

```python id="oslikj"
orphan_events = events.join(
    users,
    left_on="user_id",
    right_on="id",
    how="anti",
)
```

Value case:

```text id="yzkegv"
find fact rows with no dimension match
find records not yet processed
find deletes/missing references
incremental ingestion gap detection
```

Anti join keeps left rows without a right-side match and projects only left columns. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 13.9.4 Full reconciliation

```python id="zpjiq8"
recon = left_source.join(
    right_source,
    on="business_key",
    how="full",
    coalesce_duplicate_keys=True,
)
```

Value case:

```text id="8v21kn"
show matched and unmatched keys from both systems
audit source differences
prepare mismatch reports
```

For reconciliation, consider `coalesce_duplicate_keys=False` if key provenance must be audited.

---

## 13.9.5 Slowly changing dimension / validity interval join

```python id="75h7hy"
joined = facts.join_on(
    dim_scd,
    facts.col("entity_id") == dim_scd.col("entity_id"),
    facts.col("event_ts") >= dim_scd.col("valid_from"),
    facts.col("event_ts") < dim_scd.col("valid_to"),
    how="left",
)
```

Value case:

```text id="thdorg"
attach dimension attributes valid at event time
requires expression join
keep equality predicate explicit for optimizer
range predicates implement temporal validity
```

# 13.10 SQL equivalents

## Equi-join with same key

```python id="n69nz8"
df_api = left.join(right, on="id", how="inner")
```

```sql id="7dbyr9"
SELECT *
FROM left_table l
JOIN right_table r
  ON l.id = r.id;
```

## Left join with different keys

```python id="v6zyhd"
df_api = left.join(right, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", how="left")
```

```sql id="51uosd"
SELECT *
FROM left_table l
LEFT JOIN right_table r
  ON l.customer_id = r.id;
```

## Semi join

```python id="sqbayf"
df_api = left.join(right, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", how="semi")
```

```sql id="xuqkgm"
SELECT l.*
FROM left_table l
LEFT SEMI JOIN right_table r
  ON l.customer_id = r.id;
```

The SQL reference defines left semi join as returning rows from the left table with at least one right match and projecting only left columns. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

## Anti join

```python id="qjpgfu"
df_api = left.join(right, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", how="anti")
```

```sql id="rfd9cl"
SELECT l.*
FROM left_table l
LEFT ANTI JOIN right_table r
  ON l.customer_id = r.id;
```

The SQL reference defines left anti join as returning rows from the left table with no right-side match and projecting only left columns. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

## Range join

```python id="00x97p"
df_api = facts.join_on(
    intervals,
    facts.col("ts") >= intervals.col("start_ts"),
    facts.col("ts") < intervals.col("end_ts"),
)
```

```sql id="frjloj"
SELECT *
FROM facts f
JOIN intervals i
  ON f.ts >= i.start_ts
 AND f.ts < i.end_ts;
```

# 13.11 Generated join specification

```python id="o2z4ex"
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

JoinType = Literal["inner", "left", "right", "full", "semi", "anti"]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EquiJoinSpec:
    how: JoinType
    left_keys: tuple[str, ...]
    right_keys: tuple[str, ...]
    coalesce_duplicate_keys: bool = True


def equi_join(left, right, spec: EquiJoinSpec):
    if len(spec.left_keys) != len(spec.right_keys):
        raise ValueError("left_keys and right_keys must have identical length")

    if spec.left_keys == spec.right_keys:
        return left.join(
            right,
            on=list(spec.left_keys),
            how=spec.how,
            coalesce_duplicate_keys=spec.coalesce_duplicate_keys,
        )

    return left.join(
        right,
        left_on=list(spec.left_keys),
        right_on=list(spec.right_keys),
        how=spec.how,
        coalesce_duplicate_keys=spec.coalesce_duplicate_keys,
    )
```

Agent constraints:

```text id="rbofgq"
Validate key-list length.
Validate key existence with schema() before join.
Select/alias after join.
Never emit deprecated join_keys for new code.
```

---

# 13.12 Expression join builder

```python id="jbey8j"
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

from datafusion import lit


RangeOp = Literal["lt", "lte", "gt", "gte"]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RangeJoinSpec:
    left_eq: str
    right_eq: str
    probe_col: str
    right_start: str
    right_end: str
    how: JoinType = "inner"


def interval_join(left, right, spec: RangeJoinSpec):
    return left.join_on(
        right,
        left.col(spec.left_eq) == right.col(spec.right_eq),
        left.col(spec.probe_col) >= right.col(spec.right_start),
        left.col(spec.probe_col) < right.col(spec.right_end),
        how=spec.how,
    )
```

Projection with aliases:

```python id="vw7axe"
joined = interval_join(facts, dim, spec)

out = joined.select(
    facts.col("event_id"),
    facts.col("entity_id"),
    facts.col("event_ts"),
    dim.col("attribute").alias("entity_attribute_at_event_time"),
)
```

# 13.13 Schema guards for joins

```python id="as7d43"
def require_columns(df, columns: set[str], side: str):
    names = set(df.schema().names)
    missing = columns - names
    if missing:
        raise KeyError(f"{side} DataFrame missing columns: {sorted(missing)}")


def validate_equi_join(left, right, spec: EquiJoinSpec):
    require_columns(left, set(spec.left_keys), "left")
    require_columns(right, set(spec.right_keys), "right")
```

Use before agent-generated joins:

```python id="cqhcxm"
validate_equi_join(left, right, spec)
joined = equi_join(left, right, spec)
```

---

# 13.14 Output schema discipline

## 13.14.1 Public-output join should project immediately

```python id="05y5hf"
joined = orders.join(
    users,
    left_on="user_id",
    right_on="id",
    how="left",
)

public = joined.select(
    orders.col("order_id"),
    orders.col("user_id"),
    users.col("country").alias("user_country"),
    orders.col("amount"),
)
```

## 13.14.2 Avoid `SELECT *` style join outputs

```python id="jd18b4"
# Risky: output schema depends on duplicate names, coalescing, and source schemas.
joined = orders.join(users, left_on="user_id", right_on="id", how="left")
```

Correct:

```python id="p9ejj3"
joined.select(
    orders.col("order_id"),
    orders.col("user_id"),
    users.col("country").alias("user_country"),
)
```

Agent rule:

```text id="mkncg1"
Join output schemas are API contracts.
Always explicitly project public outputs.
Alias duplicate non-key columns.
Document key coalescing behavior.
```

---

# 13.15 Performance and deployment advisory

```text id="ti7zb2"
Join cost controls:
  - project required columns before join
  - filter inputs before join when semantically safe
  - use semi/anti for existence filtering instead of inner join + projection
  - keep equi-join predicates explicit
  - use join(...) for ordinary equi-joins
  - use join_on(...) for non-equi/range predicates
  - inspect optimized plans for complex joins
  - benchmark range joins at production cardinality
```

Example:

```python id="uqrsfc"
events_small = (
    events.select("event_id", "user_id", "amount", "event_ts")
          .filter("amount > 0")
)

users_small = users.select("id", "country")

joined = events_small.join(
    users_small,
    left_on="user_id",
    right_on="id",
    how="left",
)
```

---

# 13.16 Anti-pattern catalog

## Anti-pattern: unqualified duplicate column after join

```python id="1jxhcl"
joined = left.join_on(right, left.col("id") == right.col("id"))
out = joined.select(col("val"))
```

Correct:

```python id="ywim76"
out = joined.select(
    left.col("val").alias("left_val"),
    right.col("val").alias("right_val"),
)
```

---

## Anti-pattern: using `inner` join for existence filtering

```python id="rhcclb"
matched = left.join(right, left_on="id", right_on="id", how="inner").select(left.col("id"))
```

Correct:

```python id="vsdpyj"
matched = left.join(right, left_on="id", right_on="id", how="semi")
```

Semi joins avoid projecting right columns and represent existence filtering directly. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## Anti-pattern: using `left` join + null filter for anti-join

```python id="yr4a6d"
tmp = left.join(right, left_on="id", right_on="id", how="left")
anti = tmp.filter(right.col("id").is_null())
```

Correct:

```python id="t776h4"
anti = left.join(right, left_on="id", right_on="id", how="anti")
```

Anti join directly represents “left rows with no right match.” ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## Anti-pattern: undocumented duplicate-key policy

```python id="2u9ppj"
joined = left.join(right, on="id")
```

Correct:

```python id="fu9gq1"
joined = left.join(
    right,
    on="id",
    how="inner",
    coalesce_duplicate_keys=True,
)
```

Then project:

```python id="ki1f4x"
out = joined.select(
    left.col("id"),
    left.col("customer"),
    right.col("name").alias("provider_name"),
)
```

---

## Anti-pattern: deprecated `join_keys`

```python id="rvz6yl"
joined = left.join(right, join_keys=(["a"], ["b"]))
```

Correct:

```python id="x8apks"
joined = left.join(right, left_on="a", right_on="b")
```

`join_keys` is documented as deprecated. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## Anti-pattern: range join with hidden equality expression

```python id="5srubd"
joined = facts.join_on(
    dim,
    (facts.col("entity_id") + lit(0)) == dim.col("entity_id"),
    facts.col("ts") >= dim.col("valid_from"),
)
```

Correct:

```python id="os9yoa"
joined = facts.join_on(
    dim,
    facts.col("entity_id") == dim.col("entity_id"),
    facts.col("ts") >= dim.col("valid_from"),
)
```

Equality predicates in `join_on(...)` are documented as correctly optimized; preserve a clean equality shape where possible. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

# 13.17 Test patterns

## Inner join test

```python id="mh4y7d"
def test_inner_join(ctx):
    left = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2, 3], "x": ["a", "b", "c"]})
    right = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2, 4], "y": ["A", "B", "D"]})

    out = (
        left.join(right, on="id", how="inner")
            .sort("id")
            .to_pydict()
    )

    assert out == {"id": [1, 2], "x": ["a", "b"], "y": ["A", "B"]}
```

## Left join null behavior test

```python id="ea2dw9"
def test_left_join(ctx):
    left = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2, 3]})
    right = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2], "y": ["A", "B"]})

    out = (
        left.join(right, on="id", how="left")
            .sort("id")
            .to_pydict()
    )

    assert out["id"] == [1, 2, 3]
    assert out["y"] == ["A", "B", None]
```

## Semi join test

```python id="rc790j"
def test_semi_join(ctx):
    left = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2, 3], "x": ["a", "b", "c"]})
    right = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 3]})

    out = (
        left.join(right, on="id", how="semi")
            .sort("id")
            .to_pydict()
    )

    assert out == {"id": [1, 3], "x": ["a", "c"]}
```

## Anti join test

```python id="t8d1fg"
def test_anti_join(ctx):
    left = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2, 3], "x": ["a", "b", "c"]})
    right = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 3]})

    out = (
        left.join(right, on="id", how="anti")
            .sort("id")
            .to_pydict()
    )

    assert out == {"id": [2], "x": ["b"]}
```

## Duplicate-key coalescing test

```python id="0ckg3g"
def test_duplicate_key_coalescing(ctx):
    left = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2], "x": ["a", "b"]})
    right = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2], "y": ["A", "B"]})

    out = left.join(right, on="id").schema().names

    assert out == ["id", "x", "y"]
```

## `join_on` qualified disambiguation test

```python id="yfvlsu"
def test_join_on_qualified_cols(ctx):
    left = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2], "val": [10, 20]})
    right = ctx.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2], "val": [30, 40]})

    joined = left.join_on(right, left.col("id") == right.col("id"))

    out = (
        joined.select(
            left.col("id"),
            left.col("val").alias("left_val"),
            right.col("val").alias("right_val"),
        )
        .sort(left.col("id"))
        .to_pydict()
    )

    assert out == {
        "id": [1, 2],
        "left_val": [10, 20],
        "right_val": [30, 40],
    }
```

# 13.18 Deployment checklist

```text id="7d2pwf"
Join design:
  [ ] Choose join type intentionally: inner/left/right/full/semi/anti.
  [ ] Use semi for existence filtering.
  [ ] Use anti for missing-reference detection.
  [ ] Use full for reconciliation.

Keys:
  [ ] Use on=... only for same-name keys.
  [ ] Use left_on/right_on for different-name keys.
  [ ] Avoid deprecated join_keys.
  [ ] Validate key existence with schema().
  [ ] Validate composite key lengths.

Expression joins:
  [ ] Use join_on for inequality/range joins.
  [ ] Use left.col/right.col for qualified references.
  [ ] Keep equality predicates explicit.
  [ ] Inspect optimized plan for complex joins.

Output schema:
  [ ] Decide coalesce_duplicate_keys explicitly.
  [ ] Project immediately after joins.
  [ ] Alias duplicate non-key columns.
  [ ] Document key naming behavior.
  [ ] Test schema names.

Performance:
  [ ] Filter before join when semantics allow.
  [ ] Project needed columns before join.
  [ ] Prefer equi-join shape where possible.
  [ ] Benchmark non-equi joins with realistic cardinalities.
  [ ] Use explain/optimized plan for tuning.
```

---

## 13.19 Section compression for LLM agents

```text id="pce6zw"
Equi-join:
  df.join(right, on="id", how="inner", coalesce_duplicate_keys=True)
  df.join(right, on=["tenant_id", "id"], how="left")
  df.join(right, left_on="customer_id", right_on="id", how="inner")

Supported how:
  inner
  left
  right
  full
  semi
  anti

Deprecated:
  join_keys=(left_keys, right_keys)

Expression join:
  df.join_on(right, left.col("id") == right.col("id"), how="inner")
  df.join_on(right,
             left.col("entity_id") == right.col("entity_id"),
             left.col("ts") >= right.col("valid_from"),
             left.col("ts") < right.col("valid_to"),
             how="left")

Qualified columns:
  left.col("x")
  right.col("x")
  required for duplicate names and join_on disambiguation

Duplicate key handling:
  coalesce_duplicate_keys=True default for same-name on keys
  coalesce_duplicate_keys=False keeps both key columns
  always project/alias public outputs

Join type meaning:
  inner -> matched rows only
  left  -> all left rows + nullable right fields
  right -> all right rows + nullable left fields
  full  -> all rows from both sides
  semi  -> left rows with match; left columns only
  anti  -> left rows without match; left columns only

Optimizer:
  join_on supports inequality predicates
  equality predicates are correctly optimized
  keep equality predicates explicit
  inspect optimized_logical_plan() / execution_plan() for complex joins

Best practices:
  validate schemas
  filter/project before join
  use semi/anti directly
  avoid deprecated join_keys
  use df.col for ambiguous columns
  document output key behavior
  benchmark range joins
```

[1]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/autoapi/datafusion/dataframe/index.html "datafusion.dataframe — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"
[2]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/user-guide/common-operations/joins.html "Joins — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"
[3]: https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/sql/select.html "SELECT syntax — Apache DataFusion  documentation"

# DataFusion Advanced — 14) Aggregation, grouping sets, rollups, and cubes

This section follows the dense, agent-facing technical-reference style of the Cyclopts source material. 

## 14.0 Version anchor

Current package anchor: **`datafusion==54.0.0`**, requiring **Python >=3.10**. PyPI describes DataFusion Python as bindings to Apache Arrow DataFusion, supporting SQL/DataFrame queries, optimizer-backed execution, Python UDFs, PyArrow/Pandas-compatible exchange, and Substrait plan serialization. ([PyPI][1])

```bash id="yiqxjh"
python -m pip install "datafusion==54.0.0"
```

```python id="zrwqdv"
import datafusion
assert datafusion.__version__ == "54.0.0"
```

---

## 14.1 Core aggregation invariant

`DataFrame.aggregate(group_by, aggs)` returns a **lazy `DataFrame`** representing aggregate computation. It does not execute until a terminal operation. `group_by` is a sequence of expressions or column names; it may include a `GroupingSet` expression for rollups, cubes, or explicit grouping sets. `aggs` is a sequence of aggregate expressions. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

```python id="w7gzml"
from datafusion import SessionContext, col, lit, functions as f
from datafusion.expr import GroupingSet

ctx = SessionContext()

df = ctx.from_pydict({
    "region": ["US", "US", "CA"],
    "city": ["NYC", "SF", "TOR"],
    "sales": [100.0, 200.0, 150.0],
})

agg_df = df.aggregate(
    [col("region")],
    [
        f.count_star().alias("n_rows"),
        f.sum(col("sales")).alias("sales_total"),
        f.avg(col("sales")).alias("sales_avg"),
    ],
)

# terminal boundary
agg_df.show()
```

Default aggregation produces one output row per unique grouping-key combination. If `group_by=[]` (or, since 54, `group_by=None`), aggregation is over the entire DataFrame. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

```python id="i54cv8"
overall = df.aggregate(
    [],
    [
        f.count_star().alias("n_rows"),
        f.sum(col("sales")).alias("sales_total"),
    ],
)
```

---

## 14.2 Signature and type model

```python id="liruis"
df.aggregate(
    group_by: Sequence[Expr | str] | Expr | str | None,
    aggs: Sequence[Expr] | Expr,
) -> DataFrame
```

Since 54 the signature is deliberately permissive: `group_by` also accepts a single bare `Expr`, a single column-name string, or `None` (whole-table aggregation — see 14.22); `aggs` accepts a single `Expr` without list wrapping.

Accepted `group_by` items:

```text id="q4vbcg"
Expr
str column name
GroupingSet.rollup(...)
GroupingSet.cube(...)
GroupingSet.grouping_sets(...)
```

Accepted `aggs` items:

```text id="lak2dc"
aggregate Expr:
  f.count(...)
  f.count_star()
  f.sum(...)
  f.avg(...)
  f.min(...)
  f.max(...)
  f.array_agg(...)
  f.first_value(...)
  f.last_value(...)
  f.approx_distinct(...)
  f.approx_median(...)
  f.approx_percentile_cont(...)
  f.stddev(...)
  f.var(...)
  f.corr(...)
  f.regr_slope(...)
  ...
```

Agent rule:

```text id="gwyq7g"
All aggregate outputs should be aliased.
Unaliased aggregate expression names are unstable output-schema contracts.
```

```python id="ex86y7"
df.aggregate(
    [col("region")],
    [f.sum(col("sales")).alias("sales_total")],
)
```

# 14.3 Basic aggregation syntax

## 14.3.1 Single grouping key

```python id="bodv6s"
by_region = df.aggregate(
    [col("region")],
    [
        f.count_star().alias("n_rows"),
        f.sum(col("sales")).alias("sales_total"),
        f.avg(col("sales")).alias("sales_avg"),
        f.min(col("sales")).alias("sales_min"),
        f.max(col("sales")).alias("sales_max"),
    ],
)
```

SQL equivalent:

```sql id="aq6d83"
SELECT
  region,
  count(*) AS n_rows,
  sum(sales) AS sales_total,
  avg(sales) AS sales_avg,
  min(sales) AS sales_min,
  max(sales) AS sales_max
FROM t
GROUP BY region;
```

The DataFusion aggregation guide demonstrates `df.aggregate([group_col], [f.max(...), f.avg(...), f.min(...)])` and notes that more than one column can be used for grouping. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 14.3.2 Composite grouping keys

```python id="zg1nn4"
by_region_city = df.aggregate(
    [col("region"), col("city")],
    [
        f.count_star().alias("n_rows"),
        f.sum(col("sales")).alias("sales_total"),
    ],
)
```

SQL equivalent:

```sql id="n8fcms"
SELECT region, city, count(*) AS n_rows, sum(sales) AS sales_total
FROM t
GROUP BY region, city;
```

Agent rule:

```text id="s6uqys"
Composite group key order becomes output column order.
Use stable explicit column ordering in public APIs and tests.
```

---

## 14.3.3 Global aggregation

```python id="vqrljd"
overall = df.aggregate(
    [],
    [
        f.count_star().alias("n_rows"),
        f.sum(col("sales")).alias("sales_total"),
        f.avg(col("sales")).alias("sales_avg"),
    ],
)
```

SQL equivalent:

```sql id="mwc3k8"
SELECT count(*) AS n_rows, sum(sales) AS sales_total, avg(sales) AS sales_avg
FROM t;
```

# 14.4 Aggregate function catalog

## 14.4.1 Core aggregate functions

```text id="l4ro8c"
count
count_star
sum
avg / mean
min
max
median
first_value
last_value
nth_value
array_agg
string_agg
bool_and
bool_or
bit_and
bit_or
bit_xor
```

```python id="cz91ou"
summary = df.aggregate(
    [col("region")],
    [
        f.count_star().alias("n_rows"),
        f.count(col("sales")).alias("n_sales_non_null"),
        f.sum(col("sales")).alias("sales_sum"),
        f.avg(col("sales")).alias("sales_avg"),
        f.median(col("sales")).alias("sales_median"),
        f.min(col("sales")).alias("sales_min"),
        f.max(col("sales")).alias("sales_max"),
    ],
)
```

`avg(expression, distinct=False, filter=None)` expects a numeric expression, returns a float, and accepts an optional aggregate-level filter; since 54, `sum` and `avg` also accept `distinct=True` as first-class keyword parameters (see 14.22). ([Apache DataFusion][4])

stats = df.aggregate(
    [col("region")],
    [
        f.stddev_samp(col("sales")).alias("sales_stddev_samp"),
        f.var_samp(col("sales")).alias("sales_var_samp"),
        f.corr(col("sales"), col("margin")).alias("corr_sales_margin"),

Regression aggregate functions evaluate non-null input pairs and accept `filter=`; the API documents functions such as `regr_slope`, `regr_sxx`, and related regression aggregates. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

# 14.5 Approximate aggregate functions

## 14.5.1 `approx_distinct`

```python id="z6ypsk"
f.approx_distinct(
    expression: Expr,
    filter: Expr | None = None,
) -> Expr
```

`approx_distinct` returns an approximate number of distinct values and may be significantly faster than exact distinct-count patterns on some DataFrames; it also supports aggregate-level `filter=`. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

```python id="9v7tal"
by_region = df.aggregate(
    [col("region")],
    [
        f.approx_distinct(col("user_id")).alias("approx_users"),
    ],
)
```

SQL equivalent:

```sql id="edhafh"
SELECT region, approx_distinct(user_id) AS approx_users
FROM t
GROUP BY region;
```

---

## 14.5.2 `approx_median`

```python id="uxrqay"
f.approx_median(
    expression: Expr,
    filter: Expr | None = None,
) -> Expr
```

`approx_median` approximates the median and is documented as similar to `median()` but potentially faster for some DataFrames. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

```python id="qdnlzr"
latency = df.aggregate(
    [col("service")],
    [
        f.approx_median(col("latency_ms")).alias("approx_median_latency_ms"),
    ],
)
```

---

## 14.5.3 `approx_percentile_cont`

```python id="uud956"
f.approx_percentile_cont(
    sort_expression: Expr | SortExpr,
    percentile: float,
    num_centroids: int | None = None,
    filter: Expr | None = None,
) -> Expr
```

`approx_percentile_cont` returns an approximate continuous percentile, requires `percentile` between `0.0` and `1.0`, uses the t-digest algorithm, and exposes `num_centroids` to limit t-digest bin count. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

```python id="eybt0o"
pcts = df.aggregate(
    [col("service")],
    [
        f.approx_percentile_cont(col("latency_ms"), 0.50).alias("p50_latency_ms"),
        f.approx_percentile_cont(col("latency_ms"), 0.95).alias("p95_latency_ms"),
        f.approx_percentile_cont(
            col("latency_ms"),
            0.99,
            num_centroids=200,
        ).alias("p99_latency_ms"),
    ],
)
```

Weighted variant:

```python id="xae893"
weighted = df.aggregate(
    [col("service")],
    [
        f.approx_percentile_cont_with_weight(
            col("latency_ms"),
            col("request_weight"),
            0.95,
            num_centroids=200,
        ).alias("weighted_p95_latency_ms"),
    ],
)
```

The weighted variant accepts `sort_expression`, `weight`, `percentile`, optional `num_centroids`, and optional `filter`. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

---

## 14.5.4 Approximate aggregate policy

```text id="vbi0pe"
Use approximate aggregates for:
  high-cardinality exploratory analytics
  latency dashboards
  observability rollups
  approximate user counts
  approximate percentile summaries
  large-scale monitoring

Avoid approximate aggregates for:
  billing
  compliance
  reconciliation
  audit reports
  contractual metrics
  exact percentile requirements
```

Agent output naming rule:

```text id="54awur"
Name approximate outputs explicitly:
  approx_users
  approx_median_latency_ms
  approx_p95_latency_ms
  not users / median / p95 unless approximation is documented elsewhere
```
