# 15.9 Generated window spec builders

## 15.9.1 Common sort-key builder

```python id="g0m0ap"
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

from datafusion import col


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SortSpec:
    column: str
    direction: Literal["asc", "desc"] = "asc"
    nulls: Literal["first", "last"] = "last"


def sort_expr(spec: SortSpec):
    return col(spec.column).sort(
        ascending=(spec.direction == "asc"),
        nulls_first=(spec.nulls == "first"),
    )
```

---

## 15.9.2 Offset window builder

```python id="6chkb1"
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Literal
from datafusion import functions as f, col


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OffsetWindowSpec:
    kind: Literal["lag", "lead"]
    input: str
    output: str
    partition_by: tuple[str, ...]
    order_by: tuple[SortSpec, ...]
    shift_offset: int = 1
    default_value: Any = None


def offset_window_expr(spec: OffsetWindowSpec):
    fn = f.lag if spec.kind == "lag" else f.lead
    return fn(
        col(spec.input),
        shift_offset=spec.shift_offset,
        default_value=spec.default_value,
        partition_by=[col(c) for c in spec.partition_by],
        order_by=[sort_expr(s) for s in spec.order_by],
    ).alias(spec.output)
```

---

## 15.9.3 Ranking window builder

```python id="liqr3p"
from typing import Literal
from dataclasses import dataclass


RankKind = Literal["row_number", "rank", "dense_rank", "percent_rank", "cume_dist"]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RankWindowSpec:
    kind: RankKind
    output: str
    partition_by: tuple[str, ...]
    order_by: tuple[SortSpec, ...]


def rank_window_expr(spec: RankWindowSpec):
    fns = {
        "row_number": f.row_number,
        "rank": f.rank,
        "dense_rank": f.dense_rank,
        "percent_rank": f.percent_rank,
        "cume_dist": f.cume_dist,
    }
    return fns[spec.kind](
        partition_by=[col(c) for c in spec.partition_by],
        order_by=[sort_expr(s) for s in spec.order_by],
    ).alias(spec.output)
```

---

## 15.9.4 Aggregate-over-window builder

```python id="tfq19m"
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

from datafusion.expr import Window, WindowFrame


AggWindowKind = Literal["avg", "sum", "min", "max", "count"]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FrameSpec:
    unit: Literal["rows", "range", "groups"] = "rows"
    start: int | None = None
    end: int | None = 0


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AggWindowSpec:
    kind: AggWindowKind
    input: str
    output: str
    partition_by: tuple[str, ...]
    order_by: tuple[SortSpec, ...] = ()
    frame: FrameSpec | None = None


def agg_window_expr(spec: AggWindowSpec):
    fns = {
        "avg": f.avg,
        "sum": f.sum,
        "min": f.min,
        "max": f.max,
        "count": f.count,
    }

    window = Window(
        partition_by=[col(c) for c in spec.partition_by],
        order_by=[sort_expr(s) for s in spec.order_by],
        window_frame=(
            WindowFrame(spec.frame.unit, spec.frame.start, spec.frame.end)
            if spec.frame is not None
            else None
        ),
    )

    return fns[spec.kind](col(spec.input)).over(window).alias(spec.output)
```

---

# 15.10 Window vs aggregate selection rules

| Need                                               | Use                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| one row per group                                  | `df.aggregate(...)`                                              |
| same row count as input with group metric attached | aggregate-over-window                                            |
| previous/next value                                | `lag` / `lead`                                                   |
| top-N per group                                    | `rank` or `row_number` + filter                                  |
| deterministic single winner per group              | `row_number` with complete tie-breaker order                     |
| tie-aware leaderboard                              | `rank` or `dense_rank`                                           |
| rolling metric                                     | aggregate-over-window + `WindowFrame("rows", n, 0)`              |
| cumulative metric                                  | aggregate-over-window + `WindowFrame("rows", None, 0)`           |
| fill forward latest non-null                       | `last_value(...).over(Window(..., null_treatment=IGNORE_NULLS))` |

---

# 15.11 Determinism and ordering contract

## 15.11.1 Bad: implicit row order

```python id="9p9m8d"
df.select(
    col("x"),
    f.lag(col("x")).alias("previous_x"),
)
```

Problem:

```text id="wat3co"
No order_by:
  physical input order may be undefined
  partition execution order may be unstable
  file/object-store scan order may vary
  optimizer/runtime changes can alter results
```

## 15.11.2 Good: explicit order

```python id="5f733k"
df.select(
    col("entity_id"),
    col("event_ts"),
    col("event_id"),
    col("x"),
    f.lag(
        col("x"),
        partition_by=[col("entity_id")],
        order_by=[
            col("event_ts").sort(ascending=True, nulls_first=False),
            col("event_id").sort(ascending=True, nulls_first=False),
        ],
    ).alias("previous_x"),
)
```

Agent rule:

```text id="91dcwt"
Every window expression that depends on row sequence must document:
  partition_by keys
  order_by keys
  tie-breaker keys
  null ordering
  frame semantics
```

---

# 15.12 Performance and deployment advisory

```text id="0npawm"
Window functions can require:
  partitioning
  sorting within partitions
  buffering frame rows
  preserving row cardinality
```

Best practices:

```text id="8k3u2l"
Before window:
  - project only required columns
  - filter rows early when semantics allow
  - cast order keys to stable types
  - avoid duplicate/non-deterministic order keys

During window:
  - partition by meaningful keys
  - order deterministically
  - specify frame for rolling/running metrics
  - avoid massive unpartitioned windows over large datasets unless intended

After window:
  - filter rank/row_number outputs for top-N
  - project final schema explicitly
  - materialize only after row-cardinality budget is known
```

```python id="hf69bp"
base = (
    df.select("entity_id", "event_ts", "event_id", "amount")
      .filter(col("amount").is_not_null())
)

ranked = base.select(
    "*",
    f.row_number(
        partition_by=[col("entity_id")],
        order_by=[
            col("event_ts").sort(ascending=False, nulls_first=False),
            col("event_id").sort(ascending=True, nulls_first=False),
        ],
    ).alias("rn"),
)

latest = ranked.filter(col("rn") == lit(1)).drop("rn")
```

---

# 15.13 Anti-pattern catalog

## Anti-pattern: rank without `order_by`

```python id="lokkkg"
df.select(
    f.rank(partition_by=[col("group_id")]).alias("rank")
)
```

Correct:

```python id="7r4x58"
df.select(
    f.rank(
        partition_by=[col("group_id")],
        order_by=[col("score").sort(ascending=False, nulls_first=False)],
    ).alias("rank")
)
```

The `rank` API docs explicitly say to set `order_by` to produce meaningful results. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## Anti-pattern: lag without stable tie-breaker

```python id="4fzjaz"
f.lag(col("status"), partition_by=[col("user_id")], order_by=[col("ts")])
```

Correct:

```python id="5p4m55"
f.lag(
    col("status"),
    partition_by=[col("user_id")],
    order_by=[
        col("ts").sort(ascending=True, nulls_first=False),
        col("event_id").sort(ascending=True, nulls_first=False),
    ],
)
```

---

## Anti-pattern: aggregate when row cardinality must be preserved

```python id="9oikb7"
df.aggregate([col("group_id")], [f.avg(col("x")).alias("group_avg_x")])
```

Correct:

```python id="f479gh"
df.select(
    "*",
    f.avg(col("x")).over(
        Window(partition_by=[col("group_id")])
    ).alias("group_avg_x"),
)
```

---

## Anti-pattern: missing frame for running metric

```python id="8n80wp"
f.sum(col("amount")).over(
    Window(partition_by=[col("account_id")], order_by=[col("ts").sort()])
)
```

Safer explicit form:

```python id="19jtgw"
f.sum(col("amount")).over(
    Window(
        partition_by=[col("account_id")],
        order_by=[col("ts").sort()],
        window_frame=WindowFrame("rows", None, 0),
    )
).alias("running_amount")
```

Although the default with `order_by` is unbounded preceding through current row, explicit frames make metric definitions stable and readable. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## Anti-pattern: `IGNORE_NULLS` not documented

```python id="25tk8x"
f.last_value(col("status")).over(Window(..., null_treatment=NullTreatment.IGNORE_NULLS))
```

Correct policy:

```text id="ci7bbm"
Metric definition:
  last_known_status = last non-null status up to current row,
  ordered by event_ts/event_id,
  partitioned by entity_id,
  frame = unbounded preceding through current row,
  null treatment = IGNORE_NULLS.
```

---

# 15.14 Testing patterns

## Lag test

```python id="uvtsdk"
def test_lag(ctx):
    df = ctx.from_pydict({
        "entity_id": [1, 1, 1],
        "ts": [10, 20, 30],
        "x": [100, 200, 300],
    })

    out = (
        df.select(
            col("entity_id"),
            col("ts"),
            col("x"),
            f.lag(
                col("x"),
                default_value=0,
                partition_by=[col("entity_id")],
                order_by=[col("ts").sort()],
            ).alias("prev_x"),
        )
        .sort("ts")
        .to_pydict()
    )

    assert out["prev_x"] == [0, 100, 200]
```

## Partitioned rank test

```python id="zjgypz"
def test_partitioned_rank(ctx):
    df = ctx.from_pydict({
        "g": ["a", "a", "b", "b"],
        "v": [10, 20, 30, 20],
    })

    out = (
        df.select(
            col("g"),
            col("v"),
            f.rank(
                partition_by=[col("g")],
                order_by=[col("v").sort(ascending=False)],
            ).alias("rnk"),
        )
        .sort("g", col("rnk").sort())
        .to_pydict()
    )

    assert out["rnk"] == [1, 2, 1, 2]
```

## Moving average test

```python id="wxw10e"
def test_moving_average(ctx):
    df = ctx.from_pydict({
        "entity_id": [1, 1, 1, 1],
        "ts": [1, 2, 3, 4],
        "x": [10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0],
    })

    out = (
        df.select(
            col("ts"),
            f.avg(col("x")).over(
                Window(
                    partition_by=[col("entity_id")],
                    order_by=[col("ts").sort()],
                    window_frame=WindowFrame("rows", 2, 0),
                )
            ).alias("ma3"),
        )
        .sort("ts")
        .to_pydict()
    )

    assert out["ma3"] == [10.0, 15.0, 20.0, 30.0]
```

## Last non-null test

```python id="1lwirn"
def test_last_non_null(ctx):
    df = ctx.from_pydict({
        "entity_id": [1, 1, 1, 1],
        "ts": [1, 2, 3, 4],
        "status": ["a", None, "b", None],
    })

    out = (
        df.select(
            col("ts"),
            col("status"),
            f.last_value(col("status")).over(
                Window(
                    partition_by=[col("entity_id")],
                    order_by=[col("ts").sort()],
                    window_frame=WindowFrame("rows", None, 0),
                    null_treatment=NullTreatment.IGNORE_NULLS,
                )
            ).alias("last_status"),
        )
        .sort("ts")
        .to_pydict()
    )

    assert out["last_status"] == ["a", "a", "b", "b"]
```

---

# 15.15 Deployment checklist

```text id="5mya1i"
Window design:
  [ ] Decide if row cardinality must be preserved.
  [ ] Use window functions for per-row metrics using related rows.
  [ ] Use aggregate() when row collapse is desired.

Ordering:
  [ ] Every sequence-sensitive window has order_by.
  [ ] Every order_by has deterministic tie-breakers.
  [ ] Null ordering is explicit.
  [ ] No reliance on implicit physical row order.

Partitioning:
  [ ] partition_by is explicit for entity/group-local metrics.
  [ ] Global windows are deliberate and documented.
  [ ] High-cardinality partitions are tested at scale.

Frames:
  [ ] Running metrics use WindowFrame("rows", None, 0).
  [ ] Moving metrics use WindowFrame("rows", n, 0).
  [ ] Whole-partition metrics use full-partition frame or omit order_by intentionally.
  [ ] Range frames use exactly one order_by term.

Nulls:
  [ ] IGNORE_NULLS vs RESPECT_NULLS documented.
  [ ] Forward-fill/last-known-value uses IGNORE_NULLS.
  [ ] Null-sensitive metrics tested.

Performance:
  [ ] Project/filter before window.
  [ ] Avoid huge unpartitioned windows by accident.
  [ ] Inspect optimized_logical_plan()/execution_plan() for large workloads.
  [ ] Materialize only after cardinality is understood.

Testing:
  [ ] Tiny deterministic fixtures.
  [ ] Explicit sort before to_pydict assertions.
  [ ] Tie cases tested.
  [ ] Null cases tested.
```

---

## 15.16 Section compression for LLM agents

```text id="wl4vrx"
Mental model:
  window functions compute per-row results using related rows;
  aggregates collapse rows, windows preserve row identity.

Imports:
  from datafusion import col, lit, functions as f
  from datafusion.expr import Window, WindowFrame
  from datafusion.common import NullTreatment

Offset:
  f.lag(col("x"), shift_offset=1, default_value=None,
        partition_by=[col("id")], order_by=[col("ts").sort()])

  f.lead(col("x"), shift_offset=1, default_value=None,
         partition_by=[col("id")], order_by=[col("ts").sort()])

Ranking:
  f.row_number(partition_by=[...], order_by=[...])
  f.rank(partition_by=[...], order_by=[...])
  f.dense_rank(partition_by=[...], order_by=[...])
  f.percent_rank(partition_by=[...], order_by=[...])
  f.cume_dist(partition_by=[...], order_by=[...])
  f.ntile(lit(n), partition_by=[...], order_by=[...])

Aggregate-over-window:
  f.avg(col("x")).over(Window(partition_by=[...]))
  f.sum(col("x")).over(Window(partition_by=[...], order_by=[...],
                               window_frame=WindowFrame("rows", None, 0)))

Frames:
  WindowFrame("rows", 2, 0)       -> 2 preceding through current row
  WindowFrame("rows", None, 0)    -> unbounded preceding through current row
  WindowFrame("rows", None, None) -> entire partition

Defaults:
  order_by set     -> default frame unbounded preceding to current row
  order_by missing -> default frame entire partition

Null treatment:
  Window(..., null_treatment=NullTreatment.IGNORE_NULLS)
  Window(..., null_treatment=NullTreatment.RESPECT_NULLS)

Rules:
  always alias window outputs
  always specify order_by for lag/lead/rank/row_number/running windows
  include tie-breaker keys
  partition entity-local windows
  explicitly frame running/moving metrics
  use IGNORE_NULLS for last-known-value
  never rely on implicit row order
```

[1]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/user-guide/common-operations/windows.html "Window Functions — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"
[2]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/autoapi/datafusion/functions/index.html "datafusion.functions — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"
[3]: https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/sql/window_functions.html "Window Functions — Apache DataFusion  documentation"


# DataFusion Advanced — 16) User-defined functions: UDF, UDAF, UDWF, UDTF

This section follows the same dense, agent-facing technical-reference style as the Cyclopts source material. 

## 16.0 Core extension invariant

DataFusion Python supports four user-defined function classes:

```text id="bq80ff"
Scalar UDF  -> row-wise / element-wise expression over Arrow batches
UDAF        -> group aggregate; many rows -> one scalar per group
UDWF        -> window evaluator; partition/window rows -> per-row window output
UDTF        -> table-valued function; literal args -> TableProvider
```

DataFusion’s UDF guide explicitly says built-in expressions and functions reduce the need for custom Python functions, but user-defined functions are still supported when the built-in catalog cannot express the operation. Scalar UDFs are Python functions that take one or more PyArrow arrays and return one PyArrow array; they operate on whole record batches at a time, even when the semantics are row-by-row. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

```python id="s4gn1i"
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc

from datafusion import (
    SessionContext,
    col,
    lit,
    udf,
    udaf,
    udwf,
    udtf,
    Accumulator,
)
from datafusion.user_defined import WindowEvaluator, Volatility
```

---

## 16.1 Function family map

| Type          | Constructor                             | Python implementation unit      | DataFusion use site                            | Returns        |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| Scalar UDF    | `udf(...)` / `ScalarUDF.udf(...)`       | callable over PyArrow arrays    | `select`, `filter`, SQL scalar function        | `Expr`         |
| Aggregate UDF | `udaf(...)` / `AggregateUDF.udaf(...)`  | `Accumulator` factory/class     | `aggregate`, SQL aggregate, window aggregate   | `Expr`         |
| Window UDF    | `udwf(...)` / `WindowUDF.udwf(...)`     | `WindowEvaluator` factory/class | `select`, window expression                    | `Expr`         |
| Table UDF     | `udtf(...)` / `TableFunction.udtf(...)` | table-provider factory          | SQL `FROM fn(...)` / table function invocation | table provider |

`ScalarUDF`, `AggregateUDF`, `WindowUDF`, `TableFunction`, `Accumulator`, `WindowEvaluator`, and `Volatility` are the documented user-defined-function classes in `datafusion.user_defined`. `SessionContext` has `register_udf`, `register_udaf`, `register_udwf`, and `register_udtf` methods for context-level registration. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

# 16.2 Scalar UDFs

## 16.2.1 Contract

```text id="92k3d6"
Scalar UDF function:
  input:  one or more pyarrow.Array values
  output: one pyarrow.Array
  execution: batch-oriented
  semantics: usually element-wise / row-wise
```

```python id="8kezlc"
udf(
    func,
    input_fields,
    return_field,
    volatility,
    name=None,
)
```

`ScalarUDF.udf(...)` can be used as a function or decorator; `input_fields` can be a sequence of PyArrow `DataType` or `Field` values, and if a `DataType` is passed instead of a `Field`, DataFusion assumes nullable inputs/outputs and no metadata. The return value is a `ScalarUDF` that can be used in SQL expressions, aggregation, or window calls. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 16.2.2 Minimal scalar UDF: PyArrow-vectorized

```python id="4kb5m8"
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc
from datafusion import SessionContext, col, udf

def double_array(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.multiply(x, 2)

double_udf = udf(
    double_array,
    [pa.int64()],
    pa.int64(),
    "immutable",
    name="double_array",
)

ctx = SessionContext()
df = ctx.from_pydict({"x": [1, 2, 3]})

out = df.select(
    col("x"),
    double_udf(col("x")).alias("x2"),
)

out.to_pydict()
```

SQL registration:

```python id="h0ckss"
ctx.register_udf(double_udf)

ctx.sql("""
    SELECT x, double_array(x) AS x2
    FROM t
""")
```

`SessionContext.register_udf(udf)` registers a scalar UDF with the context; calling the UDF object with `Expr` arguments returns an `Expr`. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 16.2.3 Decorator syntax

```python id="7i54yr"
@udf([pa.int64()], pa.int64(), "immutable", name="triple")
def triple(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.multiply(x, 3)

df.select(
    col("x"),
    triple(col("x")).alias("x3"),
)
```

`ScalarUDF.udf(...)` explicitly supports both function-call style and decorator style. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 16.2.4 Nullable/type metadata via `pa.Field`

Use `pa.Field` when nullability or metadata is part of the contract.

```python id="egsojy"
input_field = pa.field(
    "x",
    pa.int64(),
    nullable=False,
    metadata={b"semantic_type": b"user_id"},
)

return_field = pa.field(
    "is_positive",
    pa.bool_(),
    nullable=False,
)

@udf([input_field], return_field, "immutable", name="is_positive")
def is_positive(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.greater(x, 0)
```

The UDF guide states that PyArrow `Field` can be used instead of `DataType` for additional control such as metadata or nullability. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 16.2.5 Python-object fallback: slow path

```python id="p0778h"
def slow_is_null(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pa.array([value.as_py() is None for value in x])
```

DataFusion’s UDF guide strongly recommends PyArrow built-in compute functions when possible because they can perform computations without copying from original arrays; converting Arrow values into Python objects and reconstructing arrays is described as one of the slowest operations and should be done sparingly. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text id="hwzwq7"
Scalar UDF fast path:
  use pyarrow.compute
  operate on whole arrays
  return pyarrow.Array
  avoid for value in array loops
  avoid value.as_py() loops
  avoid list comprehension over full columns

Scalar UDF slow path:
  Python object conversion
  per-element Python logic
  external library calls per value
  non-vectorized algorithms
```

---

## 16.2.6 Scalar UDF SQL usage

```python id="b0zwbs"
ctx.register_record_batches("t", [[batch]])
ctx.register_udf(double_udf)

df = ctx.sql("""
    SELECT
        x,
        double_array(x) AS x2
    FROM t
""")
```

Registration is required for SQL name resolution. Direct DataFrame API use can call the UDF object directly.

---

# 16.3 Volatility

## 16.3.1 Values

```text id="twpkgi"
"immutable"
"stable"
"volatile"

Volatility.Immutable
Volatility.Stable
Volatility.Volatile
```

`Volatility` can be passed either as the enum or as lowercase strings. Immutable functions always return the same output for the same input and may be inlined during planning; stable functions return the same value for a given input within a single query but may differ across queries; volatile functions may differ from evaluation to evaluation and cannot be evaluated during planning. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

```python id="l4xioi"
from datafusion.user_defined import Volatility

udf(fn, [pa.int64()], pa.int64(), Volatility.Immutable, name="fn")
udf(fn, [pa.int64()], pa.int64(), "immutable", name="fn")
```

## 16.3.2 Selection rules

```text id="daq6pr"
immutable:
  pure deterministic function
  same inputs -> same output forever
  examples: normalize_email, hash_id, unit_conversion

stable:
  fixed within query
  may differ across queries
  examples: run_date, current_config_lookup, query_start_time

volatile:
  may differ per row/evaluation
  examples: random, uuid, current_external_service_state
```

Agent rule:

```text id="50lgbk"
Do not mark time/random/external-state/network functions immutable.
Wrong volatility can cause incorrect planning/inlining behavior.
```

---

# 16.4 Aggregate UDFs / UDAFs

## 16.4.1 Contract

```text id="sa42pd"
UDAF:
  input: arrays per batch
  update: consume input batch and mutate accumulator state
  state: expose intermediate scalar state for partial aggregation
  merge: combine states from partial accumulators
  evaluate: return final scalar result
```

The UDAF guide says `udaf()` defines user-defined aggregate functions, requiring an `Accumulator`. Four methods are required: `update`, `state`, `merge`, and `evaluate`; `update` processes arrays from one batch, `state` returns scalar values representing a partial state, `merge` combines partial states, and `evaluate` returns the final result. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 16.4.2 `Accumulator` interface

```python id="xz8rul"
class Accumulator:
    def update(self, *values: pa.Array) -> None:
        ...

    def state(self) -> list[pa.Scalar]:
        ...

    def merge(self, states: list[pa.Array]) -> None:
        ...

    def evaluate(self) -> pa.Scalar:
        ...
```

The API reference defines `Accumulator.update(*values: pyarrow.Array)`, `state() -> list[pyarrow.Scalar]`, `merge(states: list[pyarrow.Array])`, and `evaluate() -> pyarrow.Scalar`. It also notes `evaluate` and `state` may return values convertible into Arrow scalars, including basic Python primitive types and Arrow-FFI-compatible objects. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 16.4.3 Minimal UDAF: sum with bias

```python id="ycpyzz"
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc

from datafusion import SessionContext, col, udaf, Accumulator


class SumWithBias(Accumulator):
    def __init__(self, bias: float = 0.0):
        self._sum = bias

    def update(self, values: pa.Array) -> None:
        s = pc.sum(values).as_py()
        if s is not None:
            self._sum += s

    def state(self) -> list[pa.Scalar]:
        return [pa.scalar(self._sum, type=pa.float64())]

    def merge(self, states: list[pa.Array]) -> None:
        s = pc.sum(states[0]).as_py()
        if s is not None:
            self._sum += s

    def evaluate(self) -> pa.Scalar:
        return pa.scalar(self._sum, type=pa.float64())


sum_with_bias = udaf(
    lambda: SumWithBias(10.0),
    pa.float64(),
    pa.float64(),
    [pa.float64()],
    "immutable",
    name="sum_with_bias",
)

ctx = SessionContext()
df = ctx.from_pydict({"x": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]})

df.aggregate(
    [],
    [sum_with_bias(col("x")).alias("biased_sum")],
).to_pydict()
```

The documented UDAF API supports passing an accumulator class, function, lambda, or decorator; if constructor arguments are needed, use a lambda or factory method, and the accumulator is constructed for every runtime use of the UDAF. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 16.4.4 Multi-input UDAF: difference between sums

```python id="hh0am7"
class SumDifference(Accumulator):
    def __init__(self):
        self._sum = 0.0

    def update(self, a: pa.Array, b: pa.Array) -> None:
        a_sum = pc.sum(a).as_py() or 0.0
        b_sum = pc.sum(b).as_py() or 0.0
        self._sum += a_sum - b_sum

    def state(self) -> list[pa.Scalar]:
        return [pa.scalar(self._sum, type=pa.float64())]

    def merge(self, states: list[pa.Array]) -> None:
        s = pc.sum(states[0]).as_py() or 0.0
        self._sum += s

    def evaluate(self) -> pa.Scalar:
        return pa.scalar(self._sum, type=pa.float64())


sum_diff = udaf(
    SumDifference,
    [pa.float64(), pa.float64()],
    pa.float64(),
    [pa.float64()],
    "stable",
    name="sum_diff",
)

df.aggregate(
    [],
    [sum_diff(col("a"), col("b")).alias("col_diff")],
)
```

The user guide’s UDAF example implements a two-column aggregate whose `update(values_a, values_b)` uses PyArrow compute sums and whose `merge(states)` combines partial states. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 16.4.5 UDAF state-type design

```text id="2busw8"
state_type:
  list[pa.DataType]
  one entry per scalar in Accumulator.state()
  merge(states) receives arrays of these state values
```

Examples:

```text id="bh3m5p"
sum:
  state_type=[pa.float64()]
  state=[current_sum]

average:
  state_type=[pa.float64(), pa.int64()]
  state=[sum, count]

variance:
  state_type=[pa.float64(), pa.float64(), pa.int64()]
  state=[sum, sum_of_squares, count]

top-k:
  state_type=[pa.list_(item_type)]  # wrapped as scalar
```

For returning list values from `evaluate` or `state`, the docs recommend wrapping values in a `pyarrow.Scalar`, such as `pa.scalar([...], type=pa.list_(pa.timestamp("ms")))`, and registering matching `return_type` and `state_type` values. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 16.4.6 UDAF SQL registration

```python id="vso6qz"
ctx.register_udaf(sum_diff)

ctx.sql("""
    SELECT sum_diff(a, b) AS col_diff
    FROM t
""")
```

`SessionContext.register_udaf(udaf)` registers a user-defined aggregate function with the context. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 16.4.7 UDAF agent rules

```text id="4p08fx"
Accumulator design:
  - keep state compact
  - use PyArrow compute in update/merge
  - avoid storing full input arrays unless unavoidable
  - make state_type exactly match state()
  - make return_type exactly match evaluate()
  - handle nulls explicitly
  - assume update is called per batch
  - assume merge combines partial states from parallel/batched execution

Performance:
  - update and merge should be vectorized
  - avoid per-row Python loops
  - avoid Python object state explosion
  - use Rust-backed UDAF for hot complex aggregations
```

---

# 16.5 Window UDFs / UDWFs

## 16.5.1 Contract

```text id="06u16n"
UDWF:
  implementation: WindowEvaluator
  input: partition arrays / frame ranges / rank info
  output: one value per input row
  use site: select/window expression
```

To implement a Python user-defined window function, call `udwf()` with a class implementing `WindowEvaluator`. The docs describe three evaluation methods: `evaluate`, `evaluate_all`, and `evaluate_all_with_rank`; `evaluate` is simplest but least performant because it computes one row at a time, while `evaluate_all` computes all rows for a partition in one pass. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 16.5.2 `WindowEvaluator` methods

```python id="9swyx5"
class WindowEvaluator:
    def evaluate(
        self,
        values: list[pa.Array],
        eval_range: tuple[int, int],
    ) -> pa.Scalar:
        ...

    def evaluate_all(
        self,
        values: list[pa.Array],
        num_rows: int,
    ) -> pa.Array:
        ...

    def evaluate_all_with_rank(...):
        ...
```

Relevant evaluator options:

```python id="c79pqp"
def uses_window_frame(self) -> bool: ...
def supports_bounded_execution(self) -> bool: ...
def include_rank(self) -> bool: ...
def is_causal(self) -> bool: ...
def memoize(self) -> None: ...
```

The API reference documents `evaluate`, `evaluate_all`, `include_rank`, `is_causal`, `memoize`, `supports_bounded_execution`, and `uses_window_frame`. `evaluate_all` must produce one output row for every input row, while `evaluate` receives an evaluation range and returns one scalar. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 16.5.3 Evaluation mode table

```text id="jbceac"
Default non-frame function:
  uses_window_frame=False
  supports_bounded_execution=False
  include_rank=False
  implement evaluate_all

Frame-dependent function:
  uses_window_frame=True
  implement evaluate

Bounded incremental function:
  supports_bounded_execution=True
  implement evaluate or optimized stateful path

Rank-only function:
  include_rank=True
  implement evaluate_all_with_rank
```

The user guide lists which evaluator method is selected by `uses_window_frame`, `supports_bounded_execution`, and `include_rank`, and says these option methods determine which evaluate function is called. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 16.5.4 UDWF example: exponential smoothing

```python id="k0sfxf"
import pyarrow as pa
from datafusion import SessionContext, col, udwf
from datafusion.user_defined import WindowEvaluator


class ExponentialSmooth(WindowEvaluator):
    def __init__(self, alpha: float):
        self.alpha = alpha

    def evaluate_all(self, values: list[pa.Array], num_rows: int) -> pa.Array:
        x = values[0]
        results: list[float] = []
        current = 0.0

        for idx in range(num_rows):
            v = x[idx].as_py()
            if idx == 0:
                current = v
            else:
                current = v * self.alpha + current * (1.0 - self.alpha)
            results.append(current)

        return pa.array(results, type=pa.float64())


exp_smooth = udwf(
    lambda: ExponentialSmooth(0.9),
    pa.float64(),
    pa.float64(),
    volatility="immutable",
    name="exp_smooth",
)

ctx = SessionContext()
df = ctx.from_pydict({"a": [1.0, 2.1, 2.9, 4.0]})

df.select(
    col("a"),
    exp_smooth(col("a")).alias("smooth_a"),
)
```

The official guide shows an `ExponentialSmooth(WindowEvaluator)` with `evaluate_all(...)`, registering it with `udwf(...)`, and using it in `df.select("a", exp_smooth(col("a")).alias("smooth_a"))`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 16.5.5 UDWF registration for SQL

```python id="pas7xr"
ctx.register_udwf(exp_smooth)

ctx.sql("""
    SELECT a, exp_smooth(a) AS smooth_a
    FROM t
""")
```

`SessionContext.register_udwf(udwf)` registers a user-defined window function with the context. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 16.5.6 UDWF agent rules

```text id="879fww"
Window evaluator design:
  - implement evaluate_all when frame-independent and possible
  - implement evaluate only when frame-specific output is required
  - implement evaluate_all_with_rank for rank-only logic
  - return one output element per input row from evaluate_all
  - use PyArrow arrays and compute where possible
  - document frame dependence
  - document bounded execution support
  - document rank dependence
  - document null behavior
  - avoid future-row dependence unless explicitly required
```

---

# 16.6 User-defined table functions / UDTFs

## 16.6.1 Contract

```text id="uoszqg"
UDTF:
  input: Expr arguments
  constraint: only literal expressions currently supported
  output: TableProvider
  registration: ctx.register_udtf(...)
  SQL use: table-valued function in FROM position
```

DataFusion’s UDF guide states that table functions take any number of `Expr` arguments, but only literal expressions are supported; table functions must return a table provider, and once created they are registered through `SessionContext.register_udtf()`. It also notes Rust-backed table functions exposed via PyO3 must expose a PyCapsule. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 16.6.2 Constructor surface

```python id="d5m8j1"
udtf(name: str) -> decorator
udtf(func, name: str) -> TableFunction

# full 54 surface (with_session added in 54 — see 16.15):
udtf(*args, with_session: bool = False, **kwargs)
TableFunction(name: str, func: Callable[..., Any], ctx: SessionContext | None = None,
              *, with_session: bool = False)
```

The `TableFunction.udtf(...)` API documents decorator style and function style and returns a `TableFunction`; calling a `TableFunction` with `Expr` arguments executes the UDTF and returns a table provider. Since 54, both constructors accept `with_session=True` to opt into session injection (16.15). ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 16.6.3 UDTF skeleton

```python id="0pm98u"
from datafusion import udtf, lit

def make_table_provider_for_path(path_literal):
    # Return an object implementing DataFusion table-provider export contract.
    # Typical implementation:
    #   - Python table provider object
    #   - Rust-backed provider exposed as PyCapsule
    #   - wrapper around an existing provider
    return provider

path_table = udtf(make_table_provider_for_path, "path_table")
ctx.register_udtf(path_table)
```

SQL use:

```python id="mowxv8"
df = ctx.sql("""
    SELECT *
    FROM path_table('/data/events.parquet')
""")
```

DataFrame/table-function use conceptually:

```python id="baqdjs"
provider = path_table(lit("/data/events.parquet"))
```

**Agent caution:** UDTF arguments are currently literal-only. Do not generate UDTFs expecting column-dependent table expansion, per-row table-returning behavior, or lateral row-wise invocation unless the target DataFusion version explicitly supports it. The official guide states only literal expressions are supported for table-function arguments. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 16.6.4 Table-provider return contract

```text id="w67c21"
UDTF function must return:
  TableProvider-compatible object
  or Rust-backed provider exported through PyCapsule
  or object matching DataFusion table-provider integration contract
```

Custom table-provider implementation details belong to the custom table provider API. For hot or complex table functions, prefer Rust-backed table providers and expose them to Python through PyO3/PyCapsule; the UDTF guide explicitly references Rust-backed and Python-based examples and PyCapsule export for Rust-backed table functions. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 16.6.5 UDTF agent rules

```text id="9i56xo"
Use UDTF when:
  literal parameters produce a dynamic table
  table shape depends on constant arguments
  provider construction belongs in SQL FROM position
  source/plugin abstraction should be SQL-callable

Avoid UDTF when:
  operation is scalar per row -> scalar UDF
  operation is group aggregate -> UDAF
  operation is windowed per row -> UDWF
  arguments need non-literal column expressions
  output can be represented as a registered table/view
```

---

# 16.7 Registration lifecycle

## 16.7.1 Context-local registration

```python id="ld90rz"
ctx.register_udf(scalar_udf)
ctx.register_udaf(aggregate_udf)
ctx.register_udwf(window_udf)
ctx.register_udtf(table_function)
```

```python id="ik3jz7"
ctx.deregister_udf("fn_name")
ctx.deregister_udaf("agg_name")
ctx.deregister_udwf("win_name")
ctx.deregister_udtf("table_fn_name")
```

`SessionContext` registers and deregisters scalar UDFs, aggregate UDFs, window UDFs, and table UDFs by name; these registrations are context-local mutable state. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

Agent rule:

```text id="0748wj"
Register functions during context bootstrap.
Do not register functions inside pure query builders.
Use fresh SessionContext per test/tenant/session where function registry isolation matters.
```

---

## 16.8 DataFrame API vs SQL API usage

```python id="s2cbq2"
# DataFrame API: direct UDF object call
df.select(my_udf(col("x")).alias("y"))

# SQL API: requires context registration
ctx.register_udf(my_udf)
ctx.sql("SELECT my_udf(x) AS y FROM t")
```

```python id="pbmzhk"
# UDAF DataFrame API
df.aggregate([col("g")], [my_udaf(col("x")).alias("metric")])

# UDAF SQL API
ctx.register_udaf(my_udaf)
ctx.sql("SELECT g, my_udaf(x) AS metric FROM t GROUP BY g")
```

```python id="bu5mxh"
# UDWF DataFrame API
df.select(my_udwf(col("x")).alias("win_x"))

# UDWF SQL API
ctx.register_udwf(my_udwf)
ctx.sql("SELECT my_udwf(x) AS win_x FROM t")
```

---

# 16.9 Rust-backed UDFs and PyCapsule path

The API supports importing UDF/UDAF/UDWF objects from PyCapsules: `ScalarUDF.from_pycapsule`, `AggregateUDF.from_pycapsule`, and `WindowUDF.from_pycapsule` instantiate Python wrapper objects around Rust-exported DataFusion function implementations. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

```text id="icqth8"
Rust-backed function path:
  implement function in Rust
  expose __datafusion_scalar_udf__ / __datafusion_aggregate_udf__ / __datafusion_window_udf__
  return PyCapsule
  wrap in Python via from_pycapsule or constructor path
  register with SessionContext
```

Use Rust-backed UDFs when:

```text id="2nos6t"
hot path
large data volume
complex per-row logic
Python object conversion is too slow
stateful aggregate is performance-critical
window evaluator needs bounded/incremental memory behavior
GIL contention or Python callback overhead dominates
```

The UDF guide says an advanced approach to avoid Python object conversion cost is to write Rust-based UDFs and expose them to Python. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

# 16.10 Deployment advisory

## 16.10.1 Built-ins-first decision tree

```text id="3p9x69"
Can built-in datafusion.functions express it?
  yes -> use built-in

Can Expr methods express it?
  yes -> use Expr method

Can pyarrow.compute express it vectorized?
  yes -> scalar UDF with Arrow compute

Does it require group state?
  yes -> UDAF

Does it require per-row window partition state?
  yes -> UDWF

Does it produce a relation/table from literal parameters?
  yes -> UDTF

Is it hot and Python is too slow?
  yes -> Rust-backed UDF/provider via PyCapsule
```

DataFusion’s guide explicitly recommends built-in expressions/functions and PyArrow compute functions before custom Python object conversion. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 16.10.2 Packaging / deployment rules

```text id="6s2i4d"
Python UDF deployment:
  - pin datafusion version
  - pin pyarrow version compatibility
  - package UDF modules with application code
  - register functions during SessionContext bootstrap
  - avoid runtime dynamic function definitions in services
  - avoid dependency imports inside function body
  - ensure worker/container image contains all UDF dependencies
  - test SQL registration and DataFrame direct-call paths
```

## 16.10.3 Runtime rules

```text id="m2zjdr"
Scalar UDF:
  - batch-oriented
  - vectorize
  - return Arrow array
  - avoid per-row Python

UDAF:
  - compact state
  - deterministic merge
  - type-accurate state_type
  - null-safe update/merge

UDWF:
  - prefer evaluate_all for frame-independent functions
  - document frame dependence
  - document bounded execution
  - return array length == partition row count

UDTF:
  - literal arguments only
  - returns table provider
  - bootstrap provider dependencies
  - prefer Rust provider for production/hot path
```

---

# 16.11 Anti-pattern catalog

## Anti-pattern: UDF for built-in operation

```python id="78qcua"
def lower_py(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pa.array([v.as_py().lower() if v.as_py() else None for v in x])
```

Correct:

```python id="l008nh"
from datafusion import functions as f

df.select(f.lower(col("name")).alias("name_lc"))
```

---

## Anti-pattern: per-row Python loop inside scalar UDF

```python id="g4fd6p"
def add_one_slow(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pa.array([v.as_py() + 1 if v.as_py() is not None else None for v in x])
```

Correct:

```python id="bynfiq"
def add_one_fast(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.add(x, 1)
```

---

## Anti-pattern: wrong volatility

```python id="b5jcpr"
@udf([], pa.float64(), "immutable", name="rand_bad")
def rand_bad() -> pa.Array:
    ...
```

Correct:

```python id="1apfwo"
@udf([], pa.float64(), "volatile", name="rand_value")
def rand_value() -> pa.Array:
    ...
```

Volatile functions may change from evaluation to evaluation and cannot be evaluated during planning. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## Anti-pattern: UDAF state stores all rows

```python id="xpk3m7"
class BadMedian(Accumulator):
    def __init__(self):
        self.values = []  # unbounded state
```

Better:

```text id="qpbkxq"
Use:
  approximate built-in percentile
  compact sketch state
  Rust-backed aggregate
  bounded-memory data structure
```

---

## Anti-pattern: UDTF expecting column arguments

```sql id="nxp3qm"
SELECT *
FROM my_table_function(column_name)
```

Current contract: UDTF arguments are `Expr` values but only literal expressions are supported. Use literal args or build a scalar/window/aggregate UDF instead. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## Anti-pattern: registration inside query builder

```python id="x0eoi3"
def build_query(ctx):
    ctx.register_udf(my_udf)
    return ctx.sql("SELECT my_udf(x) FROM t")
```

Correct:

```python id="o7r466"
def bootstrap_context():
    ctx = SessionContext()
    ctx.register_udf(my_udf)
    return ctx

def build_query(ctx):
    return ctx.sql("SELECT my_udf(x) FROM t")
```

---

# 16.12 Test patterns

## Scalar UDF test

```python id="q9tglz"
def test_scalar_udf(ctx):
    @udf([pa.int64()], pa.int64(), "immutable", name="double_test")
    def double_test(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
        return pc.multiply(x, 2)

    out = (
        ctx.from_pydict({"x": [1, 2, 3]})
        .select(double_test(col("x")).alias("y"))
        .to_pydict()
    )

    assert out == {"y": [2, 4, 6]}
```

## Scalar UDF SQL registration test

```python id="4d1e2l"
def test_scalar_udf_sql(ctx):
    @udf([pa.int64()], pa.int64(), "immutable", name="double_sql")
    def double_sql(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
        return pc.multiply(x, 2)

    ctx.register_udf(double_sql)
    ctx.register_record_batches("t", [[make_batch({"x": [1, 2, 3]})]])

    out = ctx.sql("SELECT double_sql(x) AS y FROM t").to_pydict()

    assert out == {"y": [2, 4, 6]}
```

## UDAF test

```python id="kvp7zd"
def test_udaf(ctx):
    sum_bias = udaf(
        lambda: SumWithBias(10.0),
        pa.float64(),
        pa.float64(),
        [pa.float64()],
        "immutable",
        name="sum_bias_test",
    )

    df = ctx.from_pydict({"x": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]})

    out = df.aggregate([], [sum_bias(col("x")).alias("s")]).to_pydict()

    assert out == {"s": [16.0]}
```

## UDWF test

```python id="579ym5"
def test_udwf(ctx):
    smooth = udwf(
        lambda: ExponentialSmooth(0.5),
        pa.float64(),
        pa.float64(),
        volatility="immutable",
        name="smooth_test",
    )

    df = ctx.from_pydict({"x": [1.0, 3.0, 5.0]})

    out = df.select(smooth(col("x")).alias("s")).to_pydict()

    assert len(out["s"]) == 3
```

# 16.13 Function design checklist

```text id="aamq08"
Before implementing:
  [ ] Search datafusion.functions built-ins.
  [ ] Search Expr methods.
  [ ] Check pyarrow.compute.
  [ ] Decide scalar vs aggregate vs window vs table.
  [ ] Define exact Arrow input types.
  [ ] Define exact Arrow output type.
  [ ] Define nullability/metadata with pa.Field if needed.
  [ ] Define volatility.
  [ ] Define SQL name.
  [ ] Decide whether SQL registration is required.

Scalar UDF:
  [ ] input arrays count matches input_fields length.
  [ ] returns one output Arrow array.
  [ ] output length equals input batch length.
  [ ] vectorized implementation.
  [ ] no per-row object loop unless unavoidable.

UDAF:
  [ ] update handles arrays and nulls.
  [ ] state returns scalar list matching state_type.
  [ ] merge handles arrays of partial states.
  [ ] evaluate returns scalar matching return_type.
  [ ] state is compact and mergeable.
  [ ] constructor/factory is zero-arg or wrapped.

UDWF:
  [ ] choose evaluate/evaluate_all/evaluate_all_with_rank.
  [ ] document uses_window_frame.
  [ ] document supports_bounded_execution.
  [ ] document include_rank.
  [ ] output row count equals input row count.
  [ ] null/frame/order behavior tested.

UDTF:
  [ ] arguments are literal-only.
  [ ] return value is table provider.
  [ ] SQL use site documented.
  [ ] provider lifecycle and credentials are bootstrap-owned.

Deployment:
  [ ] register in context bootstrap.
  [ ] deregister in tests if context reused.
  [ ] avoid global context for tenant-specific functions.
  [ ] benchmark against built-ins.
  [ ] use Rust-backed implementation for hot paths.
```

---

## 16.14 Section compression for LLM agents

```text id="bzjsk1"
Scalar UDF:
  udf(func, input_fields, return_field, volatility, name=None) -> ScalarUDF
  @udf(input_fields, return_field, volatility, name=None)
  func(*arrays: pa.Array) -> pa.Array
  df.select(my_udf(col("x")).alias("y"))
  ctx.register_udf(my_udf) for SQL

UDAF:
  class MyAccum(Accumulator):
    update(*arrays) -> None
    state() -> list[pa.Scalar]
    merge(states: list[pa.Array]) -> None
    evaluate() -> pa.Scalar

  udaf(accum_factory, input_types, return_type, state_type, volatility, name=None)
  df.aggregate([group], [my_udaf(col("x")).alias("metric")])
  ctx.register_udaf(my_udaf) for SQL

UDWF:
  class MyEval(WindowEvaluator):
    evaluate(values, eval_range) -> pa.Scalar        # general, least performant
    evaluate_all(values, num_rows) -> pa.Array       # partition-wide, faster
    evaluate_all_with_rank(...) -> pa.Array          # rank-based
    uses_window_frame() -> bool
    supports_bounded_execution() -> bool
    include_rank() -> bool

  udwf(factory_or_evaluator, input_types, return_type, volatility, name=None)
  df.select(my_udwf(col("x")).alias("win_x"))
  ctx.register_udwf(my_udwf) for SQL

UDTF:
  udtf(func, name) -> TableFunction
  ctx.register_udtf(table_fn)
  SQL FROM table_fn(literal_args)
  literal expression args only
  returns TableProvider

Volatility:
  immutable -> same input, same output; may inline during planning
  stable    -> same within one query, may differ across queries
  volatile  -> may differ per evaluation; not planned/inlined

Performance defaults:
  built-ins first
  PyArrow compute second
  Python UDF only when needed
  Rust-backed UDF for hot paths
  avoid as_py loops
  avoid full Python object conversion
  keep UDAF state compact
  document types, nulls, volatility, frame behavior, registration scope
```

## 16.15 UDTF session injection: `with_session=True` (new in 54)

The 54.0.0 changelog lists “pass `SessionContext` into UDTF calls” as a breaking change; at the released Python surface it landed as an **opt-in flag**, so existing UDTFs keep working unchanged. Shapes verified against the installed `datafusion==54.0.0` wheel (see [`datafusion_python_54vs53.md`](datafusion_python_54vs53.md) §1.1).

```python id="udtf54a"
udtf(*args, with_session: bool = False, **kwargs)

TableFunction(
    name: str,
    func: Callable[..., Any],
    ctx: SessionContext | None = None,
    *,
    with_session: bool = False,
)
```

With `with_session=True`, the **calling `SessionContext` is injected as a `session` keyword argument on each invocation** of the table function. The UDTF can then resolve session-dependent state — configuration, registered tables, catalogs, registered functions — during planning:

```python id="udtf54b"
from datafusion import SessionContext, udtf

@udtf("tables_snapshot", with_session=True)
def tables_snapshot(prefix_literal, *, session):
    # session is the live SessionContext that invoked this UDTF.
    # Use it read-only: e.g. resolve a registered table into a provider,
    # or branch on session configuration.
    ...
    return provider

ctx = SessionContext()
ctx.register_udtf(tables_snapshot)
df = ctx.sql("SELECT * FROM tables_snapshot('staging_')")
```

Contract (live-verified):

```text id="udtf54c"
with_session=False (default):
  invocation signature unchanged: func(*literal_expr_args)
  no migration required for existing UDTFs

with_session=True:
  invocation signature: func(*literal_expr_args, session=<SessionContext>)
  func MUST accept a keyword argument named exactly `session`
  injected object is the calling SessionContext (isinstance check passes)
  positional literal args still arrive as raw expression objects
```

**Don’t-retain rule:** the injected session is loaned for the duration of the call. Do not store it on `self`, in module globals, in closures that outlive the invocation, or in the returned table provider. A retained session couples the provider to a context lifecycle it does not own, defeats context isolation (2.14/2.15), and can keep catalog state alive across tenant/session boundaries. Resolve what you need (provider handle, config values) inside the call and let `session` go.

Wrapper audit: any indirection layer that wraps `udtf(...)` or constructs `TableFunction(...)` positionally must be re-checked against the new keyword-only `with_session` parameter.

## 16.16 Pickling UDFs and expressions for spawn-based multiprocessing (new in 54)

DataFusion 54 makes most `Expr` values and decorator-defined aggregate/window UDFs picklable, enabling `multiprocessing` **spawn**-based workflows that ship expressions or UDF definitions to worker processes (the changelog lists UDAF/UDWF pickling; the boundaries below were live-verified against the installed wheel).

```python id="pkl54a"
import pickle
from datafusion import col, lit

expr = (col("a") + lit(1)).alias("b")
restored = pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(expr))   # works
```

Live-verified pickling matrix:

```text id="pkl54b"
Picklable:
  plain Expr trees (col/lit/operators/alias)                    -> yes
  Expr containing a scalar-UDF call (my_udf(col("x")))          -> yes
  UDAF defined via @udaf(...) decorator on Accumulator class    -> yes
  UDWF defined via @udwf(...) decorator on WindowEvaluator      -> yes

NOT picklable (TypeError: cannot pickle 'datafusion.…UDF' object):
  ScalarUDF object itself (udf(func, ...) result)               -> no
  UDAF built via factory call udaf(MyAccum, ...)                -> no
  UDWF built via factory call udwf(MyEvaluator, ...)            -> no
```

Rules for spawn-based parallelism:

```text id="pkl54c"
Define UDAF/UDWF with the decorator form at module scope so workers can
  re-import the defining module during unpickling.
Ship scalar UDFs as Exprs (my_udf(col("x"))), not as ScalarUDF objects.
Do not pickle registered SessionContext state; re-register in each worker.
Test pickle.dumps on the exact composition you ship — support is
  construction-path-sensitive, not type-universal.
```

[1]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/user-guide/common-operations/udf-and-udfa.html "User-Defined Functions — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"
[2]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/autoapi/datafusion/user_defined/index.html "datafusion.user_defined — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"
[3]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/autoapi/datafusion/context/index.html "datafusion.context — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"

# DataFusion Advanced — 17) Query plans, optimizer behavior, and explainability

This section follows the same dense, agent-facing technical-reference style as the Cyclopts source material. 

## 17.0 Version anchor

Current package anchor: **`datafusion==54.0.0`**. DataFusion 54.0.0’s release notes emphasize SQL lambdas and higher-order array functions, dynamic filter pushdown, statistics propagation, improved spilling (including memory-limited nested-loop joins), and Parquet execution work — plus EXPLAIN-visible display changes (lowered aggregate names, `count(1)` displayed as `count(*)`) — so plan text, optimizer behavior, and physical-plan shape should be treated as version-sensitive. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

```bash id="u2wf1o"
python -m pip install "datafusion==54.0.0"
```

```python id="c1lif0"
import datafusion

assert datafusion.__version__ == "54.0.0"
```

---

## 17.1 Core invariant: `DataFrame` is a logical-plan wrapper

`DataFrame` is not eager data; it is a lazily built plan handle. DataFusion’s library docs describe DataFrames as thin wrappers over `LogicalPlan`, adding plan-building and execution functionality, and the Python API exposes `logical_plan()`, `optimized_logical_plan()`, and `execution_plan()` for inspection. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

```text id="xa9tji"
SQL query text
  -> SQL planner
  -> LogicalPlan
  -> optimizer
  -> optimized LogicalPlan
  -> physical planner
  -> ExecutionPlan
  -> RecordBatch stream

DataFrame API calls
  -> Expr + DataFrame transforms
  -> LogicalPlan
  -> optimizer
  -> optimized LogicalPlan
  -> physical planner
  -> ExecutionPlan
  -> RecordBatch stream
```

```python id="s2jx74"
from datafusion import SessionContext, col, lit, functions as f

ctx = SessionContext()

df = (
    ctx.read_parquet("events.parquet")
    .filter(col("amount") > lit(0))
    .aggregate(
        [col("country")],
        [f.count_star().alias("n_rows"), f.sum(col("amount")).alias("gross_amount")],
    )
    .sort(col("gross_amount").sort(ascending=False))
    .limit(20)
)

# Plan handles; no result materialization here.
logical = df.logical_plan()
optimized = df.optimized_logical_plan()
physical = df.execution_plan()
```

---

## 17.2 Plan-stage taxonomy

| Stage                    | Python API                                     | Meaning                                                            | Stable enough for tests?                                             |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| unoptimized logical plan | `df.logical_plan()`                            | direct logical representation of SQL/DataFrame operations          | good for coarse semantic assertions                                  |
| optimized logical plan   | `df.optimized_logical_plan()`                  | logical plan after optimizer rewrites                              | useful but optimizer-version-sensitive                               |
| physical/execution plan  | `df.execution_plan()`                          | concrete executable operator tree using data layout/runtime config | most environment/version-sensitive                                   |
| explain output           | `df.explain(...)` / SQL `EXPLAIN ...`          | formatted logical/physical plan and optional runtime metrics       | useful for debugging; snapshot carefully                             |
| runtime metrics          | `df.explain(analyze=True)` / `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` | executed plan with operator metrics                                | performance diagnostics only; not deterministic across hardware/data |

DataFusion’s explain-usage guide distinguishes logical plans from physical plans: logical plans are generated from SQL/DataFrame/other frontends without underlying data-organization knowledge, while physical plans are generated with hardware configuration and data organization considered, so the same query can produce different physical plans on different hardware/configurations/data layouts. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

# 17.3 `DataFrame.explain(...)`

## 17.3.1 Signature

```python id="q1u97s"
df.explain(
    verbose: bool = False,
    analyze: bool = False,
    format: ExplainFormat | None = None,
) -> None
```

`DataFrame.explain(...)` prints an explanation of the DataFrame’s current plan. If `analyze=True`, it runs the plan and reports metrics. The DataFrame API documents `verbose`, `analyze`, and `format`, and says the DataFrame method defaults to `ExplainFormat.INDENT`. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

```python id="os8oxe"
df.explain()
df.explain(verbose=True)
df.explain(analyze=True)
```

---

## 17.3.2 Explain formats

```python id="yw4hih"
from datafusion import ExplainFormat

df.explain(format=ExplainFormat.INDENT)
df.explain(format=ExplainFormat.TREE)
df.explain(format=ExplainFormat.GRAPHVIZ)
df.explain(format=ExplainFormat.PGJSON)
```

`ExplainFormat` controls plan rendering and exposes `INDENT`, `TREE`, `GRAPHVIZ`, and `PGJSON`; `GRAPHVIZ` emits DOT-format graph output, `TREE` uses box-drawing visual format, `INDENT` is indented text, and `PGJSON` is PostgreSQL-compatible JSON for visualization tooling. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

```text id="wvruzu"
ExplainFormat.INDENT:
  default DataFrame.explain rendering
  compact text
  good for logs and tests

ExplainFormat.TREE:
  visual box-drawing tree
  good for human debugging
  harder for stable text snapshots

ExplainFormat.GRAPHVIZ:
  DOT graph output
  good for visual plan diagrams
  useful in docs and architecture review

ExplainFormat.PGJSON:
  JSON-compatible plan output
  good for visualization tooling
  potentially better for structured assertions
```

---

## 17.3.3 Runtime metrics with `analyze=True`

```python id="awblzp"
df.explain(analyze=True)
df.explain(analyze=True, format=ExplainFormat.TREE)
```

`analyze=True` executes the DataFrame and reports runtime metrics, so it is a terminal operation, not a passive inspection call. DataFusion’s SQL `EXPLAIN` reference likewise exposes `EXPLAIN [ANALYZE] [VERBOSE] [FORMAT format] statement`. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

```text id="kemodf"
explain(analyze=False):
  plan rendering only
  no query execution

explain(analyze=True):
  executes the query
  collects runtime/operator metrics
  may scan files, run joins, run aggregates, run UDFs
  use for performance diagnostics
```

Agent rule:

```text id="sfrxys"
Never call explain(analyze=True) inside validation-only or lint-only paths.
Use analyze=True only for benchmark/performance/debug workloads.
```

---

## 17.3.4 Verbose explain

```python id="aoc6w5"
df.explain(verbose=True)
```

SQL `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` shows more detailed output, but DataFusion’s SQL reference notes that verbose explain only supports the `indent` format. Treat DataFrame `verbose=True` as a developer-facing diagnostic output mode, not a stable public artifact. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

---

# 17.4 SQL `EXPLAIN`

## 17.4.1 Syntax

```sql id="li3hzj"
EXPLAIN [ANALYZE] [VERBOSE] [FORMAT format] statement
```

The SQL reference defines `EXPLAIN` as showing the logical and physical execution plan for a SQL statement and documents the optional `ANALYZE`, `VERBOSE`, and `FORMAT` clauses. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

```python id="4ch6li"
ctx.sql("""
    EXPLAIN FORMAT TREE
    SELECT country, count(*) AS n
    FROM events
    GROUP BY country
""").show()
```

```python id="a05fxe"
ctx.sql("""
    EXPLAIN ANALYZE
    SELECT country, count(*) AS n
    FROM events
    GROUP BY country
""").show()
```

## 17.4.2 SQL vs DataFrame explain

| Need                                           | Use                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| explain a DataFrame builder pipeline           | `df.explain(...)`                                                                    |
| explain raw SQL text                           | `ctx.sql("EXPLAIN ...").show()`                                                      |
| get runtime metrics for DataFrame              | `df.explain(analyze=True)`                                                           |
| get runtime metrics for SQL                    | `ctx.sql("EXPLAIN ANALYZE ...").show()`                                              |
| render DOT graph                               | `df.explain(format=ExplainFormat.GRAPHVIZ)` or SQL `FORMAT GRAPHVIZ` where supported |
| assert logical-plan internals programmatically | `df.logical_plan()` / `df.optimized_logical_plan()`                                  |

---

# 17.5 Plan object APIs

## 17.5.1 `df.logical_plan()`

```python id="8eqk3q"
lp = df.logical_plan()
print(lp.display())
print(lp.display_indent())
print(lp.display_indent_schema())
```

`DataFrame.logical_plan()` returns the unoptimized `LogicalPlan`. `LogicalPlan` is a node in a tree of relational operators such as projection or filter; it represents transforming an input relation into an output relation, and logical plans can be created by the SQL query planner, the DataFrame API, or programmatically. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

Available `LogicalPlan` methods:

```text id="ij9qve"
__repr__() -> str
display() -> str
display_indent() -> str
display_indent_schema() -> str
display_graphviz() -> str
inputs() -> list[LogicalPlan]
to_proto() -> bytes
from_proto(ctx, data: bytes) -> LogicalPlan
to_variant() -> Any
__eq__(other) -> bool
```

The Python plan API documents display methods, Graphviz DOT output, schema-indent output, `inputs()`, protobuf serialization/deserialization, equality, and variant conversion for `LogicalPlan`. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

---

## 17.5.2 `df.optimized_logical_plan()`

```python id="odc5lc"
olp = df.optimized_logical_plan()
print(olp.display_indent())
```

`DataFrame.optimized_logical_plan()` returns the optimized `LogicalPlan`; use it to verify logical rewrites such as projection pruning, predicate movement, rewritten limits, simplified expressions, and join/filter positioning. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

```python id="g5vz0i"
def assert_filter_reaches_scanish_area(df):
    text = df.optimized_logical_plan().display()
    assert "Filter" in text or "predicate=" in text
```

Agent rule:

```text id="jgttud"
Use optimized logical plans for semantic performance assertions.
Do not assert exact full text unless version-pinned.
```

---

## 17.5.3 `df.execution_plan()`

```python id="8j2f6l"
ep = df.execution_plan()

print(ep.display())
print(ep.display_indent())
print(ep.partition_count)
```

`DataFrame.execution_plan()` returns the execution/physical plan. `ExecutionPlan` represents nodes in the DataFusion physical plan, exposes child physical plans, display methods, protobuf serialization/deserialization, and `partition_count`. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

Available `ExecutionPlan` methods/properties:

```text id="n2a7g4"
__repr__() -> str
children() -> list[ExecutionPlan]
display() -> str
display_indent() -> str
to_proto() -> bytes
from_proto(ctx, data: bytes) -> ExecutionPlan
partition_count -> int
```

`ExecutionPlan.children()` returns an empty list for leaf nodes such as scans, a single child for unary nodes, or two children for binary nodes such as joins; `partition_count` returns the number of partitions in the physical plan. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

---

## 17.5.4 Plan-tree traversal helpers

```python id="x7psbg"
def walk_logical(plan, depth: int = 0):
    print("  " * depth + plan.display().splitlines()[0])
    for child in plan.inputs():
        walk_logical(child, depth + 1)


def walk_physical(plan, depth: int = 0):
    print("  " * depth + plan.display().splitlines()[0])
    for child in plan.children():
        walk_physical(child, depth + 1)
```

Use cases:

```text id="85krgv"
custom plan linting
operator inventory
debugging scan/join/aggregate nesting
coarse plan-shape tests
extension/plugin validation
```

---

# 17.6 Graphviz and visual plan output

## 17.6.1 Logical plan Graphviz

```python id="7gubpt"
dot = df.logical_plan().display_graphviz()
Path("logical_plan.dot").write_text(dot)
```

`LogicalPlan.display_graphviz()` prints graph visualization output in DOT format, intended for Graphviz-compatible visualization. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

## 17.6.2 Explain Graphviz

```python id="jv4qv6"
df.explain(format=ExplainFormat.GRAPHVIZ)
```

`ExplainFormat.GRAPHVIZ` is documented as Graphviz DOT format for graph rendering. ([Apache DataFusion][4])

## 17.6.3 Deployment rule

```text id="d6p64o"
Graphviz output:
  - useful in docs, incident reports, architecture review
  - not ideal for exact tests
  - can expose table names, paths, predicates, and literals
  - treat as diagnostic artifact; sanitize before sharing externally
```

---

# 17.7 Protobuf serialization

## 17.7.1 Logical plan protobuf

```python id="nyie3r"
lp = df.logical_plan()

blob: bytes = lp.to_proto()
lp2 = LogicalPlan.from_proto(ctx, blob)

assert lp == lp2
```

`LogicalPlan.to_proto()` converts a logical plan to protobuf bytes, and `LogicalPlan.from_proto(ctx, data)` reconstructs it; tables created in memory from record batches are currently not supported. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

## 17.7.2 Execution plan protobuf

```python id="z9xoux"
ep = df.execution_plan()

blob: bytes = ep.to_proto()
ep2 = ExecutionPlan.from_proto(ctx, blob)
```

`ExecutionPlan.to_proto()` converts a physical plan into protobuf bytes, and `ExecutionPlan.from_proto(ctx, data)` reconstructs it; record-batch in-memory tables are currently not supported. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

## 17.7.3 Serialization policy

```text id="wx0f22"
Use plan protobuf for:
  plan persistence experiments
  cross-process plan transport
  engine-extension tests
  logical-plan regression artifacts
  plan replay under same version/runtime/catalog

Avoid assuming:
  cross-version compatibility without tests
  support for in-memory record-batch tables
  portability across missing catalogs/table providers
  physical-plan equivalence across hardware/runtime configs
```

---

# 17.8 Executing plans explicitly

## 17.8.1 Execute logical plan

```python id="84bspo"
lp = df.logical_plan()

df2 = ctx.execute_logical_plan(lp)
batches = df2.collect()
```

`SessionContext.execute_logical_plan(plan)` executes a `LogicalPlan` and returns a `DataFrame`; the docs show retrieving a plan from `df.logical_plan()` and executing it through the context. ([Apache DataFusion][7])

## 17.8.2 Execute physical plan

```python id="7p9bcg"
ep = df.execution_plan()

stream = ctx.execute(ep, partitions=ep.partition_count)
for rb in stream:
    process(rb)
```

`SessionContext.execute(plan, partitions)` executes an `ExecutionPlan` and returns a `RecordBatchStream`. ([Apache DataFusion][7])

Agent rule:

```text id="7ha7mq"
Most agents should execute DataFrames, not raw plans.
Use raw plan execution for:
  custom planner pipelines
  serialization/replay experiments
  extension tests
  physical-plan diagnostics
```

---

# 17.9 Optimizer behavior surface

## 17.9.1 Config-driven optimizer behavior

DataFusion exposes many optimizer configuration keys. Examples include dynamic filter pushdown, join dynamic filter pushdown, top-k pushdown/repartitioning, window-limit and window-top-N optimizations, aggregate repartitioning, join reordering, hash-join preference, piecewise merge join, sort pushdown, and leaf-expression pushdown. The config reference also includes explain-related settings such as logical-only/physical-only explain output, show statistics, show partition sizes, show schema, explain format, and analyze metric categories. ([Apache DataFusion][8])

```python id="jad5zg"
from datafusion import SessionConfig, SessionContext

config = (
    SessionConfig()
    .with_target_partitions(8)
    .set("datafusion.optimizer.join_reordering", "true")
    .set("datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join", "true")
    .set("datafusion.optimizer.enable_dynamic_filter_pushdown", "true")
    .set("datafusion.explain.show_statistics", "true")
    .set("datafusion.explain.show_schema", "true")
    .set("datafusion.explain.format", "indent")
)

ctx = SessionContext(config=config)
```

Important config examples:

```text id="8z8o58"
datafusion.optimizer.max_passes:
  number of optimizer passes

datafusion.optimizer.join_reordering:
  statistics-driven join input reordering

datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join:
  prefer HashJoin over SortMergeJoin; faster but memory-sensitive

datafusion.optimizer.enable_dynamic_filter_pushdown:
  push dynamic filters generated by TopK, Join, Aggregate into scans

datafusion.optimizer.enable_window_topn:
  can replace Filter(rn<=K) -> Window(ROW_NUMBER) -> Sort with PartitionedTopKExec;
  docs warn high-cardinality keys may regress memory/runtime

datafusion.explain.analyze_level:
  summary vs dev-level runtime metric detail

datafusion.explain.analyze_categories:
  rows / bytes / timing / uncategorized / none / all
```

The configuration docs explicitly describe these behaviors and warnings, including the high-cardinality caveat for `enable_window_topn` and memory tradeoff for hash joins. ([Apache DataFusion][8])

---

## 17.9.2 Removing optimizer rules

```python id="ky3v76"
removed = ctx.remove_optimizer_rule("rule_name")
assert isinstance(removed, bool)
```

`SessionContext.remove_optimizer_rule(name)` removes an optimizer rule by name and returns `True` if a rule with that name was found and removed; the API example shows removing a nonexistent rule returns `False`. ([Apache DataFusion][7])

```python id="dz4k58"
if not ctx.remove_optimizer_rule("nonexistent_rule"):
    print("rule not found")
```

Agent use cases:

```text id="j90326"
optimizer regression isolation
debugging unexpected rewrites
benchmarking a rule's impact
extension compatibility testing
reproducing bug reports
```

Agent rules:

```text id="h1bg3r"
Do not remove optimizer rules in production by default.
Gate rule removal behind explicit debug/config flags.
Record removed-rule names in logs/test metadata.
Add plan snapshots before/after removal.
```

---

# 17.10 Explain-reading heuristics

DataFusion’s explain-usage guide says query plans are trees read from bottom to top; the bottom nodes are inputs/scans, and upper nodes consume those inputs. It also states that understanding a query plan can reveal performance causes, such as too many files being read, but tuning depends on why the plan is slow. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

```text id="qa7zfy"
Read physical plans bottom-up:
  DataSourceExec / scan nodes
    -> filters / projections / repartitions
    -> joins / aggregates / windows / sorts
    -> projection / limit / final sink
```

Look for:

```text id="xvyu8q"
scan:
  file_groups
  projection columns
  predicates
  pruning hints
  number of files/partitions

filter:
  pushed into scan or applied after scan

projection:
  unnecessary columns removed early?

join:
  join type
  hash vs sort-merge shape
  build/probe side
  repartitioning

aggregate:
  partial/final aggregate split
  repartition by group keys

sort/top-k:
  sort with fetch vs full sort
  limit pushed down?

window:
  sort/repartition requirements
  frame complexity
```

---

# 17.11 Performance diagnostics workflow

## 17.11.1 Static plan triage

```python id="ko92pb"
print("UNOPTIMIZED LOGICAL")
print(df.logical_plan().display_indent())

print("OPTIMIZED LOGICAL")
print(df.optimized_logical_plan().display_indent())

print("PHYSICAL")
print(df.execution_plan().display_indent())
```

Use when:

```text id="0h0zym"
query fails
optimizer rewrite looks suspicious
projection/filter pushdown is missing
join type/shape is unexpected
physical partitioning is unexpected
```

## 17.11.2 Runtime metrics

```python id="iqssvo"
df.explain(analyze=True, format=ExplainFormat.INDENT)
```

Use when:

```text id="3phpox"
query is slow
operator row counts are needed
operator timing is needed
bytes/rows/timing categories matter
file scan behavior must be verified
```

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` can be tuned via `datafusion.explain.analyze_level` and `datafusion.explain.analyze_categories`; config docs describe `summary` vs `dev` and metric categories such as rows, bytes, timing, uncategorized, none, and all. ([Apache DataFusion][8])

# 17.12 Regression testing strategy

## 17.12.1 Coarse logical-plan assertions

```python id="wg9wba"
def test_plan_has_filter_and_projection(ctx):
    df = (
        ctx.read_parquet("events.parquet")
        .select("user_id", "amount")
        .filter(col("amount") > lit(0))
    )

    plan = df.optimized_logical_plan().display()

    assert "Projection" in plan
    assert "Filter" in plan or "predicate=" in plan
```

## 17.12.2 Exact snapshots only under strict version pinning

```python id="rfc63o"
def test_optimized_plan_snapshot(ctx, snapshot):
    import datafusion
    assert datafusion.__version__ == "54.0.0"

    plan = df.optimized_logical_plan().display_indent()
    snapshot.assert_match(plan, "optimized_plan_53_0_0.txt")
```

Agent rule:

```text id="6xn69n"
Exact plan snapshots:
  require datafusion version pin
  require config pin
  require source schema/path layout pin
  require explain format pin
  should be updated deliberately during DataFusion upgrades
```

## 17.12.3 Physical plan snapshots: higher sensitivity

```python id="9xuo6b"
def test_physical_plan_shape(ctx):
    ep = df.execution_plan()
    text = ep.display_indent()

    assert ep.partition_count >= 1
    assert "Exec" in text
```

Physical plans are sensitive to hardware configuration and data organization; DataFusion’s docs explicitly say the same query may generate different physical plans across hardware/config/data. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

# 17.13 Plan serialization tests

```python id="wzl64t"
from datafusion.plan import LogicalPlan

def test_logical_plan_proto_roundtrip(ctx):
    df = ctx.read_parquet("events.parquet").select("user_id")

    lp = df.logical_plan()
    blob = lp.to_proto()

    lp2 = LogicalPlan.from_proto(ctx, blob)

    assert lp == lp2
```

Caveat: `LogicalPlan.to_proto()` / `from_proto()` currently do not support tables created in memory from record batches, per the plan API docs. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

# 17.14 Explain artifact capture

```python id="zt2q6e"
from contextlib import redirect_stdout
from io import StringIO
from datafusion import ExplainFormat

def capture_explain(df, *, analyze: bool = False, format=ExplainFormat.INDENT) -> str:
    buf = StringIO()
    with redirect_stdout(buf):
        df.explain(analyze=analyze, format=format)
    return buf.getvalue()
```

Use cases:

```text id="ccxv20"
test snapshot
debug log attachment
performance report
benchmark artifact
CI upgrade diff
```

Security rule:

```text id="04kjez"
Explain output may include:
  table names
  file paths
  predicates
  literal values
  UDF names
  object-store URI fragments

Sanitize before external sharing.
```

# 17.15 Optimizer customization pattern

```python id="issadh"
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OptimizerDebugConfig:
    remove_rules: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    show_plans: bool = False


def apply_optimizer_debug(ctx: SessionContext, cfg: OptimizerDebugConfig) -> None:
    for rule_name in cfg.remove_rules:
        removed = ctx.remove_optimizer_rule(rule_name)
        if not removed:
            raise ValueError(f"Optimizer rule not found: {rule_name}")
```

Use:

```python id="iafww9"
ctx = SessionContext()
apply_optimizer_debug(
    ctx,
    OptimizerDebugConfig(remove_rules=("some_rule_name",)),
)
```

Deployment rule:

```text id="qq6lsp"
Only enable optimizer-rule removal in:
  regression tests
  targeted debug sessions
  benchmark variants
  bug reproduction harnesses
```
