# 22.9 Optimized-plan unparsing caution

Unparsing an optimized plan may expose optimizer-generated shapes that are less readable or less portable than user-authored SQL. The Rust `plan_to_sql` documentation explicitly states conversion can fail when a plan cannot be converted to SQL. Additionally, recent DataFusion issue reports around the unparser show dialect-specific and expression-specific bugs can occur, so production agents should treat unparser output as a generated artifact requiring validation rather than a proof of universal SQL portability. ([Docs.rs][2])

```python id="41ic1j"
sql = Unparser(Dialect.postgres()).plan_to_sql(df.optimized_logical_plan())
```

Safer lineage default:

```python id="q6gsvi"
sql = Unparser(Dialect.postgres()).plan_to_sql(df.logical_plan())
```

Agent policy:

```text id="qfgq5g"
Use logical_plan() for lineage.
Use optimized_logical_plan() only for optimizer-debug SQL experiments.
Always validate optimized-plan unparse output before target-engine execution.
```

---

# 22.10 Parameterization caveat

The unparser outputs SQL text; it does not preserve Python-side `param_values` objects or `named_params` semantics. DataFusion’s SQL parameter docs state that named `$name` replacement converts Python objects to strings, DataFrame parameters are temporary views, and `param_values` substitutes scalar objects after parsing; those are Python API invocation semantics, not necessarily recoverable from a logical plan unparse. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

```python id="ncxef8"
df = ctx.sql(
    "SELECT * FROM events WHERE amount > $min_amount",
    param_values={"min_amount": 100.123456789},
)

sql = Unparser(Dialect.default()).plan_to_sql(df.logical_plan())
```

Policy:

```text id="o5mpv9"
Do not assume unparsed SQL remains parameterized.
For lineage:
  record original parameterized SQL + param_values separately.

For pushdown:
  build parameterized target SQL explicitly,
  or validate literal-rendered SQL carefully.
```

Lineage envelope:

```python id="66vjbf"
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SQLLineageEnvelope:
    source_sql: str | None
    param_values: dict | None
    unparsed_sql: str
    dialect: str
    plan_stage: str  # logical | optimized
```

---

# 22.11 Relationship to SQL parser and dialects

DataFusion’s SQL parser supports dialect-specific behavior through session configuration, and its parameter docs explicitly mention dialect limitations for named placeholders in `hive` and `mysql`. The unparser dialect controls emitted SQL style, while parser dialect controls how incoming SQL is interpreted. These are related but separate concerns. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

```text id="u1a5qn"
Parser dialect:
  SQL text -> LogicalPlan

Unparser dialect:
  LogicalPlan -> SQL text
```

Agent rule:

```text id="p07lbc"
Document both:
  source parser dialect
  target unparser dialect

Do not assume:
  parser dialect == unparser dialect
  unparsed SQL can be parsed by every target engine
```

---

# 22.12 Generated-code patterns

## 22.12.1 Unparser factory

```python id="v1tnvm"
from datafusion.unparser import Dialect, Unparser


def make_dialect(name: str) -> Dialect:
    if name == "default":
        return Dialect.default()
    if name == "duckdb":
        return Dialect.duckdb()
    if name == "mysql":
        return Dialect.mysql()
    if name in {"postgres", "postgresql"}:
        return Dialect.postgres()
    if name == "sqlite":
        return Dialect.sqlite()
    raise ValueError(f"Unsupported unparser dialect: {name}")


def unparse_plan(plan, *, dialect_name: str = "default", pretty: bool = True) -> str:
    return (
        Unparser(make_dialect(dialect_name))
        .with_pretty(pretty)
        .plan_to_sql(plan)
    )
```

---

## 22.12.2 DataFrame lineage helper

```python id="tmutoy"
def dataframe_to_sql(
    df,
    *,
    dialect_name: str = "default",
    pretty: bool = True,
    optimized: bool = False,
) -> str:
    plan = df.optimized_logical_plan() if optimized else df.logical_plan()
    return unparse_plan(plan, dialect_name=dialect_name, pretty=pretty)
```

---

## 22.12.3 Multi-dialect artifact helper

```python id="jm1gh4"
def dataframe_sql_artifacts(df, *, pretty: bool = True) -> dict[str, str]:
    plan = df.logical_plan()
    artifacts = {}

    for dialect_name in ["default", "duckdb", "mysql", "postgres", "sqlite"]:
        try:
            artifacts[dialect_name] = unparse_plan(
                plan,
                dialect_name=dialect_name,
                pretty=pretty,
            )
        except Exception as exc:
            artifacts[dialect_name] = f"-- UNPARSE_FAILED: {exc}"

    return artifacts
```

---

## 22.12.4 Lineage artifact writer

```python id="0pux3j"
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from pathlib import Path
import datafusion
import hashlib
import json


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class UnparseArtifact:
    datafusion_version: str
    dialect: str
    pretty: bool
    plan_stage: str
    sql: str
    sql_sha256: str


def make_unparse_artifact(df, *, dialect_name: str, pretty: bool, optimized: bool) -> UnparseArtifact:
    sql = dataframe_to_sql(
        df,
        dialect_name=dialect_name,
        pretty=pretty,
        optimized=optimized,
    )

    return UnparseArtifact(
        datafusion_version=datafusion.__version__,
        dialect=dialect_name,
        pretty=pretty,
        plan_stage="optimized" if optimized else "logical",
        sql=sql,
        sql_sha256=hashlib.sha256(sql.encode()).hexdigest(),
    )


def write_unparse_artifact(path: str | Path, artifact: UnparseArtifact) -> None:
    Path(path).write_text(json.dumps(asdict(artifact), indent=2, sort_keys=True))
```

# 22.15 Limitations and risk policy

```text id="wpit1g"
Unparser can fail:
  not every LogicalPlan can be converted to SQL
  unsupported expressions/functions may fail
  optimized plans may contain harder-to-render shapes
  dialect-specific rendering bugs can exist
  target engine may not support emitted SQL

Unparser output can differ:
  from source SQL text
  across DataFusion versions
  across dialects
  between logical and optimized plans
  after optimizer rewrites
```

Rust `plan_to_sql` explicitly returns an error if the plan cannot be converted to SQL. Recent issue reports also show specific unparser edge cases can exist around dialects and expressions; for example, PostgreSQL dialect unparsing after optimization and `IS DISTINCT FROM` support have active bug reports as of 2026. ([Docs.rs][2])

Deployment rule:

```text id="7fhh1p"
Treat unparsed SQL as generated code:
  validate
  test
  snapshot with version
  do not assume universal target-engine compatibility
```

---

# 22.16 Security and governance

```text id="8tjm0h"
Unparsed SQL may expose:
  table names
  catalog/schema names
  column names
  literal values
  predicates
  file/table-provider naming conventions
  business logic in CASE/filter expressions
```

Policy:

```text id="fgaq6r"
Before external sharing:
  redact sensitive identifiers
  redact literal values
  classify lineage artifacts
  store hashes for identity
  restrict dialect artifacts to approved audiences
```

Unparsed SQL should not be used as an injection-safety layer. It is SQL text produced from a plan, but if it is sent to a remote engine, that engine executes it as code.

---

# 22.17 Anti-pattern catalog

## Anti-pattern: assuming unparsed SQL equals original SQL

```python id="lc9gvx"
source_sql = "SELECT * FROM events WHERE amount > 0"
df = ctx.sql(source_sql)
assert Unparser(Dialect.default()).plan_to_sql(df.logical_plan()) == source_sql
```

Correct:

```text id="gi95pu"
Unparser emits semantically reconstructed SQL.
It may normalize identifiers, projections, aliases, nesting, and formatting.
Compare outputs/results, not original SQL strings.
```

---

## Anti-pattern: unparse optimized plan for user-facing lineage

```python id="q0dghb"
sql = Unparser(Dialect.default()).plan_to_sql(df.optimized_logical_plan())
```

Safer:

```python id="ntfm8n"
sql = Unparser(Dialect.default()).plan_to_sql(df.logical_plan())
```

---

## Anti-pattern: pushing unparsed SQL to remote engine without validation

```python id="17gn0x"
remote.execute(Unparser(Dialect.postgres()).plan_to_sql(df.logical_plan()))
```

Correct:

```text id="qg2r8z"
Validate:
  parse in target engine
  execute on fixture data
  compare result with DataFusion output
  record unsupported functions/datatypes/dialect issues
```

---

## Anti-pattern: direct `Dialect(...)` construction

```python id="4fxpd2"
dialect = Dialect(...)
```

Correct:

```python id="3d076r"
dialect = Dialect.default()
dialect = Dialect.duckdb()
dialect = Dialect.mysql()
dialect = Dialect.postgres()
dialect = Dialect.sqlite()
```

The `Dialect` constructor is documented as not typically called by end users; use static factories. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## Anti-pattern: losing original parameter bindings

```python id="2o758v"
df = ctx.sql("SELECT * FROM t WHERE x > $x", param_values={"x": 1.234})
sql = Unparser(Dialect.default()).plan_to_sql(df.logical_plan())
# param_values are no longer a separate binding artifact.
```

Correct:

```text id="n8n579"
Store:
  original SQL
  param_values
  unparsed SQL
  logical plan hash
```

DataFusion’s SQL docs distinguish string parameter replacement, DataFrame temporary views, and `param_values` scalar substitution; those invocation details are not equivalent to a standalone unparsed SQL string. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

```text id="tsp6i5"
Construction:
  [ ] Import Dialect and Unparser from datafusion.unparser.
  [ ] Use Dialect.default/duckdb/mysql/postgres/sqlite factories.
  [ ] Construct Unparser(dialect).
  [ ] Use with_pretty(True) for human artifacts.

  [ ] Store dialect.
  [ ] Store pretty flag.
  [ ] Store source SQL and params if available.
  [ ] Store unparsed SQL hash.
  [ ] Store table/schema contracts.

Testing:
  [ ] Smoke-test plan_to_sql.

  [ ] Matrix-test dialect emission.
  [ ] Snapshot under version pin.
  [ ] External-engine test for pushdown dialects.

Security:
```

## 22.19 Section compression for LLM agents

```text id="d5206y"
Purpose:
  datafusion.unparser converts LogicalPlan -> SQL string.

Imports:
  from datafusion.unparser import Dialect, Unparser

Dialects:
  Dialect.default()
  Dialect.duckdb()
  Dialect.mysql()
  Dialect.postgres()
  Dialect.sqlite()

Core API:
  unparser = Unparser(Dialect.default())
  sql = unparser.plan_to_sql(df.logical_plan())

Pretty:
  sql = Unparser(Dialect.default()).with_pretty(True).plan_to_sql(plan)

Plan source:
  df.logical_plan()           -> preferred for lineage/user-facing SQL
  df.optimized_logical_plan() -> optimizer-debug only; more version-sensitive

Use cases:
  query lineage
  SQL generation from DataFrame API pipelines
  cross-dialect compatibility checks
  generated-query audit artifacts
  remote-engine pushdown experiments

Caveats:
  unparsed SQL may differ from original SQL
  conversion can fail if plan cannot be represented as SQL
  dialect output must be validated against target engine
  parameter bindings are not preserved as Python param_values
  optimized-plan unparsing can expose hard-to-render optimizer shapes
  snapshots are DataFusion-version-sensitive

Generated-code defaults:
  use static Dialect factories
  use pretty=True for human artifacts
  store DataFusion version + dialect + plan stage + hash
  validate by parse/execute roundtrip on fixture data
  never push unparsed SQL to remote engine without target-engine validation
```

# DataFusion Advanced — 23) Custom table providers and Python/Rust extension points

This section follows the same dense, agent-facing technical-reference style as the Cyclopts source material. 

## 23.0 Core extension invariant

A **custom table provider** makes a non-built-in data source queryable by DataFusion as a normal table. DataFusion’s official Python custom-provider path is: implement a Rust `TableProvider`, expose it to Python through PyO3 as an `FFI_TableProvider` inside a `PyCapsule`, then register that Python object with `SessionContext.register_table(...)`. DataFusion Python custom table providers require **DataFusion 43.0.0 or later**. ([datafusion.apache.org][1])

```text id="0an0f2"
external data source
  -> Rust TableProvider
  -> FFI_TableProvider
  -> PyCapsule
  -> Python object with __datafusion_table_provider__
  -> ctx.register_table("name", provider)
  -> ctx.table("name") / SQL SELECT * FROM name
```

```python id="qrib4w"
from datafusion import SessionContext

ctx = SessionContext()

provider = MyTableProvider(...)          # Python object backed by Rust provider / PyCapsule export
ctx.register_table("custom_source", provider)

df = ctx.table("custom_source")
df.show()
```

---

## 23.1 Object model map

| Layer                     | Implementation language | DataFusion role                                          | Required output                                 |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Python package facade     | Python + PyO3 module    | user imports/configures provider object                  | Python object                                   |
| provider bridge           | PyO3/Rust               | exposes provider through `__datafusion_table_provider__` | `PyCapsule`                                     |
| `TableProvider`           | Rust                    | queryable table abstraction                              | `ExecutionPlan` from `scan(...)`                |
| `ExecutionPlan`           | Rust                    | physical operator node                                   | `SendableRecordBatchStream` from `execute(...)` |
| stream                    | Rust async stream       | actual data production                                   | Arrow `RecordBatch` stream                      |
| DataFusion Python context | Python binding          | table registration and query execution                   | `ctx.register_table(...)`                       |

The DataFusion custom-provider guide describes the full path as `TableProvider + ExecutionPlan + stream`: `TableProvider::scan()` returns an `ExecutionPlan`; `ExecutionPlan::execute()` returns a `SendableRecordBatchStream`; and the stream produces data during execution. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

---

## 23.2 Registration surface: `ctx.register_table(...)`

### Signature

```python id="0kg1tw"
ctx.register_table(
    name: str,
    table: datafusion.catalog.Table
         | datafusion.context.TableProviderExportable
         | datafusion.DataFrame
         | pyarrow.dataset.Dataset,
) -> None
```

`SessionContext.register_table(...)` registers any object convertible into a DataFusion `Table`; the registered table can be referenced from SQL executed against that same context. The older `register_table_provider(...)` API is deprecated in favor of `register_table(...)`. ([datafusion.apache.org][3])

```python id="i6ig1g"
ctx.register_table("capsule_table", provider)

ctx.sql("SELECT * FROM capsule_table LIMIT 10").show()
ctx.table("capsule_table").show()
```

Accepted registration objects:

```text id="1k6fsm"
datafusion.catalog.Table
object with __datafusion_table_provider__ PyCapsule protocol
datafusion.DataFrame      -> registered as view-like table
pyarrow.dataset.Dataset   -> registered as dataset-backed table
```

The `datafusion.catalog.Table` API states that it can wrap built-in DataFusion tables such as CSV/Parquet, PyArrow datasets, DataFusion DataFrames converted into views, and externally provided tables implemented with the FFI PyCapsule interface. ([datafusion.apache.org][4])

---

## 23.3 Python protocol: `__datafusion_table_provider__`

The current Python type hint `TableProviderExportable` is a protocol for objects that expose a `__datafusion_table_provider__` PyCapsule. The API reference shows the method shape as `__datafusion_table_provider__(session: Any) -> object`; the custom-provider guide’s Rust/PyO3 example shows a method returning a `PyCapsule` containing `FFI_TableProvider`. Treat the method as the Python-visible ABI hook that DataFusion Python calls to obtain the Rust provider. ([datafusion.apache.org][3])

```python id="lcsigw"
class TableProviderExportableProtocol:
    def __datafusion_table_provider__(self, session) -> object:
        """Return PyCapsule wrapping FFI_TableProvider."""
        ...
```

Agent rule:

```text id="9h3kwv"
Do not fake this protocol with a pure Python object returning arbitrary data.
The returned object must be the expected PyCapsule/FFI provider payload.
```

---

## 23.4 Rust/PyO3 export skeleton

The official custom-provider guide shows a PyO3 method that creates a capsule named `datafusion_table_provider`, wraps `self.clone()` in `Arc`, builds `FFI_TableProvider::new(...)`, and returns a `PyCapsule`. ([datafusion.apache.org][1])

```rust id="yg8b22"
#[pymethods]
impl MyTableProvider {
    fn __datafusion_table_provider__<'py>(
        &self,
        py: Python<'py>,
    ) -> PyResult<Bound<'py, PyCapsule>> {
        let name = cr"datafusion_table_provider".into();

        let provider = Arc::new(self.clone());
        let provider = FFI_TableProvider::new(provider, false, None);

        PyCapsule::new_bound(py, provider, Some(name.clone()))
    }
}
```

Python use:

```python id="3p0bqo"
from datafusion import SessionContext
from my_provider_package import MyTableProvider

ctx = SessionContext()

provider = MyTableProvider(...)
ctx.register_table("my_table", provider)

ctx.table("my_table").show()
```

---

# 23.5 Rust `TableProvider` contract

## 23.5.1 Minimal provider methods

A minimal read-only Rust `TableProvider` needs `schema()`, `table_type()`, and async `scan(...)`. The `scan(...)` method receives the optimizer’s pushdown hints: `projection`, `filters`, and `limit`, and returns an `ExecutionPlan`. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

```rust id="2wnwbo"
#[async_trait::async_trait]
impl TableProvider for MyTable {
    fn schema(&self) -> SchemaRef {
        Arc::clone(&self.schema)
    }

    fn table_type(&self) -> TableType {
        TableType::Base
    }

    async fn scan(
        &self,
        state: &dyn Session,
        projection: Option<&Vec<usize>>,
        filters: &[Expr],
        limit: Option<usize>,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        Ok(Arc::new(MyExecPlan::new(
            Arc::clone(&self.schema),
            projection,
            filters,
            limit,
        )))
    }
}
```

### Pushdown hints

```text id="4zp2kr"
projection:
  needed column indexes
  use to reduce output width

filters:
  predicates DataFusion would like source to apply
  use to skip files/partitions/row groups/remote records when source can do better

limit:
  row-count cap
  use to stop source reads early when possible
```

The custom-provider guide says `projection` reduces width, `filters` reduce rows, and `limit` can avoid unnecessary work if the source can stop early. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

---

## 23.5.2 Keep `scan()` lightweight

`scan()` runs during planning, not execution; it should describe how data will be produced, not produce the data. The official guide warns against I/O, network calls, or heavy computation in `scan()`, because planning can become slow, blocked, or deadlocked across multi-table/subquery plans. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

```text id="0rflaj"
scan() should:
  validate projection/filter/limit
  construct ExecutionPlan metadata
  decide partition pruning from cheap metadata
  return quickly

scan() should not:
  open long-lived network connections
  fetch full remote pages
  read files
  materialize RecordBatches
  block on slow async operations
```

---

# 23.6 Rust `ExecutionPlan` contract

## 23.6.1 Minimal execution-plan methods

An `ExecutionPlan` is a physical-plan node. The custom-provider guide lists required methods such as `name()`, `properties()`, `children()`, `with_new_children(...)`, and `execute(partition, context)`, with `execute(...)` returning a `SendableRecordBatchStream`. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

```rust id="qtv0gt"
impl ExecutionPlan for MyExecPlan {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "MyExecPlan"
    }

    fn properties(&self) -> &Arc<PlanProperties> {
        &self.properties
    }

    fn children(&self) -> Vec<&Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        vec![]
    }

    fn with_new_children(
        self: Arc<Self>,
        children: Vec<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>>,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        assert!(children.is_empty());
        Ok(self)
    }

    fn execute(
        &self,
        partition: usize,
        context: Arc<TaskContext>,
    ) -> Result<SendableRecordBatchStream> {
        // Return stream; actual data production happens when stream is polled.
        ...
    }
}
```

## 23.6.2 Plan properties

```text id="f36upf"
ExecutionPlan properties to get right:
  output partitioning
  output ordering
  schema
  equivalence properties
```

The guide emphasizes output partitioning and output ordering: partitioning determines parallelism, and correct output-ordering declarations can let the optimizer avoid unnecessary `SortExec` operators. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

---

## 23.6.3 Keep `execute()` lightweight

`execute()` is called once per partition and should construct/return a stream without doing heavy blocking work; actual data production belongs in the stream polling layer. The guide explicitly says not to block on async operations inside `execute()`. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

```text id="g2y7ls"
execute() should:
  map partition id -> source shard/range/file set
  construct RecordBatch stream
  set up channels or stream factory
  return quickly

execute() should not:
  synchronously read all rows
  block on network pages
  materialize full partition
  perform CPU-heavy transformation eagerly
```

---

# 23.7 Stream layer: where real data production belongs

```text id="wjx7eo"
Layer 1: TableProvider::scan()
  runs during planning
  builds ExecutionPlan

Layer 2: ExecutionPlan::execute()
  runs during execution, once per partition
  builds stream

Layer 3: RecordBatchStream polling
  performs I/O
  performs compute / decoding
  yields RecordBatch values
```

The DataFusion custom-provider guide summarizes this separation directly: `scan()` should build execution metadata, `execute()` should construct the stream, and the `RecordBatchStream` polling layer should perform I/O, computation, and data production. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

---

# 23.8 Filter pushdown contract

## 23.8.1 `supports_filters_pushdown(...)`

A provider can implement `supports_filters_pushdown(...)` to tell DataFusion which filters it can evaluate at the source. The official guide defines three responses: `Exact`, `Inexact`, and `Unsupported`. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

```rust id="sb6edc"
fn supports_filters_pushdown(
    &self,
    filters: &[&Expr],
) -> Result<Vec<TableProviderFilterPushDown>> {
    Ok(filters.iter().map(|f| {
        match f {
            Expr::BinaryExpr(BinaryExpr { left, op: Operator::Eq, right })
                if is_partition_column(left) || is_partition_column(right) =>
            {
                TableProviderFilterPushDown::Exact
            }
            _ => TableProviderFilterPushDown::Unsupported,
        }
    }).collect())
}
```

### Pushdown response semantics

```text id="j5sqtc"
Exact:
  source guarantees output already satisfies predicate
  DataFusion does not add FilterExec for that predicate

Inexact:
  source reduces data but may still emit nonmatching rows
  DataFusion keeps FilterExec above scan

Unsupported:
  source ignores predicate
  DataFusion handles filtering
```

The guide explains these exact meanings and warns that pushdown should be implemented only when the data source can do strictly better than DataFusion’s in-memory vectorized filter, typically by eliminating I/O such as skipping files, partitions, or row groups. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

---

## 23.8.2 Pushdown value case

```text id="7qu3hr"
Source-level pruning can skip:
  remote API pages
  database shards
  object-store prefixes
  files
  partitions
  row groups
  key ranges
  time ranges
```

The guide’s example describes a billion-row table partitioned by `region`; by pushing `region = 'us-east-1'` into the scan, the provider can skip unrelated partitions and avoid most I/O before DataFusion applies any remaining filters. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

---

# 23.9 Projection and limit pushdown

```text id="9i6t7p"
Projection pushdown:
  read only required columns
  reduce network payload
  reduce decode work
  reduce Arrow batch width

Limit pushdown:
  stop source reads early
  avoid unnecessary pages/files
  useful for preview/top-k/table sampling
```

`scan(...)` receives `projection` and `limit` in addition to `filters`, and the guide describes both as pushdown hints that reduce source work. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

Agent rule:

```text id="s011px"
Custom providers should handle projection and limit before adding exotic features.
Projection + filter + limit pushdown define the minimum production-grade scan contract.
```

---

# 23.10 Partitioning and parallelism

`ExecutionPlan::execute()` is called once per partition, and each partition produces an independent stream scheduled by DataFusion’s Tokio runtime. The guide recommends starting by matching the source’s natural layout: one file per partition, one shard per partition, or one key range per partition; it also warns that too many partitions add scheduling overhead and may require downstream repartitioning. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

```text id="z0ygpw"
Natural partition strategies:
  file/object -> partition
  database shard -> partition
  region -> partition
  key range -> partition
  time range -> partition
```

Advanced partitioning policy:

```text id="8qi6hk"
If source naturally matches target_partitions:
  optimizer less likely to insert RepartitionExec

If source declares Hash([key], N):
  downstream group-by/join on same key may avoid repartition

If source declares UnknownPartitioning:
  DataFusion must assume worst case and may insert repartition operators
```

The custom-provider guide explicitly discusses `target_partitions`, hash partitioning, and avoiding unnecessary `RepartitionExec` by exposing correct output partitioning. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

---

# 23.11 Output ordering

```text id="abchv3"
Output ordering:
  declare only if source is actually sorted
  can avoid downstream SortExec
  useful for time-series, range-partitioned, sorted-object, indexed-source data
```

The guide states that declaring natural output ordering lets the optimizer avoid inserting `SortExec` when a query requires ordered data, but correctness depends on accurately reporting source ordering. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

Agent rule:

```text id="z1h8vf"
Never lie about ordering.
Wrong ordering metadata can produce incorrect query results or missing sorts.
```

---

# 23.12 Existing implementations to study

The DataFusion guide recommends several built-in providers as references: `MemTable`, `StreamTable`, `ListingTable`, and `ViewTable`. `ListingTable` is the file-based source behind Parquet, CSV, and JSON support and demonstrates filter/projection pushdown, file pruning, and schema inference. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

```text id="3t56y5"
MemTable:
  in-memory Vec<RecordBatch>
  tests and small datasets

StreamTable:
  stream factory
  continuous or external streams

ListingTable:
  files/object-store sources
  file pruning
  schema inference
  filter/projection pushdown

ViewTable:
  wraps a logical plan
  SQL view-like provider
```

---

# 23.13 Table provider factories for SQL DDL

## 23.13.1 `ctx.register_table_factory(...)`

### Signature

```python id="kfc7lz"
ctx.register_table_factory(
    format: str,
    factory: datafusion.catalog.TableProviderFactory
           | datafusion.catalog.TableProviderFactoryExportable,
) -> None
```

`register_table_factory(...)` registers a table-provider factory that can be referenced by SQL DDL statements executed against the context. The `format` parameter becomes the value used in the `STORED AS ${format}` clause; the factory is a PyCapsule implementing `TableProviderFactoryExportable`. ([datafusion.apache.org][3])

```python id="9nhk01"
ctx.register_table_factory("MYFORMAT", my_factory)

ctx.sql("""
    CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE my_source
    STORED AS MYFORMAT
    LOCATION 'custom://resource/path'
""").collect()
```

## 23.13.2 Factory use cases

```text id="rg452a"
Use table provider factory when:
  SQL DDL should create provider-backed tables
  custom STORED AS format is needed
  plugin wants SQL-first registration
  users should create tables without Python registration calls

Use direct ctx.register_table when:
  Python bootstrap owns provider construction
  provider requires Python-side credentials/config objects
  table names are static deployment config
```

---

# 23.14 Data source integration patterns

## 23.14.1 Direct provider registration

```python id="c2rqxc"
provider = MyTableProvider(config)
ctx.register_table("external_events", provider)

df = ctx.sql("""
    SELECT count(*) AS n
    FROM external_events
    WHERE dt >= '2026-01-01'
""")
```

Use when:

```text id="ykx883"
application bootstrap owns provider config
credentials come from Python deployment layer
table name is fixed
schema is known at registration time
```

---

## 23.14.2 Catalog/schema registration

```python id="vu5peq"
from datafusion.catalog import Catalog, Schema

catalog = Catalog.memory_catalog(ctx)
schema = Schema.memory_schema(ctx)

schema.register_table("external_events", provider)
catalog.register_schema("analytics", schema)
ctx.register_catalog_provider("company", catalog)

ctx.sql("""
    SELECT *
    FROM company.analytics.external_events
""").show()
```

`Schema.register_table(...)` accepts `Table`, `TableProviderExportable`, `DataFrame`, or `pyarrow.dataset.Dataset`, and `SessionContext.register_catalog_provider(...)` attaches a catalog provider to the context. ([datafusion.apache.org][4])

Use when:

```text id="8b7l2f"
multiple providers need namespace organization
catalog/schema/table hierarchy matters
tenant/domain isolation requires qualified names
```

---

## 23.14.3 DDL factory registration

```python id="py77xx"
ctx.register_table_factory("CUSTOM", custom_factory)

ctx.sql("""
    CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE external_events
    STORED AS CUSTOM
    LOCATION 'custom://events'
""").collect()
```

Use when:

```text id="0judst"
SQL users should define custom-backed tables
format/plugin system resembles Parquet/CSV/JSON DDL
table creation should be declarative
```

---

# 23.15 Python vs Rust extension decision

## 23.15.1 Python-side extension points

```text id="k8lkhc"
Python is good for:
  provider configuration
  credential loading
  dynamic table registration
  catalog/schema orchestration
  thin plugin facades
  tests and mock providers
  DataFrame-as-view registration
  pyarrow.dataset integration
  delegating to Rust/PyCapsule provider objects
```

Current official Python APIs expose abstract Python catalog and schema providers, in-memory `Catalog`/`Schema` helpers, `Schema.register_table(...)`, and `Table` wrappers around built-in tables, PyArrow datasets, DataFrames-as-views, and FFI PyCapsule tables. ([datafusion.apache.org][4])

## 23.15.2 Rust-side provider implementation

```text id="fuum9e"
Rust is preferred for:
  hot scan paths
  pushdown implementation
  async stream production
  high-volume decoding
  partition planning
  predicate pruning
  custom file/database protocols
  memory safety
  avoiding Python GIL
  direct integration with DataFusion traits
```

The Python extension guide explains that users may implement a custom data source in Rust and expose it through PyO3 for performance and DataFusion integration reasons; it also explains why directly depending on `datafusion-python` as a Rust dependency is not generally compatible because Rust lacks a stable ABI, so DataFusion Python uses FFI/PyCapsule-style boundaries instead. ([datafusion.apache.org][5])

## 23.15.3 Decision table

| Requirement                               |                        Python glue |               Rust provider |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------: | --------------------------: |
| load credentials/config                   |                          excellent | possible but less ergonomic |
| register static tables                    |                          excellent |               not necessary |
| implement schema/table catalog lookup     |                               good | good for hot metadata paths |
| read millions/billions of rows            |                               poor |                   excellent |
| push filter/projection/limit into source  |            thin orchestration only |                   excellent |
| async stream + partitions                 | poor/direct support not documented |                   excellent |
| avoid GIL                                 |                                 no |                         yes |
| package as Python wheel                   |                                yes |        yes via PyO3/maturin |
| maximize DataFusion optimizer integration |                            limited |                   excellent |

---

# 23.16 Delta Lake and Iceberg examples as provider-backed sources

DataFusion Python supports registering provider-backed table sources such as Delta Lake through `ctx.register_table(...)` in DataFusion 43.0.0 and later, while older Delta Lake interop through Arrow Dataset lacks features such as filter pushdown and may have significant performance differences. DataFusion Python 45.0.0 and later supports Iceberg table registration through the custom table-provider interface, using `pyiceberg` or `pyiceberg-core`; the docs note that the integration relies on Iceberg Rust functionality rather than all features in PyIceberg. ([datafusion.apache.org][6])

```python id="qqvkjo"
from deltalake import DeltaTable
from datafusion import SessionContext

ctx = SessionContext()

delta_table = DeltaTable("path_to_table")
ctx.register_table("my_delta_table", delta_table)

df = ctx.table("my_delta_table")
df.show()
```

Iceberg-style pattern:

```python id="eoyl7x"
from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog
from datafusion import SessionContext

ctx = SessionContext()

catalog = load_catalog("catalog", type="in-memory")
iceberg_table = catalog.load_table("default.test")

ctx.register_table("test", iceberg_table)
ctx.table("test").show()
```

Agent rule:

```text id="o7i0rb"
Prefer native custom table-provider registration over Arrow Dataset fallback when pushdown/performance matters.
```

---

# 23.17 Provider capability contract

```text id="0t2qly"
A production-grade custom provider should document:
  schema
  table type
  supported projection pushdown
  supported filter pushdown
  Exact/Inexact/Unsupported filter semantics
  limit pushdown
  natural partitioning
  natural ordering
  statistics availability
  write support, if any
  supported DDL factory options
  credential/config lifecycle
  failure/retry semantics
```

Minimum viable provider:

```text id="71s9fg"
schema()
table_type()
scan() -> ExecutionPlan
ExecutionPlan.execute() -> SendableRecordBatchStream
```

Production provider:

```text id="zwc9cs"
projection pushdown
filter pushdown
limit pushdown
partitioning metadata
ordering metadata when true
statistics
parallel partitions
nonblocking stream production
EXPLAIN-verified plan shape
```

---

# 23.18 Query planning and `EXPLAIN` validation

The provider guide recommends `EXPLAIN` as the first tool for understanding what DataFusion is doing with a custom table provider; it shows plan differences before/after filter pushdown and explains how `FilterExec`, `SortExec`, and `RepartitionExec` reveal missing provider capabilities. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

```python id="n5tnwc"
df = ctx.sql("""
    SELECT *
    FROM external_events
    WHERE region = 'us-east-1'
      AND event_type = 'click'
""")

df.explain(analyze=False)
df.explain(analyze=True)
```

Expected validation targets:

```text id="6kiiea"
projection pushdown:
  scan plan lists only needed columns

filter pushdown Exact:
  no FilterExec for pushed predicate

filter pushdown Inexact:
  scan narrows data but FilterExec remains

limit pushdown:
  source plan records limit or fewer partitions/pages

partitioning:
  partition_count matches natural source layout or target policy

ordering:
  no unnecessary SortExec when source ordering is correctly declared
```

---

## 23.19.1 Registration smoke test

```python id="wf0y81"
def test_provider_registration(ctx):
    provider = MyTableProvider(...)

    ctx.register_table("custom_source", provider)

    assert ctx.table_exist("custom_source")

    df = ctx.table("custom_source")
    assert df.schema().names
```

```python id="0z6ac5"
def test_provider_sql_visibility(ctx):
    provider = MyTableProvider(...)
    ctx.register_table("custom_source", provider)

    out = ctx.sql("""
        SELECT count(*) AS n
        FROM custom_source
    """).to_pydict()

```

```python id="rpx3b3"
def test_provider_projection_plan(ctx):
    provider = MyTableProvider(...)
    ctx.register_table("custom_source", provider)

    df = ctx.sql("""
        SELECT id
        FROM custom_source
    """)

```

```python id="jzl91i"
        SELECT id
        FROM custom_source
        WHERE region = 'us-east-1'
```

# 23.20 Packaging/deployment pattern

```text id="w1muik"
Python wheel package:
  my_provider/
    __init__.py
    config.py
    bootstrap.py
    _rust_extension.so / .pyd

Rust crate:
  implements TableProvider
  implements ExecutionPlan
  exposes PyO3 classes
  exposes __datafusion_table_provider__
  optionally exposes TableProviderFactory PyCapsule
```

Bootstrap:

```python id="ou83b6"
from datafusion import SessionContext
from my_provider import MyTableProvider, MyTableProviderFactory

def register_custom_sources(ctx: SessionContext, cfg) -> None:
    provider = MyTableProvider(cfg.source_uri, cfg.credentials_ref)
    ctx.register_table("external_events", provider)

def register_custom_ddl(ctx: SessionContext) -> None:
    ctx.register_table_factory("CUSTOM", MyTableProviderFactory())
```

Deployment rules:

```text id="rdr5xg"
Pin:
  datafusion version
  provider package version
  Rust crate versions
  PyO3/maturin build target
  platform wheels

Validate:
  import provider package
  ctx.register_table smoke test
  schema test
  pushdown plan tests
  integration query tests
```

# 23.21 Anti-pattern catalog

## Anti-pattern: doing I/O in `scan()`

```rust id="z0d6ov"
// Bad: scan runs during planning.
async fn scan(...) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
    let rows = remote_client.fetch_all().await?;
    Ok(Arc::new(MyExecPlan::from_rows(rows)))
}
```

Correct:

```rust id="qklf0h"
async fn scan(...) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
    Ok(Arc::new(MyExecPlan::new(metadata, projection, filters, limit)))
}
```

`scan()` should build an execution plan quickly and leave actual data production to stream polling. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

---

## Anti-pattern: doing heavy work in `execute()`

```rust id="l4gnhl"
// Bad: materializes partition before returning stream.
fn execute(...) -> Result<SendableRecordBatchStream> {
    let batches = read_all_batches_for_partition(partition)?;
    Ok(stream_from_batches(batches))
}
```

Correct:

```rust id="gmaw1u"
fn execute(...) -> Result<SendableRecordBatchStream> {
    Ok(build_lazy_stream_for_partition(partition))
}
```

The provider guide says `execute()` should construct and return a stream; actual I/O and computation should occur when the stream is polled. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

---

## Anti-pattern: claiming `Exact` filter pushdown incorrectly

```rust id="gcvxlr"
// Bad if source only skips files but does not guarantee row-level predicate.
TableProviderFilterPushDown::Exact
```

Correct:

```rust id="2oil81"
// Inexact: source reduces data but DataFusion must still filter rows.
TableProviderFilterPushDown::Inexact
```

The guide defines `Exact` as guaranteeing no output rows violate the predicate; `Inexact` means the source reduces data but DataFusion still needs a `FilterExec`; `Unsupported` means DataFusion handles it entirely. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

---

## Anti-pattern: lying about ordering

```text id="2qxvua"
Bad:
  declare source sorted by timestamp because most files are usually sorted.

Correct:
  declare ordering only when every partition satisfies the ordering contract.
```

Incorrect ordering metadata can cause DataFusion to skip required sorts.

---

## Anti-pattern: too many partitions

```text id="sgp8it"
Bad:
  one partition per tiny remote object/page when there are millions of pages.

Effect:
  scheduling overhead
  memory overhead
  downstream repartitioning
```

Correct:

```text id="xsg00t"
Coalesce natural source units into partition count near target_partitions.
Expose shard/file/range partitioning deliberately.
```

The provider guide notes that too many partitions are not free and that matching target partition counts can avoid extra repartition operators. ([datafusion.apache.org][2])

---

## Anti-pattern: using deprecated Python registration API

```python id="um23l9"
ctx.register_table_provider("custom_source", provider)
```

Correct:

```python id="jv9503"
ctx.register_table("custom_source", provider)
```

`register_table_provider(...)` is deprecated in favor of `register_table(...)`. ([datafusion.apache.org][3])

---

## Anti-pattern: assuming Arrow Dataset fallback equals native provider

```python id="ycicyt"
ctx.register_dataset("delta_table", delta_table.to_pyarrow_dataset())
```

Correct when native provider is available:

```python id="p0ehsn"
ctx.register_table("delta_table", delta_table)
```

The DataFusion Python docs warn that older Delta Lake interop through Arrow Dataset does not support features such as filter pushdown and may have significant performance differences compared with table-provider registration. ([datafusion.apache.org][6])

---

# 23.22 Python vs Rust implementation guide

## Use Python-side glue when

```text id="llgexk"
config composition
credentials lookup
catalog/schema setup
register_table wiring
register_table_factory wiring
test fixtures
thin provider object construction
DataFrame/DataSet registration
dynamic table naming
```

## Use Rust TableProvider when

```text id="1zkftu"
source scan is hot
source is remote or high-volume
pushdown matters
parallel partitions matter
ordering/partitioning metadata matters
streaming needs async correctness
GIL overhead is unacceptable
data decoding is nontrivial
provider must integrate deeply with DataFusion optimizer/runtime
```

## Hybrid package pattern

```text id="gf0w96"
Python:
  user-facing config object
  provider constructor
  secret-manager integration
  context bootstrap helpers

Rust:
  TableProvider
  ExecutionPlan
  RecordBatchStream
  pushdown
  partitioning
  object decoding
  PyCapsule export
```

---

# 23.23 Provider checklist

```text id="uigede"
Rust provider:
  [ ] schema() returns stable SchemaRef.
  [ ] table_type() is correct.
  [ ] scan() is lightweight.
  [ ] scan() consumes projection/filter/limit hints.
  [ ] supports_filters_pushdown() is honest.
  [ ] ExecutionPlan properties declare partitioning accurately.
  [ ] ExecutionPlan properties declare ordering only when true.
  [ ] execute() returns stream quickly.
  [ ] stream does I/O and yields RecordBatch values.
  [ ] stream handles errors/backpressure/cancellation.
  [ ] partition count matches natural source layout or target policy.
  [ ] EXPLAIN confirms expected plan shape.
  [ ] integration tests verify SQL and DataFrame paths.

Python package:
  [ ] exposes provider constructor.
  [ ] exposes __datafusion_table_provider__ PyCapsule.
  [ ] registers via ctx.register_table(...).
  [ ] avoids deprecated register_table_provider(...).
  [ ] pins compatible datafusion version.
  [ ] ships platform wheels.
  [ ] keeps credentials outside query builders.

DDL factory:
  [ ] exposes TableProviderFactoryExportable PyCapsule.
  [ ] registered with ctx.register_table_factory(format, factory).
  [ ] SQL CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE STORED AS format tested.
  [ ] DDL options documented.
```

---

## 23.24 Section compression for LLM agents

```text id="n2daqu"
Custom provider path:
  Rust TableProvider
  -> FFI_TableProvider
  -> PyO3 PyCapsule
  -> Python object with __datafusion_table_provider__
  -> ctx.register_table("name", provider)

Requirement:
  DataFusion 43.0.0+
  expose FFI_TableProvider via PyCapsule

Python protocol:
  TableProviderExportable.__datafusion_table_provider__(session: Any) -> object
  returned object must be provider PyCapsule

Register:
  ctx.register_table(name, table_or_provider_or_dataframe_or_dataset) -> None
  ctx.table(name)
  ctx.sql("SELECT * FROM name")
  ctx.register_table_provider(...) deprecated

DDL factory:
  ctx.register_table_factory(format, factory) -> None
  SQL:
    CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE t
    STORED AS FORMAT
    LOCATION '...'

Rust TableProvider:
  schema()
  table_type()
  scan(state, projection, filters, limit) -> ExecutionPlan

Pushdown:
  projection -> read only needed columns
  filters -> source-level pruning
  limit -> stop early

Filter pushdown responses:
  Exact
  Inexact
  Unsupported

ExecutionPlan:
  name()
  properties()
  children()
  with_new_children(...)
  execute(partition, context) -> SendableRecordBatchStream

Layer discipline:
  scan() = planning metadata only
  execute() = construct stream only
  RecordBatchStream polling = I/O + data production

Performance:
  expose natural partitioning
  expose ordering only when true
  match target_partitions when useful
  implement filter/projection/limit pushdown
  verify with EXPLAIN

Python vs Rust:
  Python = config, credentials, registration, dynamic orchestration, tests
  Rust = hot scanning, pushdown, async streams, partitioning, memory safety, optimizer integration

Best practices:
  register providers in bootstrap
  keep credentials out of query builders
  avoid I/O in scan()
  avoid blocking in execute()
  use ctx.register_table(...)
  use native provider over Arrow Dataset fallback when pushdown matters
  test SQL visibility, schema, projection/filter pushdown, partitioning, and DDL factory behavior
```

## 23.25 FFI physical-optimizer rules and plan codecs (new in 54)

DataFusion 54 extends the PyCapsule FFI seam beyond table providers and functions to two new extension classes: **user-defined physical optimizer rules** and **logical/physical extension codecs**. The behavioral claims are changelog-sourced (54.0.0 changelog; not exercised here — both require a compiled Rust extension crate), but the Python entry points below were verified present, with these signatures, on the installed `datafusion==54.0.0` wheel. See [`datafusion_python_54vs53.md`](datafusion_python_54vs53.md) §2.6.

### Physical optimizer rules over FFI

```python id="ffi54a"
SessionContext.add_physical_optimizer_rule(rule: PhysicalOptimizerRuleExportable) -> None

# Protocol (datafusion.context.PhysicalOptimizerRuleExportable):
#   __datafusion_physical_optimizer_rule__() -> PyCapsule wrapping FFI_PhysicalOptimizerRule
```

The rule object follows the same export pattern as `TableProviderExportable` (23.2): a Rust crate builds an `FFI_PhysicalOptimizerRule`, wraps it in a `PyCapsule`, and exposes it through the dunder; Python appends it to the session. Per the method contract, the underlying `SessionState` is rebuilt from its current state with the rule appended — previously registered tables, UDFs, and catalogs are preserved, so ordering between registration and rule installation is not a correctness trap (but install rules during bootstrap anyway, per 23.20 discipline).

### Logical and physical extension codecs over FFI

```python id="ffi54b"
SessionContext.with_logical_extension_codec(codec)  -> SessionContext   # builder-style, returns new context
SessionContext.with_physical_extension_codec(codec) -> SessionContext

# Protocols: objects exposing
#   __datafusion_logical_extension_codec__()  -> PyCapsule
#   __datafusion_physical_extension_codec__() -> PyCapsule
# SessionContext itself also exposes both dunders for capsule re-export.
```

Extension codecs teach plan (de)serialization — the `to_proto()`/`from_proto()` seam of §17 and the Substrait/proto round-trips of §21 — how to encode plan nodes that reference custom extensions (FFI table providers, Rust UDFs, custom exec nodes). Without a codec, serializing a plan containing extension nodes fails; with one, plans that traverse the FFI boundary can round-trip. Only FFI codecs are supported: the codec implementation itself lives in Rust.

Placement guidance:

```text id="ffi54c"
Use an FFI physical optimizer rule when:
  a Rust extension must rewrite physical plans (operator substitution,
  provider-specific repartitioning) inside a Python-driven session
Use extension codecs when:
  plans containing FFI extension nodes must serialize (to_proto, Substrait,
  plan shipping between processes)
Keep using remove_optimizer_rule(name) for built-in rule removal (17.x);
  add_physical_optimizer_rule only APPENDS user rules.
Attribution: rule/codec runtime behavior is changelog-sourced — validate against
  your extension crate before relying on ordering or codec-fallback details.
```

[1]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/user-guide/io/table_provider.html "Custom Table Provider — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"
[2]: https://datafusion.apache.org/library-user-guide/custom-table-providers.html "Custom Table Provider — Apache DataFusion  documentation"
[3]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/autoapi/datafusion/context/index.html "datafusion.context — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"
[4]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/autoapi/datafusion/catalog/index.html "datafusion.catalog — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"
[5]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/contributor-guide/ffi.html "Python Extensions — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"
[6]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/user-guide/data-sources.html "Data Sources — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"

# DataFusion Advanced — 24) DataFrame display, notebook UX, and rendering

This section follows the same dense, agent-facing technical-reference style as the Cyclopts source material. 

## 24.0 Core display invariant

DataFusion rendering is a **preview/materialization concern**, not a transformation concern. DataFusion provides configurable plain-text and HTML rendering; `datafusion.dataframe_formatter` controls Jupyter rendering through `_repr_html_`, terminal/string rendering through `__repr__`, and other string/HTML representation needs. In Jupyter, evaluating `df` or calling `display(df)` triggers HTML rendering; in a terminal, `print(df)` uses plain-text rendering. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

```text id="19pivz"
Display surfaces:
  df.show(num=20)        -> explicit console execution + print
  repr(df) / print(df)   -> __repr__ plain-text representation
  df in notebook cell    -> _repr_html_ HTML representation
  display(df)            -> _repr_html_ HTML representation
```

Agent rule:

```text id="pwm6cb"
Display code is adapter/UI code.
Production transformation functions should return DataFrame objects, not display them.
```

---

## 24.1 Console rendering: `df.show(...)`

## 24.1.1 Signature

```python id="jdofrz"
df.show(num: int = 20) -> None
```

`show(num=20)` executes the DataFrame and prints the result to the console; `num` controls the number of lines shown. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

```python id="f6fybd"
df.show()
df.show(50)
```

Safe preview:

```python id="su0qws"
(
    df.select("user_id", "country", "amount")
      .filter("amount > 0")
      .limit(20)
      .show()
)
```

Agent rules:

```text id="puujvu"
show():
  explicit terminal display boundary
  use in CLI/notebook/debug code
  never use inside reusable library transformations
  cap preview with limit(...) when result cardinality is unknown
```

---

## 24.2 Plain-text rendering: `repr(df)`, `print(df)`, `__repr__`

## 24.2.1 API surface

```python id="jusz1g"
repr(df)      # calls DataFrame.__repr__()
print(df)     # also uses string representation
```

`DataFrame.__repr__()` returns a string representation of the DataFrame; `DataFrame.default_str_repr(...)` is the default string representation helper used by the formatter and implemented in Rust for performance. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

```python id="mu2lnc"
s = repr(df)
print(df)
```

Formatter-level string rendering:

```python id="d4puop"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import get_formatter

formatter = get_formatter()
text = formatter.format_str(batches, schema, has_more=True)
```

`DataFrameHtmlFormatter.format_str(...)` formats record batches as a string and is used by DataFrame’s `__repr__` implementation. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 24.2.2 Agent safety policy

```text id="ry4egz"
repr(df) / print(df):
  convenient interactive preview
  can trigger preview data retrieval in interactive contexts
  should not be used for logging large DataFrames
  should not be used for production serialization
```

Correct production logging:

```python id="yz24ef"
def log_dataframe_plan(df, logger):
    logger.info("optimized_plan=%s", df.optimized_logical_plan().display())
```

Correct preview logging:

```python id="6o77tw"
def log_preview(df, logger, *, max_rows: int = 20):
    logger.info("preview:\n%s", repr(df.limit(max_rows)))
```

---

## 24.3 HTML rendering: `_repr_html_`

## 24.3.1 Notebook behavior

```python id="6c20ln"
df          # Jupyter/IPython displays HTML table
display(df) # explicit display also uses HTML rendering
```

DataFusion’s rendering guide states that in Jupyter, displaying a DataFrame triggers HTML rendering, and explicit `display(df)` also uses HTML rendering. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

`DataFrame._repr_html_()` is the DataFrame HTML representation hook. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

```python id="aacb10"
html = df._repr_html_()
```

Formatter-level HTML rendering:

```python id="rxqp7n"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import get_formatter

formatter = get_formatter()
html = formatter.format_html(batches, schema, has_more=True)
```

`DataFrameHtmlFormatter.format_html(...)` formats record batches as HTML and is used by DataFrame’s `_repr_html_` implementation. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 24.3.2 Notebook UX rules

```text id="ejyv81"
Notebook display:
  df as last cell expression -> HTML preview
  display(df) -> HTML preview
  print(df) -> plain text preview
  df.show(n) -> console-style output
```

Agent default for generated notebooks:

```python id="r14ebq"
preview = (
    df.select("user_id", "country", "amount")
      .filter("amount > 0")
      .limit(25)
)

display(preview)
```

Avoid:

```python id="414bfi"
# Risky in notebooks when df points at a large remote scan.
df
```

---

# 24.4 Formatter configuration

## 24.4.1 `configure_formatter(...)`

```python id="rcr3fj"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import configure_formatter

configure_formatter(
    max_cell_length=25,
    max_width=1000,
    max_height=300,
    max_memory_bytes=2 * 1024 * 1024,
    min_rows=10,
    max_rows=10,
    enable_cell_expansion=True,
    custom_css=None,
    show_truncation_message=True,
    style_provider=None,
    use_shared_styles=True,
)
```

The rendering guide documents these global formatter settings: maximum cell length, HTML width/height, maximum memory for rendering, min/max displayed rows, cell expansion, custom CSS, truncation messages, style provider, and shared styles; settings affect all DataFrames displayed after configuration. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 24.4.2 Formatter parameter map

| Parameter                 | Scope            | Purpose                              |
| ------------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `max_cell_length`         | text + HTML      | truncate long cell text              |
| `max_width`               | HTML             | constrain rendered table width       |
| `max_height`              | HTML             | constrain rendered table height      |
| `max_memory_bytes`        | text + HTML      | cap memory used for rendering        |
| `min_rows`                | text + HTML      | minimum rows to display              |
| `max_rows`                | text + HTML      | maximum rows to display              |
| `repr_rows`               | deprecated alias | backward compatibility for row count |
| `enable_cell_expansion`   | HTML             | allow expanding truncated cells      |
| `custom_css`              | HTML             | inject custom CSS                    |
| `show_truncation_message` | text + HTML      | show message when data is truncated  |
| `style_provider`          | HTML             | custom cell/header style provider    |
| `use_shared_styles`       | HTML             | share CSS/JS across notebook tables  |

`DataFrameHtmlFormatter` documents defaults including `max_cell_length=25`, `max_width=1000`, `max_height=300`, `max_memory_bytes=2 * 1024 * 1024`, `min_rows=10`, `max_rows=None`, `repr_rows=None`, `enable_cell_expansion=True`, `custom_css=None`, `show_truncation_message=True`, `style_provider=None`, and `use_shared_styles=True`; the API also documents that `repr_rows` is deprecated in favor of `max_rows`. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 24.4.3 Notebook-safe global defaults

```python id="ip2j5k"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import configure_formatter

configure_formatter(
    max_cell_length=80,
    max_width=1200,
    max_height=400,
    max_memory_bytes=4 * 1024 * 1024,
    min_rows=10,
    max_rows=25,
    enable_cell_expansion=True,
    show_truncation_message=True,
    use_shared_styles=True,
)
```

The rendering guide recommends configuring the global formatter at the beginning of notebooks, setting appropriate `max_memory_bytes`, keeping `use_shared_styles=True` for performance in notebooks with multiple DataFrames, resetting when needed, and enabling cell expansion when long content may need full display. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

# 24.5 Direct formatter management

## 24.5.1 `get_formatter()`

```python id="l3azl4"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import get_formatter

formatter = get_formatter()
print(formatter.max_rows)
print(formatter.max_cell_length)
```

`get_formatter()` returns the current global `DataFrameHtmlFormatter`; it is used by DataFrame’s `_repr_html_` implementation and can also be used directly for custom rendering. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

## 24.5.2 `set_formatter(...)`

```python id="gpge2m"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import DataFrameHtmlFormatter, set_formatter

custom_formatter = DataFrameHtmlFormatter(
    max_cell_length=50,
    max_rows=20,
    enable_cell_expansion=False,
)

set_formatter(custom_formatter)
```

`set_formatter(...)` sets the global formatter instance; the rendering guide shows creating a fully custom `DataFrameHtmlFormatter` and applying it globally. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

## 24.5.3 `reset_formatter()`

```python id="yzq4gn"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import reset_formatter

reset_formatter()
```

`reset_formatter()` resets the global formatter to default settings. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

# 24.6 Custom styles and custom formatting

## 24.6.1 Custom style provider

```python id="6jei19"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import configure_formatter

class CompactStyleProvider:
    def get_cell_style(self):
        return "border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 4px; text-align: left;"

    def get_header_style(self):
        return (
            "background-color: #f6f8fa; color: #111; "
            "border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 4px; text-align: left;"
        )

configure_formatter(style_provider=CompactStyleProvider())
```

A style provider implements `get_cell_style()` and `get_header_style()` and can be passed through `configure_formatter(style_provider=...)`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 24.6.2 Type-specific cell formatters

```python id="whtlwz"
from datetime import date
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import get_formatter

formatter = get_formatter()

formatter.register_formatter(float, lambda v: f"{v:.2f}")
formatter.register_formatter(date, lambda v: v.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
```

The rendering guide documents registering custom formatters for specific Python types; a cell formatter is any callable that accepts a value and returns a string. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rule:

```text id="ub2ay3"
Cell formatters affect display only.
Do not use display formatters as data-cleaning or serialization logic.
```

---

## 24.6.3 Custom cell and header builders

```python id="5zfo69"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import get_formatter

formatter = get_formatter()

def my_cell_builder(value, row, col, table_id):
    color = "red" if isinstance(value, (int, float)) and value < 0 else "black"
    return f"<td style='color: {color}; padding: 8px;'>{value}</td>"

def my_header_builder(field):
    return f"<th style='background: #333; color: white; padding: 8px;'>{field.name}</th>"

formatter.set_custom_cell_builder(my_cell_builder)
formatter.set_custom_header_builder(my_header_builder)
```

The rendering guide documents full HTML control through custom cell/header builder functions; the cell builder receives `(value, row, col, table_id)`, and the header builder receives a schema field. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Security rule:

```text id="cw45w7"
Custom builders return HTML.
Escape or sanitize untrusted cell values.
Avoid injecting raw user-controlled strings into HTML.
```

---

# 24.7 Shared styles and notebook performance

```python id="re3t5h"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import configure_formatter

configure_formatter(use_shared_styles=True)
```

`use_shared_styles=True` is enabled by default and optimizes notebooks with many DataFrames by including CSS and JavaScript only once per notebook session, reducing HTML size, preventing style duplication, improving rendering performance, and keeping styling consistent. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Disable only when:

```python id="8xsetm"
configure_formatter(use_shared_styles=False)
```

Use cases for disabling:

```text id="7a1wvg"
isolated exported HTML fragments
per-table standalone HTML needs
debugging formatter CSS/JS behavior
```

Default policy:

```text id="q5leyx"
Notebook:
  use_shared_styles=True

Standalone HTML export:
  evaluate whether each fragment needs embedded styles
```

---

# 24.8 Memory and display controls

```python id="d3qwc6"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import configure_formatter

configure_formatter(
    max_memory_bytes=4 * 1024 * 1024,
    min_rows=20,
    max_rows=50,
)
```

The rendering guide documents `max_memory_bytes`, `min_rows`, and `max_rows` as controls for how much data is displayed and how much memory rendering may use; these parameters balance comprehensive display against performance considerations. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text id="v8upok"
Notebook max_rows:
  small default for remote/large scans
  higher only for bounded local fixtures

max_memory_bytes:
  mandatory in shared notebooks
  lower for service-rendered previews
  higher only for trusted local exploration

max_cell_length:
  keep low for payload/text-heavy columns
  increase only when long strings are important
```

---

# 24.9 Display operations vs production materialization

## 24.9.1 Display-preview APIs

```text id="4rr9i0"
df.show(n)
repr(df)
print(df)
df._repr_html_()
display(df)
```

Use for:

```text id="dp7vmg"
notebook exploration
CLI preview
debugging
documentation examples
small deterministic tests
```

## 24.9.2 Production materialization APIs

```text id="n7bzt3"
df.execute_stream()
df.write_parquet(...)
df.write_csv(...)
df.write_json(...)
df.to_arrow_table()
df.to_pandas()
df.collect()
```

Use according to output contract:

```text id="9b4867"
large output:
  execute_stream()
  write_parquet()

bounded in-memory output:
  to_arrow_table()
  collect()

small user-facing output:
  limit(n).to_pydict()
  limit(n).to_pandas()
```

Agent rule:

```text id="i80q5s"
Never confuse display rendering with durable materialization.
A notebook preview is not an export, cache, checkpoint, or production result.
```

---

# 24.10 Generated notebook patterns

## 24.10.1 Safe notebook setup cell

```python id="eny7mf"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import configure_formatter

configure_formatter(
    max_cell_length=80,
    max_width=1200,
    max_height=400,
    max_memory_bytes=4 * 1024 * 1024,
    min_rows=10,
    max_rows=25,
    enable_cell_expansion=True,

)
```

## 24.10.2 Safe preview helper

```python id="5g2ur9"
def preview(df, *, rows: int = 25):
    return df.limit(rows)
```

Notebook use:

```python id="8qyxeh"
preview(df, rows=25)
```

## 24.10.3 Console preview helper

```python id="ub4q95"
def show_preview(df, *, rows: int = 25) -> None:
    df.limit(rows).show(rows)
```

## 24.10.4 Schema-first exploration

```python id="x79upn"
print(df.schema())

df.limit(20).show()
```

Use schema inspection before display when data may be wide, remote, or expensive.

---

# 24.11 Generated CLI patterns

```python id="5qpo2r"
def cli_preview(df, *, rows: int = 20) -> None:
    (
        df.limit(rows)
          .show(rows)
    )
```

```python id="4zseai"
def cli_schema(df) -> None:
    print(df.schema())
```

```python id="31oihx"
def cli_plan(df) -> None:
    print(df.optimized_logical_plan().display_indent())
```

CLI rule:

```text id="esif0f"
Preview command:
  limit + show

Export command:
  write_parquet / execute_stream

Debug command:
  schema / explain / plan display
```

---

# 24.12 Logging policy

Bad:

```python id="cqylys"
logger.info("df=%s", df)
```

Problem:

```text id="c5e9pw"
Implicit repr may render data.
Logs can become expensive.
Logs can leak sensitive values.
Logs can include large HTML/text tables in notebook-captured logs.
```

Good:

```python id="k5u3sw"
logger.info("schema=%s", df.schema())
logger.info("plan=%s", df.optimized_logical_plan().display())
```

Bounded preview logging only in debug mode:

```python id="dbyjtn"
if debug_preview:
    logger.debug("preview:\n%s", repr(df.limit(10)))
```

---

# 24.13 Sensitive-data rendering policy

```text id="27hz2n"
Display can expose:
  PII columns
  raw payloads
  tokens / secrets accidentally present in data
  object-store paths embedded as values
  business-sensitive aggregates
```

Safer preview projection:

```python id="555od6"
safe_preview = df.select(
    "event_id",
    "event_type",
    "country",
    "amount",
).limit(20)

display(safe_preview)
```

Redaction before display:

```python id="bk9ivg"
from datafusion import lit

safe = df.select(
    "event_id",
    lit("<redacted>").alias("email"),
    "country",
    "amount",
).limit(20)
```

Agent rule:

```text id="sew2ko"
Display allowlist columns.
Do not display raw wide tables from untrusted or sensitive sources.
```

---

# 24.14 HTML customizer safety

Custom cell builders return HTML strings, so treat them as HTML-generation functions. The rendering guide’s custom builder example interpolates `value` into an HTML string; for untrusted values, escape before interpolation. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

```python id="a7qh9e"
import html
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import get_formatter

formatter = get_formatter()

def safe_cell_builder(value, row, col, table_id):
    escaped = html.escape("" if value is None else str(value))
    return f"<td style='padding: 4px;'>{escaped}</td>"

formatter.set_custom_cell_builder(safe_cell_builder)
```

---

# 24.15 Anti-pattern catalog

## Anti-pattern: naked DataFrame at end of notebook cell

```python id="tg48mf"
df
```

Correct:

```python id="1jtyiy"
df.limit(25)
```

Better for sensitive/wide data:

```python id="dq9ky4"
df.select("safe_col_a", "safe_col_b").limit(25)
```

---

## Anti-pattern: production function calls `show()`

```python id="2ved5x"
def transform(df):
    out = df.filter("amount > 0")
    out.show()
    return out
```

Correct:

```python id="5x3j4z"
def transform(df):
    return df.filter("amount > 0")
```

Adapter:

```python id="0byjmx"
transform(df).limit(20).show()
```

---

## Anti-pattern: logging `repr(df)` unbounded

```python id="xsgaks"
logger.info("%r", df)
```

Correct:

```python id="xf5l01"
logger.info("schema=%s", df.schema())
logger.debug("preview=%s", repr(df.limit(10)))
```

---

## Anti-pattern: display formatter as data contract

```python id="5gp70u"
formatter.register_formatter(float, lambda v: f"${v:,.2f}")
# Then relying on displayed currency text downstream.
```

Correct:

```python id="fxg92j"
# Display concern only:
formatter.register_formatter(float, lambda v: f"{v:,.2f}")

# Data concern:
df.select((col("amount") / lit(100)).alias("amount_dollars"))
```

---

## Anti-pattern: custom HTML with unescaped values

```python id="y2l8ao"
def unsafe_cell_builder(value, row, col, table_id):
    return f"<td>{value}</td>"
```

Correct:

```python id="c0n33k"
import html

def safe_cell_builder(value, row, col, table_id):
    return f"<td>{html.escape(str(value))}</td>"
```

---

# 24.16 Testing patterns

## 24.16.1 Formatter reset test

```python id="tylemb"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import configure_formatter, reset_formatter, get_formatter

def test_formatter_reset():
    configure_formatter(max_cell_length=10, max_rows=5)
    assert get_formatter().max_cell_length == 10

    reset_formatter()
    assert get_formatter().max_cell_length == 25
```

Defaults such as `max_cell_length=25` are documented on `DataFrameHtmlFormatter`. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 24.16.2 Repr smoke test

```python id="ii6j1i"
def test_repr_smoke(ctx):
    df = ctx.from_pydict({"x": [1, 2, 3]})
    text = repr(df.limit(2))

    assert isinstance(text, str)
    assert "x" in text
```

---

## 24.16.3 HTML repr smoke test

```python id="etmres"
def test_html_repr_smoke(ctx):
    df = ctx.from_pydict({"x": [1, 2, 3]})
    html = df.limit(2)._repr_html_()

    assert isinstance(html, str)
    assert "<" in html
```

---

## 24.16.4 Custom formatter test

```python id="uqw11f"
from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import get_formatter, reset_formatter

def test_custom_float_formatter(ctx):
    try:
        formatter = get_formatter()
        formatter.register_formatter(float, lambda v: f"{v:.1f}")

        df = ctx.from_pydict({"x": [1.234]})
        html = df._repr_html_()

        assert "1.2" in html
    finally:
        reset_formatter()
```

# 24.17 Deployment checklist

```text id="42qnyo"
Display boundaries:
  [ ] No show() inside transformation functions.
  [ ] No naked df display in generated notebooks without limit().
  [ ] No production logging of repr(df) without limit().
  [ ] Display code lives in notebook/CLI/debug adapters.

Preview safety:
  [ ] Use limit(n).
  [ ] Project safe columns.
  [ ] Avoid raw wide table previews.
  [ ] Use schema() before displaying unfamiliar sources.
  [ ] Use max_rows and max_memory_bytes in notebook setup.

Formatter:
  [ ] configure_formatter(...) at notebook start.
  [ ] max_cell_length set for payload-heavy data.
  [ ] max_memory_bytes set for shared notebooks.
  [ ] use_shared_styles=True for multi-DataFrame notebooks.
  [ ] reset_formatter() in tests.
  [ ] avoid deprecated repr_rows; use max_rows.

HTML:
  [ ] Escape values in custom builders.
  [ ] Treat custom_css/custom builders as UI code.
  [ ] Avoid injecting untrusted raw HTML.
  [ ] Test _repr_html_ smoke paths.

Production:
  [ ] Use write_parquet/execute_stream for real outputs.
  [ ] Use to_pandas/to_pydict only when bounded.
  [ ] Keep display separate from materialization.
```

---

## 24.18 Section compression for LLM agents

```text id="uo552a"
Console:
  df.show(num=20) -> None
  executes DataFrame and prints result
  use limit(n).show(n) for preview

Plain text:
  repr(df) / print(df)
  DataFrame.__repr__() -> str
  DataFrame.default_str_repr(...) used by formatter

HTML:
  df._repr_html_() -> str
  in Jupyter:
    df
    display(df)
  both trigger HTML rendering

Formatter:
  from datafusion.dataframe_formatter import (
      configure_formatter,
      get_formatter,
      set_formatter,
      reset_formatter,
      DataFrameHtmlFormatter,
  )

configure_formatter:
  max_cell_length
  max_width
  max_height
  max_memory_bytes
  min_rows
  max_rows
  enable_cell_expansion
  custom_css
  show_truncation_message
  style_provider
  use_shared_styles

Direct:
  formatter = get_formatter()
  formatter.register_formatter(type, callable)
  formatter.set_custom_cell_builder(fn)
  formatter.set_custom_header_builder(fn)
  set_formatter(DataFrameHtmlFormatter(...))
  reset_formatter()

Notebook defaults:
  configure_formatter(
      max_cell_length=80,
      max_memory_bytes=4 * 1024 * 1024,
      max_rows=25,
      use_shared_styles=True,
      show_truncation_message=True,
  )

Best practices:
  display is UI/debug code
  materialization is output/adapter code
  always limit previews
  project safe preview columns
  never log unbounded repr(df)
  never use show() in library transformations
  escape untrusted values in custom HTML builders
  use write_parquet/execute_stream for production outputs
```

[2]: https://datafusion.apache.org/python/autoapi/datafusion/dataframe/index.html "datafusion.dataframe — Apache Arrow DataFusion  documentation"
